questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: Your company runs the same containerized API in AKS clusters in three Azure regions. You want every cluster to pull images from a network-close copy while all pipelines keep using a single registry name such as contoso.azurecr.io/api:1.4. What should you do?

options.text: Enable zone redundancy on a Standard registry in the primary region
Create a Standard registry in each region and use az acr import to copy each image after every build
Upgrade the registry to the Premium SKU and add geo-replicas in the three regions
Keep a Basic registry and enable regional webhooks so each cluster is notified about new images

questions.explanation: Geo-replication creates replicas of one registry in several regions behind a single global endpoint, and Azure routes each pull to the closest healthy replica. It requires the Premium SKU. Separate registries per region would need different login servers and extra copy jobs, webhooks only notify and do not replicate content, and zone redundancy protects against zone failures inside one region, not cross-region latency.
questions.source_title: Geo-replication in Azure Container Registry

questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: After a node scale-out, some AKS pods run a different version of your app even though every manifest references contoso.azurecr.io/web:latest. Which tagging practice prevents this?

options.text: Keep using :latest but restart all pods after every push
Delete untagged manifests after each push so old layers cannot be pulled
Use stable tags such as :1.0 for deployments and unique tags for base images
Deploy images with unique tags (for example a build ID or commit SHA) and reserve stable tags for base images

questions.explanation: Stable tags keep moving as new images are pushed, so nodes that pull at different times can get different images. Microsoft recommends unique tags for deployments and stable tags for maintaining base images. Restarting pods only hides the problem, swapping the two tag types is the opposite of the recommendation, and deleting untagged manifests does nothing about a tag that points to a newer image.
questions.source_title: Recommendations for tagging and versioning container images

questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: A production image contoso.azurecr.io/payments:2.3.1 must never be overwritten or deleted, even by users who have push rights. Which command should you run?

options.text: az acr repository update --name contoso --image payments:2.3.1 --write-enabled false
az acr import --name contoso --source payments:2.3.1 --force
az acr config retention update --registry contoso --status Disabled --type UntaggedManifests
az acr repository untag --name contoso --image payments:2.3.1

questions.explanation: Image locking sets the write-enabled (and optionally delete-enabled) attributes on an image or repository so it cannot be updated or deleted. Untagging removes the tag and leaves an orphaned manifest, disabling a retention policy only stops automatic cleanup of untagged manifests, and import with --force would actually overwrite an existing tag.
questions.source_title: Lock a container image in an Azure container registry

questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: Your Premium registry fills up with orphaned manifests every time a stable tag is re-pushed. You want the registry itself to delete untagged manifests after 7 days without running any task or script. What should you configure?

options.text: A webhook that calls an Azure Function to delete old manifests
An ACR task that runs acr purge --untagged --ago 7d on a schedule
Content trust on the repository
A retention policy for untagged manifests set to 7 days

questions.explanation: A retention policy (a Premium feature) makes the registry delete untagged manifests automatically after the configured number of days, between 0 and 365. A scheduled acr purge task also works but is a task, which the requirement excludes. A webhook plus function is custom code, and content trust signs images and has nothing to do with cleanup.
questions.source_title: Set a retention policy to retain untagged manifests

questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: You want to delete all tags in the repository samples/devimage that are older than 30 days, every day at 01:00 UTC, using only Azure Container Registry features. What should you use?

options.text: The registry retention policy for untagged manifests
Image locking with --delete-enabled true
az acr repository delete run manually from Cloud Shell each morning
An ACR task created with a --schedule cron expression that runs the acr purge command with --filter and --ago 30d

questions.explanation: acr purge deletes tags and manifests by age and by repository/tag regular-expression filter, and running it as an ACR task with a timer trigger automates it. The retention policy only affects untagged manifests, so it would not delete old tagged images. A manual command is not automated, and the delete-enabled attribute only controls whether deletion is allowed.
questions.source_title: Automatically purge images from an Azure container registry

questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: A release pipeline deploys images by manifest digest (repo@sha256:...) instead of by tag. A teammate proposes a nightly acr purge task with --untagged to save storage. What is the main risk?

options.text: Purged images can be restored for 90 days, which keeps storage usage high
acr purge cannot run inside an ACR task
Images referenced only by digest may be deleted, and later pulls by that digest will fail
--untagged deletes every tag in the registry, including locked tags

questions.explanation: Microsoft warns that systems pulling by manifest digest can break when untagged manifests are purged, because those manifests have no tag and match the untagged filter. Purge is commonly run as a task, deleted image data is unrecoverable rather than recoverable for 90 days, and by default purge skips artifacts whose write or delete attributes are locked.
questions.source_title: Automatically purge images from an Azure container registry

questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: Security policy requires that your container registry is reachable only through a private endpoint in your virtual network, with public network access disabled. Which SKU is required?

options.text: Standard
Any SKU, because private endpoints are free on all tiers
Premium
Basic

questions.explanation: Private Link and public network access controls are Premium-tier features of Azure Container Registry. Basic and Standard provide the same data-plane APIs and Entra authentication, but they lack the advanced networking features. That is why the Premium tier is also required for geo-replication and other enterprise scenarios.
questions.source_title: Azure Container Registry SKU features and limits

questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: A build pipeline must push images to a registry, and a separate AKS cluster must only pull them. Following least privilege, which roles should you assign?

options.text: Contributor to both identities at the resource group scope
Enable the registry admin user and share its password with both
Owner to the pipeline identity and Reader to the AKS kubelet identity
AcrPush to the pipeline identity and AcrPull to the AKS kubelet identity

questions.explanation: AcrPush lets an identity push and pull, and AcrPull lets it pull only, which matches each workload exactly. Owner and Contributor grant management-plane rights far beyond what is needed, and Reader does not grant image pulls. The admin user is a shared credential intended for testing and is not recommended for headless services.
questions.source_title: Authenticate with ACR from AKS

questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: You built an image locally called orders-api:v1. Before running docker push to the registry contoso, what must you do?

options.text: Run az acr build with the --no-push flag
Set the image label registry=contoso in the Dockerfile
Tag it with the registry login server, for example contoso.azurecr.io/orders-api:v1
Rename the registry to orders-api so the names match

questions.explanation: Docker decides where to push from the image name, so the image must be tagged with the fully qualified login server name (<registry>.azurecr.io/<repository>:<tag>). Renaming the registry is unnecessary, az acr build with --no-push builds in the cloud without pushing, and a label in the Dockerfile does not change the push target.
questions.source_title: About registries, repositories, and artifacts

questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: Several teams share one registry and you want images grouped by team so access and cleanup are easier to manage. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Use repository namespaces such as payments/api and search/indexer
Create one tag per team, for example api:payments and api:search
Use a different Docker Hub organization for each team
Store each team's images in a separate blob container of the registry storage account

questions.explanation: Repository names can include namespaces (path segments), which group related repositories by team or product inside one registry. Tags identify versions of an image, not owners. ACR storage is managed by Azure and is not exposed as your own blob containers, and Docker Hub organizations are unrelated to your Azure registry.
questions.source_title: About registries, repositories, and artifacts

questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: Your builds depend on node:20-alpine from Docker Hub. To protect builds from upstream outages and rate limits, you want a copy of that image in your own registry without pulling it to a workstation first. Which command should you use?

options.text: az acr import --name contoso --source docker.io/library/node:20-alpine --image base/node:20-alpine
az acr task logs --registry contoso
docker pull node:20-alpine followed by docker push from a developer laptop
az acr repository update --name contoso --image node:20-alpine

questions.explanation: az acr import copies an image from another registry (public or Azure) directly into your registry on the server side, with no local Docker engine involved. Microsoft recommends keeping copies of public base content in your own registry. Pull and push from a laptop works but depends on a workstation, repository update only changes attributes, and task logs only show build output.
questions.source_title: How to consume and maintain public content with ACR Tasks

questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: The image contoso.azurecr.io/web has one manifest tagged both 1.7 and latest. You run az acr repository delete --name contoso --image web:1.7. What happens?

options.text: The image becomes untagged and is removed later by the retention policy
Only the 1.7 tag is removed and latest keeps working
Nothing is deleted because the image has more than one tag
The manifest, its unique layers, and every tag pointing to it, including latest, are deleted

questions.explanation: Deleting by tag deletes the image itself: the tag, all unique layers referenced by the image, and all other tags associated with it. To remove only one tag and keep the image, use az acr repository untag instead. There is no protection for multi-tagged images unless the image is locked.
questions.source_title: Delete container images in Azure Container Registry

questions.skill_name: Build, store, version, and manage images with Azure Container Registry
questions.stem: Which statement about Azure Container Registry service tiers is correct?

options.text: Zone redundancy is a Premium-only feature that must be enabled at creation
Basic, Standard, and Premium expose the same programmatic capabilities and data-plane APIs, and all have zone redundancy enabled by default in supported regions
Only Standard and Premium support webhooks
Only Premium supports Microsoft Entra authentication

questions.explanation: According to the SKU documentation, all three tiers share the same programmatic capabilities and data-plane APIs, and all have zone redundancy enabled by default where regions support availability zones. Tiers differ in included storage, throughput, and advanced features such as geo-replication and private endpoints. Entra authentication and webhooks are available in every tier.
questions.source_title: Azure Container Registry SKU features and limits

questions.skill_name: Build and run images with ACR Tasks
questions.stem: A developer has no Docker engine installed but needs to build the Dockerfile in the current folder and push the result to the registry contoso. Which command should they run?

options.text: az acr repository update --name contoso --image app:v1
az acr build --registry contoso --image app:v1 .
az acr import --name contoso --source ./Dockerfile
docker build -t contoso.azurecr.io/app:v1 . && docker push contoso.azurecr.io/app:v1

questions.explanation: az acr build is an ACR Tasks quick task: it uploads the build context, builds the image in Azure, and pushes it to the registry, so no local Docker engine is needed. The docker commands require a local engine, az acr import copies existing images from another registry and cannot build from a Dockerfile, and repository update only changes image attributes.
questions.source_title: Automate container image builds with ACR Tasks

questions.skill_name: Build and run images with ACR Tasks
questions.stem: You want every application image that is built FROM contoso.azurecr.io/base/dotnet:8 to be rebuilt automatically when the base image is patched. Which ACR Tasks capability should you use?

options.text: A webhook on the base repository that deletes dependent images
A quick task (az acr build) run by each developer after patch day
A task with a base image update trigger, keeping the base image on a stable tag
A retention policy on the base repository

questions.explanation: ACR Tasks discovers base image dependencies during a build and can retrigger the task when that base image is updated. To be tracked, the base image must use a stable tag such as dotnet:8. For base images in Azure container registries the run triggers immediately. A manual quick task is not automatic, deleting images does not rebuild them, and retention policies only clean up untagged manifests.
questions.source_title: About base image updates for ACR Tasks

questions.skill_name: Build and run images with ACR Tasks
questions.stem: You must rebuild a maintenance image every night at 21:00 UTC even when no code changes. How do you create this task?

options.text: az acr task create with --schedule "0 21 * * *"
az acr build with --platform linux/amd64
az acr task create with --commit-trigger-enabled true only
az acr run with a YAML file stored in the repository

questions.explanation: Adding --schedule with a cron expression to az acr task create gives the task a timer trigger. Timer-triggered tasks can still have source commit and base image triggers, and can be run manually. A commit trigger only fires on code changes, az acr build is a one-off quick task, and az acr run executes once rather than on a schedule.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Run an ACR task on a defined schedule

questions.skill_name: Build and run images with ACR Tasks
questions.stem: You want an image to be built and pushed every time code is committed to the main branch of a GitHub repository. Which approach should you use?

options.text: az acr task create with --context pointing to the repository and branch, a Dockerfile, and a Git access token so ACR can register the commit trigger
A webhook on the registry that listens for git push events
az acr build run from a developer laptop after every commit
A timer-triggered task that runs every minute

questions.explanation: ACR Tasks supports source code commit triggers: when you create a task against a Git context with a personal access token, ACR registers a webhook in the source repository and runs the task on each commit. Manual quick builds are not automated, a per-minute timer wastes runs and adds delay, and registry webhooks fire on registry events such as push, not on Git commits.
questions.source_title: az acr task (Azure CLI reference)

questions.skill_name: Build and run images with ACR Tasks
questions.stem: You define build, test, and push steps in acr-task.yaml and want to run them once right now without creating a task. Which command should you use?

options.text: az acr task logs --registry contoso --file acr-task.yaml
az acr run --registry contoso -f acr-task.yaml .
az acr build --registry contoso --file acr-task.yaml .
az acr task create --registry contoso --file acr-task.yaml

questions.explanation: Multi-step tasks are defined in YAML, and az acr run executes the file immediately as a one-off run. az acr task create registers a reusable task that runs on triggers. az acr build treats the file as a Dockerfile, not as a multi-step task definition, and task logs only shows output.
questions.source_title: Run multi-step build, test, and patch tasks in ACR Tasks

questions.skill_name: Build and run images with ACR Tasks
questions.stem: In a multi-step ACR task you want each build to get a unique image tag automatically. Which value should you use in the YAML?

options.text: The Git branch name, so all builds from main share one tag
The literal tag latest on every build
A random tag typed by the developer in the YAML before each commit
The run ID variable, for example -t $Registry/app:$ID

questions.explanation: ACR Tasks exposes run variables, and the run ID ($ID in YAML, {{.Run.ID}} in task templates) is unique for every run, which is the documented way to produce unique tags. latest and a branch name are stable tags that get overwritten, and hand-typed tags are error-prone and not automatic.
questions.source_title: Run multi-step build, test, and patch tasks in ACR Tasks

questions.skill_name: Build and run images with ACR Tasks
questions.stem: A task named nightly-build already exists. You need to start it immediately for testing. What should you run?

options.text: az acr task run --registry contoso --name nightly-build
az acr task update --registry contoso --name nightly-build --schedule now
az acr build --registry contoso --name nightly-build .
az acr task create --registry contoso --name nightly-build

questions.explanation: az acr task run starts an existing task manually, and every task can be run manually regardless of its triggers. Creating it again fails or redefines it, az acr build does not take a task name, and the schedule parameter expects a cron expression rather than the word now.
questions.source_title: How to consume and maintain public content with ACR Tasks

questions.skill_name: Build and run images with ACR Tasks
questions.stem: You must produce a container image for ARM-based edge devices, but your build agents are x64 machines with no emulation. What should you do?

options.text: Use ACR Tasks and set the target platform, for example az acr build --platform linux/arm64
Build on the x64 agent with docker build and push; Docker converts the image when ARM devices pull it
Enable geo-replication in a region that has ARM hardware
Set the WEBSITES_PORT setting to the ARM port

questions.explanation: ACR Tasks provides cloud-based image builds for Linux, Windows, and ARM platforms, and the --platform option selects the target OS and architecture. Docker does not convert an image's architecture when it is pulled, geo-replication only replicates content, and WEBSITES_PORT is an App Service setting unrelated to builds.
questions.source_title: Automate container image builds with ACR Tasks

questions.skill_name: Build and run images with ACR Tasks
questions.stem: An ACR task in registry contoso must pull a base image from a second private registry, fabrikam.azurecr.io. How should you give the task access?

options.text: Enable the admin user on contoso
Add fabrikam as a geo-replica of contoso
Lock the base image in fabrikam with --write-enabled false
Add a custom registry credential to the task with az acr task credential add

questions.explanation: az acr task credential add stores a login for another registry (for example using a managed identity or username and password) so the task can authenticate during the run. Enabling the admin user on the task's own registry does not grant access to fabrikam, locking an image controls writes only, and geo-replication replicates a single registry rather than connecting two registries.
questions.source_title: az acr task (Azure CLI reference)

questions.skill_name: Build and run images with ACR Tasks
questions.stem: Your application images use FROM node:20 from Docker Hub, and base image triggers react slowly or are throttled. What does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: Set the task timeout to the maximum value
Switch every Dockerfile to FROM node:latest
Disable the base image trigger and rebuild weekly by hand
Keep a copy of the base image in an Azure container registry and reference that copy in your Dockerfiles

questions.explanation: Microsoft recommends copying public base content into your own Azure container registry and building from that copy. This removes the dependency on the public registry, and base images in Azure container registries trigger dependent task runs immediately. Moving to latest makes builds less predictable, manual rebuilds lose automation, and a longer timeout does not change trigger behavior.
questions.source_title: About base image updates for ACR Tasks

questions.skill_name: Build and run images with ACR Tasks
questions.stem: You want a task to build the image, run the unit tests inside the freshly built image, and push only if the tests pass. Which ACR Tasks feature should you use?

options.text: A timer trigger that runs every five minutes
A base image update trigger on the test image
A quick task created with az acr build --no-push
A multi-step task with build, cmd, and push steps

questions.explanation: Multi-step tasks support build, push, and cmd step types, so you can run a container from the new image as a cmd step to execute tests. If a step fails the run fails and later steps such as push do not run. A quick build with --no-push cannot run tests, and triggers decide when a task runs, not what it does.
questions.source_title: ACR Tasks reference: YAML

questions.skill_name: Build and run images with ACR Tasks
questions.stem: A scheduled ACR task failed last night and you need to read the build output of its most recent run. Which command should you use?

options.text: kubectl logs nightly-build
az acr task logs --registry contoso --name nightly-build
az acr config retention show --registry contoso
az acr repository show-tags --name contoso --repository app

questions.explanation: az acr task logs streams or shows the logs of a task run; by default it shows the most recent run of the named task. show-tags lists tags in a repository, kubectl logs reads pod logs in Kubernetes rather than ACR task runs, and retention show only displays the retention policy configuration.
questions.source_title: az acr task (Azure CLI reference)

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: You deploy a custom Linux container to Azure App Service. The app inside listens on port 8000, and the site returns errors because App Service cannot reach it. What should you configure?

options.text: Set WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE to true
Enable Always On
Set the PORT environment variable inside the Dockerfile to 80
Set the WEBSITES_PORT app setting to 8000

questions.explanation: For custom containers, WEBSITES_PORT tells App Service which container port to route requests to; by default App Service tries to detect ports 80 and 8080. Changing an environment variable inside the image does not change where App Service forwards traffic, Always On keeps the app loaded but does not fix routing, and the storage setting controls the shared /home directory.
questions.source_title: Environment variables and app settings in Azure App Service

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: A containerized Node.js app on App Service needs a value called DB_HOST. You add DB_HOST as an app setting in the portal. How does the code read it?

options.text: As an environment variable named DB_HOST inside the container
Only through the App Service REST API at runtime
It can't; app settings apply only to code-based apps, not containers
From a file at /home/site/appsettings.json that App Service generates

questions.explanation: App Service injects app settings into the container as environment variables, so the code reads process.env.DB_HOST (or the equivalent in other languages). No settings file is generated for this purpose, no REST call is needed, and custom containers support app settings the same way code-based apps do.
questions.source_title: Configure a custom container for Azure App Service

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: Your App Service container needs a database password that is stored as the secret DbPassword in the key vault contoso-kv. You don't want the value stored in app settings. What should you put in the app setting?

options.text: $(KeyVault:contoso-kv:DbPassword)
@Microsoft.KeyVault(VaultName=contoso-kv;SecretName=DbPassword)
keyvaultref:https://contoso-kv.vault.azure.net/secrets/DbPassword
${secrets.DbPassword}

questions.explanation: App Service resolves Key Vault references written as @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...) or @Microsoft.KeyVault(VaultName=...;SecretName=...), using the app's managed identity. The keyvaultref: format belongs to Azure Container Apps secrets, and the other two are not recognized syntaxes, so App Service would pass them through as plain text.
questions.source_title: Use Key Vault references as app settings

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: You want an App Service app to pull its container image from Azure Container Registry without storing registry credentials. Which two steps are required? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.

options.text: Set acrUseManagedIdentityCreds to true in the app's site configuration
Grant the managed identity the Key Vault Secrets User role on the registry
Enable a managed identity on the app and grant it the AcrPull role on the registry
Enable the registry admin user and copy its password into DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_PASSWORD

questions.explanation: App Service can authenticate to ACR with a system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity: the identity needs AcrPull on the registry, and the site configuration must tell App Service to use managed identity credentials (acrUseManagedIdentityCreds). The admin user is exactly the stored credential you wanted to avoid, and Key Vault roles have no effect on registry access.
questions.source_title: Configure a custom container for Azure App Service

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: An app uses a user-assigned managed identity to pull from ACR, but image pulls fail with an authorization error. The identity has AcrPull, and acrUseManagedIdentityCreds is true. What is the most likely missing setting?

options.text: acrUserManagedIdentityID set to the client ID of the user-assigned identity
WEBSITES_PORT set to 443
keyVaultReferenceIdentity set to the system-assigned identity
Always On set to true

questions.explanation: When acrUseManagedIdentityCreds is true and no user-assigned identity is specified, App Service uses the system-assigned identity. To use a user-assigned identity you must also set acrUserManagedIdentityID to that identity's client ID. The port, Key Vault reference identity, and Always On settings have nothing to do with image pull authentication.
questions.source_title: Configure a custom container for Azure App Service

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: An app setting uses @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=https://contoso-kv.vault.azure.net/secrets/ApiKey/) with no version. The secret is rotated and a new version is created. What happens?

options.text: The app restarts immediately when the new version is created
The app picks up the latest version automatically, within 24 hours
The reference stops resolving because a version is required
The app keeps the old value until the reference is edited to include the new version ID

questions.explanation: If the reference omits the secret version, App Service uses the latest version and refreshes cached Key Vault reference values every 24 hours, so a rotated secret is picked up within that window without a redeploy. A reference that includes a version stays pinned to that version. App Service does not restart on every new version, and versionless references are valid.
questions.source_title: Use Key Vault references as app settings

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: Your app has both a system-assigned and a user-assigned managed identity. Key Vault references must be resolved with the user-assigned identity, which is the only one granted access to the vault. What should you configure?

options.text: Set acrUserManagedIdentityID to the user-assigned identity
Add the client ID of the identity to every Key Vault reference string
Disable the system-assigned identity; App Service then switches automatically
Set the app's keyVaultReferenceIdentity property to the resource ID of the user-assigned identity

questions.explanation: Key Vault references use the system-assigned identity by default. To use a user-assigned identity, set the keyVaultReferenceIdentity property (for example with az webapp update --set keyVaultReferenceIdentity=<identity resource ID>). The reference syntax has no client ID field, and acrUserManagedIdentityID only affects image pulls from ACR.
questions.source_title: Use Key Vault references as app settings

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: A key vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model. Which role should you assign to an App Service managed identity so that it can resolve Key Vault references for secrets, with least privilege?

options.text: Contributor on the key vault
Key Vault Administrator
Key Vault Secrets User
Key Vault Secrets Officer

questions.explanation: Key Vault Secrets User allows reading secret contents, which is all a Key Vault reference needs. Secrets Officer can also create and delete secrets, Administrator has full data-plane control, and Contributor is a management-plane role that does not grant reading secret values under the RBAC model. Least privilege points to Secrets User.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Use Azure Key Vault with a virtual machine in .NET

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: On App Service for Linux, your custom container writes temporary files to /home, and you notice that the files are shared between all scaled-out instances. You want each instance to use only its own local storage. What should you do?

options.text: Set WEBSITES_PORT to 0
Scale in to one instance
Enable a sidecar container
Set WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE to false

questions.explanation: For Linux containers, if WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE isn't specified, the /home directory is shared across scaled instances by default; setting it to false disables that sharing. WEBSITES_PORT controls request routing, scaling in removes redundancy rather than changing storage behavior, and a sidecar adds another container without changing /home.
questions.source_title: Environment variables and app settings in Azure App Service

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: Your team pushes contoso.azurecr.io/web:prod after every release and wants the App Service app to pull and restart with the new image automatically. What should you enable?

options.text: A retention policy on the registry
A timer-triggered ACR task that restarts the web app
Continuous deployment from Azure Container Registry for the app (the registry webhook that notifies App Service)
Health check on the App Service app

questions.explanation: App Service supports CI/CD from Container Registry: when enabled, a webhook on the registry notifies App Service when the configured image tag is pushed, and App Service pulls the new image and restarts. ACR tasks can't restart a web app by themselves, retention policies only clean up untagged manifests, and health check monitors instances without changing their image.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Build and run a custom image in Azure App Service

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: A custom container on App Service fails to start, and you need to see its stdout and stderr output, including the startup logs. What should you do?

options.text: Query the ContainerAppConsoleLogs table in Log Analytics
Open the registry's webhook history
Run kubectl logs against the App Service plan
Enable application logging for the container (file system) in App Service logs, then view the log stream

questions.explanation: App Service captures container output once container logging is enabled in App Service logs, and you can then view it through the log stream or download it. Registry webhooks don't record container output, kubectl only works against Kubernetes clusters, and ContainerAppConsoleLogs is the table for Azure Container Apps, not App Service.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Build and run a custom image in Azure App Service

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: You converted an App Service app to a sidecar-enabled custom container app. You notice that changes to WEBSITES_PORT and DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_USERNAME no longer have any effect. Why?

options.text: Sidecar apps only read settings from Key Vault
Those settings don't apply to sidecar-enabled apps; containers and their registry authentication are configured on the sitecontainers definitions instead
App Service ignores all app settings after a restart
The settings must be prefixed with SIDECAR_

questions.explanation: For apps that aren't sidecar-enabled, the main container is configured through app settings such as DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_URL, DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_USERNAME, DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_PASSWORD, and WEBSITES_PORT. For sidecar-enabled apps those settings don't apply; each container, its port, and its image-pull authentication are defined as Microsoft.Web/sites/sitecontainers resources.
questions.source_title: Configure sidecars in Azure App Service

questions.skill_name: Deploy containers to App Service (environment variables and secrets)
questions.stem: You want an App Service app setting called FeatureColor to take its value from the key App:Color in Azure App Configuration, without changing application code. Which configuration is correct?

options.text: Use a Key Vault reference that points at the App Configuration endpoint
Copy the value from App Configuration into the app setting during each deployment
Grant the app the App Configuration Reader role and read the value with the REST API
Use an App Configuration reference such as @Microsoft.AppConfiguration(Endpoint=https://contoso.azconfig.io; Key=App:Color) and grant the app's identity App Configuration Data Reader

questions.explanation: App Service and Functions support App Configuration references in app settings; they resolve with the app's managed identity, which needs the App Configuration Data Reader data-plane role. Copying values during deployment drifts out of date, Key Vault references only point at Key Vault, and App Configuration Reader is a control-plane role that does not grant access to key-values.
questions.source_title: Use App Configuration references for App Service and Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: A container app uses the default revision mode. You deploy a new image and the new revision fails its health probes. What happens to production traffic?

options.text: Traffic stays on the old revision, because in single revision mode traffic moves only after the new revision is running and healthy
Both revisions are deactivated until you redeploy
Traffic is split 50/50 between the old and new revisions
Traffic moves to the new revision immediately and the app returns errors

questions.explanation: Single revision mode is the default. New revisions are provisioned and scaled, and traffic is diverted from the old revision only once the new replicas are running; if an update fails, traffic remains on the old revision and old revisions are deprovisioned automatically after a successful switch. Traffic splitting requires multiple revision mode.
questions.source_title: Update and deploy changes in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: You want to send 10 percent of requests to a new revision of a container app and keep 90 percent on the current revision. What must you configure?

options.text: Create a second container app and put Azure Front Door in front
Set the app to multiple revision mode and assign traffic weights of 90 and 10 to the two revisions
Keep single revision mode and set maxReplicas to 10 on the new revision
Add a revision label called canary; labels automatically receive 10 percent

questions.explanation: Traffic splitting requires multiple revision mode, and the combined weight of all traffic rules must equal 100 percent. Replica counts don't control traffic share, and labels give a revision its own FQDN without requiring any traffic weight. A second app with Front Door works but is unnecessary when Container Apps supports weighted splitting natively.
questions.source_title: Traffic splitting in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: Which change to a container app creates a new revision?

options.text: Switching the revision mode from single to multiple
Changing a container image or an environment variable in the template section
Adding a new secret to the configuration section
Changing the ingress target port

questions.explanation: Revision-scope changes are changes to the properties.template section, such as container images, environment variables, scale rules, and the revision suffix, and they create a new revision. Application-scope changes in properties.configuration, such as secrets, ingress, registry credentials, and revision mode, apply to all revisions without creating a new one.
questions.source_title: Update and deploy changes in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: In a blue-green rollout, the green revision should receive no production traffic, but testers must call it directly. What should you use?

options.text: Give the green revision a traffic weight of 1 percent
Put the green revision in a different Container Apps environment
Assign the label green to the revision and have testers call its label FQDN
Expose the green revision with a NodePort service

questions.explanation: A revision label gets its own FQDN (app name, three dashes, and label), so testers can reach a specific revision directly while its traffic weight stays at 0 percent. A 1 percent weight would still send real users to it, a separate environment is a separate deployment, and NodePort is a Kubernetes concept that Container Apps doesn't expose.
questions.source_title: Blue-green deployment in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: Your blue-green pipeline needs predictable revision names such as myapp--v2-3-0 so it can set traffic weights by name. What should the pipeline set on each deployment?

options.text: maxInactiveRevisions to 0
A new secret named after the release
template.revisionSuffix to a value that identifies the release
configuration.activeRevisionsMode to single

questions.explanation: Setting template.revisionSuffix gives deterministic revision names in the form <app>--<suffix>, which a pipeline can reference when assigning traffic or labels. Single revision mode disables traffic splitting, secrets are application-scope and don't name revisions, and the inactive revision limit only controls how many old revisions are kept.
questions.source_title: Blue-green deployment in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: You run az containerapp revision set-mode --mode multiple on an existing app. What is the effect?

options.text: The app now allows multiple active revisions, and no new revision is created by this change
A new revision is created and receives 100 percent of traffic
Traffic is automatically split evenly across all revisions
All existing revisions are deleted and recreated

questions.explanation: Revision mode is an application-scope setting. Changing it with az containerapp revision set-mode controls whether several revisions can be active at once, and Microsoft notes that changing the revision mode doesn't create a new revision. Traffic weights are still yours to configure, and existing revisions are untouched.
questions.source_title: Manage revisions in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: Two container apps, orders and inventory, run in the same Container Apps environment. Which statement about the environment is correct?

options.text: Apps in one environment must use the same container image
They share the environment's virtual network and write logs to the same Log Analytics workspace
Each app must be in a separate resource group
Each app gets its own isolated virtual network

questions.explanation: An environment is a secure boundary around a group of container apps: apps in the same environment share the same virtual network and send logs to the same logging destination. Each app can use its own images, and resource group placement is independent of environment membership.
questions.source_title: Azure Container Apps environments

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: A new workload needs GPU-capable dedicated hardware while other apps in the same environment should keep scale-to-zero serverless billing. Which environment type supports this?

options.text: Two separate AKS clusters
A Consumption-only environment with maxReplicas set to 1
A workload profiles environment, with a Dedicated profile for the GPU app and the Consumption profile for the others
A Consumption-only environment

questions.explanation: Workload profiles environments (the default, v2) support both the Consumption plan and Dedicated workload profiles in the same environment. Consumption-only environments are legacy and run only on-demand Consumption compute, so they can't host dedicated or GPU profiles. AKS isn't required for this scenario.
questions.source_title: Compute and billing structures in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: You are creating a workload profiles Container Apps environment in your own virtual network. Which subnet configuration is valid?

options.text: A /29 subnet shared with virtual machines
A dedicated subnet of /27 or larger, delegated to Microsoft.App/environments
Any existing subnet; the environment creates its own subnet automatically
A /23 subnet that must not be delegated

questions.explanation: Workload profiles environments need a dedicated subnet of /27 or larger that is delegated to Microsoft.App/environments. The legacy Consumption-only environment instead requires /23 or larger and must not be delegated. Subnet size can't be changed after the environment is created, so plan it carefully.
questions.source_title: Provide a virtual network to an Azure Container Apps environment

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: A container app must read a queue connection string that is stored in Key Vault, using a user-assigned managed identity. How should you define the secret?

options.text: @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=<KEY_VAULT_SECRET_URI>) as an environment variable value
Mount the key vault as an Azure Files volume
queue-conn=keyvaultref:<KEY_VAULT_SECRET_URI>,identityref:<MANAGED_IDENTITY_RESOURCE_ID>, and reference it from an environment variable with secretRef
Copy the value into the image at build time

questions.explanation: Container Apps secrets can reference Key Vault with the format <name>=keyvaultref:<secret URI>,identityref:<identity resource ID>, and containers consume the secret through an environment variable with secretRef. The @Microsoft.KeyVault syntax is for App Service and Functions, baking secrets into images is insecure, and Key Vault can't be mounted as an Azure Files share.
questions.source_title: Manage secrets in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: The frontend container app must call the internal-only container app named catalog in the same environment. What is the simplest way to address it?

options.text: Expose catalog with external ingress and call its public FQDN
Use the public IP address of the catalog replica
Call it by its app name, for example http://catalog, which resolves inside the environment
Create a Kubernetes Service object for catalog

questions.explanation: Container apps in the same environment can call each other by app name, and the environment's DNS resolves it to the app's internal endpoint. Replica IPs change, making catalog external defeats the internal-only requirement, and Container Apps doesn't let you create Kubernetes Service objects directly.
questions.source_title: Communicate between container apps

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: After an incident you must roll a container app back to the previous revision immediately. The app is in multiple revision mode, and both revisions are active. What is the fastest safe action?

options.text: Set the previous revision's traffic weight to 100 percent and the faulty revision's to 0 percent
Restart the faulty revision
Delete the container app and redeploy the old image
Switch the app to single revision mode

questions.explanation: In multiple revision mode you can shift traffic between active revisions instantly by changing weights, which is the built-in rollback mechanism. Deleting and redeploying causes downtime, switching to single mode keeps traffic on the latest revision, and restarting the faulty revision doesn't remove the bad code.
questions.source_title: Traffic splitting in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: You update the value of a secret that an environment variable references through secretRef. Running replicas still see the old value. Why?

options.text: The secret name must change every time the value changes
Secret changes are application-scope and don't create a new revision; you must restart the revision or deploy a new revision to pick up the value
secretRef values are cached for 24 hours like App Service Key Vault references
Secrets are only read when the environment is recreated

questions.explanation: Secrets live in the application configuration, so updating them doesn't generate a new revision, and existing replicas keep the value they started with until the revision is restarted or a new revision is created. Recreating the environment isn't needed, the 24-hour cache belongs to App Service Key Vault references, and secret names don't need to change.
questions.source_title: Manage secrets in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Deploy to Azure Container Apps (environments and revisions)
questions.stem: A revision in multiple revision mode is no longer needed, but you want to keep it available for a quick rollback without it consuming resources. What should you do?

options.text: Delete the container app
Deactivate the revision with az containerapp revision deactivate
Set its traffic weight to 0 percent and leave it active
Remove its label

questions.explanation: Deactivating a revision stops its replicas so it no longer runs or receives traffic, and it can be activated again later. A revision with 0 percent traffic stays active and can keep replicas running, deleting the app removes everything, and removing a label only removes the label FQDN.
questions.source_title: Manage revisions in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: You create a container app with HTTP ingress and don't define any scale settings. What scaling behavior does the app get?

options.text: The default HTTP rule with a minimum of 0 and a maximum of 10 replicas per revision
A minimum of 1 and a maximum of 100 replicas
No scaling until you add a KEDA rule
A fixed single replica that never scales

questions.explanation: If no scale rule is defined, Container Apps applies the default HTTP scale rule with 0 minimum replicas and 10 maximum replicas per revision, so the app can scale to zero when idle. You can raise the maximum up to 1,000. Replicas are scaled automatically, so no extra rule is required for HTTP traffic.
questions.source_title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: An HTTP scale rule is added without specifying concurrentRequests. At roughly what load does Container Apps add another replica?

options.text: When CPU reaches 80 percent
About 10 concurrent requests per replica, the default
About 100 concurrent requests per replica
When memory reaches 80 percent

questions.explanation: The HTTP scale rule's concurrentRequests defaults to 10 (minimum 1). Concurrency is calculated every 15 seconds as the requests in the past 15 seconds divided by 15. CPU and memory thresholds are separate custom rule types and aren't the default.
questions.source_title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: A worker uses a custom KEDA rule on a Service Bus queue with minReplicas 0. After the queue empties, the last replica keeps running for about five minutes before the app scales to zero. Why?

options.text: KEDA polls the queue only once every 5 minutes
Service Bus keeps messages locked for 5 minutes
Custom rules have a 300-second cool-down period that applies when scaling in from the final replica to 0
Scale-to-zero is not supported for Service Bus rules

questions.explanation: Custom scale rules use a 30-second polling interval and a 300-second cool-down period, and the cool-down applies only when scaling in from the final replica to zero. That's why the app waits about five minutes after the queue reaches zero. Service Bus scaling does support scale to zero, and the polling interval is 30 seconds, not 5 minutes.
questions.source_title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: You want a container app to scale on the length of the Service Bus queue orders, adding a replica for every 5 messages and authenticating with a connection string kept in a secret named sb-conn. Which CLI parameters are correct?

options.text: --scale-rule-type cpu --scale-rule-metadata "value=5"
--scale-rule-http-concurrency 5 --secrets sb-conn
--scale-rule-type azure-servicebus --scale-rule-metadata "queueName=orders" "namespace=contoso-sb" "messageCount=5" --scale-rule-auth "connection=sb-conn"
--scale-rule-type servicebus-queue --scale-rule-auth "sb-conn"

questions.explanation: Custom rules use the KEDA scaler type (azure-servicebus), its metadata as key=value pairs (queue name, namespace, and messageCount as the target per replica), and --scale-rule-auth to map the scaler's connection trigger parameter to a secret. HTTP concurrency and CPU rules don't read queue length, and servicebus-queue isn't the KEDA scaler name.
questions.source_title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: You want a Service Bus scale rule to authenticate with the app's managed identity instead of a connection string. In the Azure portal you can't find the option. What should you do?

options.text: Managed identity isn't supported for any KEDA scaler in Container Apps
Give the identity Contributor on the container app
Configure the rule with the CLI (--scale-rule-identity) or with Bicep/ARM (identity in the custom rule), because the portal doesn't support managed identity for scale rules
Create the rule as an HTTP rule instead

questions.explanation: Container Apps supports managed identity for the Azure Queue Storage, Service Bus, and Event Hubs scalers, but the portal doesn't expose it; you set it with --scale-rule-identity in the CLI or identity in the custom block of Bicep/ARM. An HTTP rule can't read queue length, and Contributor on the app doesn't authenticate the scaler to Service Bus.
questions.source_title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: A background worker container app has ingress disabled. You set no minReplicas and no custom scale rule. What is the risk?

options.text: The app can scale to zero and never restart, because nothing will trigger it to scale out again
The app will scale to 1,000 replicas
The app can't be deployed without ingress
Revisions will be deactivated every night

questions.explanation: Without ingress, the default HTTP rule never fires. Microsoft warns that if ingress is disabled and you define neither minReplicas nor a custom rule, the app scales to zero and has no way to start again. Set minReplicas to 1 or more, or add an event-driven rule such as a queue scaler.
questions.source_title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: A team adds a CPU scale rule to a container app and expects it to scale to zero overnight. It never goes below one replica. Why?

options.text: CPU rules only work with multiple revision mode
CPU and memory scale rules don't allow a container app to scale to zero
CPU rules require a Dedicated workload profile
The cool-down period for CPU rules is 24 hours

questions.explanation: CPU and memory are measured inside running replicas, so these rules can't scale to zero; Microsoft recommends preferring HTTP or event-driven rules when possible. CPU rules work on the Consumption plan and in any revision mode, and there's no 24-hour cool-down.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Scale a container app

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: A queue rule targets messageCount=5. There are 100 messages waiting and maxReplicas is 10. How many replicas will the revision run when it fully scales out?

options.text: 5, because messageCount is the replica limit
100, one replica per message
10, because the desired count of ceil(100 / 5) = 20 is capped by maxReplicas
20, because maxReplicas is a soft limit

questions.explanation: KEDA computes desiredReplicas = ceil(currentMetricValue / targetMetricValue), which is 20 here, but replicas never exceed maxReplicas. messageCount is the target number of messages per replica, not a replica cap.
questions.source_title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: Traffic drops sharply, but your container app keeps its extra replicas for a few minutes before scaling in. What explains this?

options.text: Revisions in single mode can't scale in
HTTP rules only scale in at midnight
The scale-up stabilization window of 300 seconds
The scale-down stabilization window of 300 seconds

questions.explanation: Container Apps uses a 0-second scale-up stabilization window and a 300-second scale-down stabilization window, so scale-in happens only after the scale-down conditions have held for 300 seconds. This avoids flapping. Scale-up isn't delayed, and both revision modes support scaling in.
questions.source_title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: A container app in multiple revision mode has two active revisions. Each revision's scale settings use minReplicas 1 and maxReplicas 10. What is the maximum total number of replicas?

options.text: 11, the sum of one minimum and one maximum
20, because scale limits apply per revision
10, because limits apply to the whole app
1,000, because multiple revision mode removes limits

questions.explanation: Scale limits define the minimum and maximum number of replicas per revision. With two active revisions each limited to 10, the app can run up to 20 replicas in total. Multiple revision mode doesn't remove these limits.
questions.source_title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: A container app must scale on the number of messages in an Azure Storage queue. Which rule should you add?

options.text: An HTTP rule with concurrentRequests set to the queue length
A memory rule
A TCP rule on port 443
A custom rule of type azure-queue with queueName and queueLength metadata

questions.explanation: Container Apps uses KEDA, which provides the azure-queue scaler for Azure Storage queues; queueLength is the target number of messages per replica, and authentication uses a secret or a managed identity. HTTP and TCP rules only measure incoming requests or connections, and memory rules measure resource usage, not queue depth.
questions.source_title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: You are designing scaling for a public HTTP API on Container Apps. Which guidance does Microsoft give?

options.text: Set minReplicas equal to maxReplicas to disable scaling
Use a TCP rule for all HTTP APIs
Prefer HTTP scale rules over CPU or memory rules when possible
Always combine CPU and memory rules for APIs

questions.explanation: The scaling tutorial recommends HTTP scale rules over CPU or memory rules where possible, because they react directly to demand and allow scale to zero. TCP rules are for non-HTTP traffic, and fixing minReplicas and maxReplicas removes scaling altogether.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Scale a container app

questions.skill_name: Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
questions.stem: A latency-sensitive API on Container Apps must never suffer a cold start, but should still scale out under load. What should you configure?

options.text: Set maxReplicas to 1
Set minReplicas to 0 and lower the polling interval
Remove all scale rules
Set minReplicas to 1 or more and keep an HTTP scale rule

questions.explanation: Scale to zero happens only when minReplicas is 0, and the first request after scaling to zero waits for a replica to start. Keeping at least one replica avoids that cold start while the HTTP rule still adds replicas under load. maxReplicas 1 prevents scaling out, and removing rules falls back to the default rule with a minimum of 0.
questions.source_title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: You have an AKS cluster and a manifest file store.yaml that defines Deployments and Services. Which command sequence deploys it?

options.text: az aks create --manifest store.yaml
az aks get-credentials --resource-group rg --name aks1, then kubectl apply -f store.yaml
kubectl run -f store.yaml without credentials
az acr build --file store.yaml

questions.explanation: az aks get-credentials downloads credentials and configures kubectl to talk to the cluster, and kubectl apply -f creates or updates every object defined in the manifest. az aks create has no manifest option, kubectl needs cluster credentials, and az acr build builds container images, not Kubernetes objects.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Deploy an AKS cluster using Azure CLI

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: A Deployment manifest is rejected with an error that the selector doesn't match the template labels. Which fix is correct?

options.text: Set replicas to 0
Delete the selector; Kubernetes infers it
Add a Service of type LoadBalancer
Make spec.selector.matchLabels match the labels in spec.template.metadata.labels

questions.explanation: A Deployment manages the pods whose labels match its selector, so spec.selector.matchLabels must match the pod template's labels; the AKS sample manifests use app: <name> in both places. The selector is required for apps/v1 Deployments, a Service doesn't affect Deployment validation, and replicas has no relation to the error.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Deploy an AKS cluster using Azure CLI

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: The store-front Deployment must be reachable from the internet with a public IP, while the product-service Deployment must be reachable only inside the cluster. Which Service types should you use?

options.text: LoadBalancer for store-front and ClusterIP for product-service
ClusterIP for both
LoadBalancer for both
NodePort for product-service and ClusterIP for store-front

questions.explanation: A LoadBalancer Service gets an external IP from the Azure load balancer, which is how the AKS quickstart exposes the storefront. ClusterIP, the default, gives a cluster-internal IP only, which is what the backend services use. Swapping them or exposing both publicly breaks the requirement.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Deploy an AKS cluster using Azure CLI

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: You push an image to contoso.azurecr.io/store-front:v1. What must the image field in your AKS manifest contain?

options.text: Only store-front:v1; AKS searches attached registries automatically
The registry resource ID
docker.io/store-front:v1
The full name including the ACR login server: contoso.azurecr.io/store-front:v1

questions.explanation: Kubernetes pulls exactly the image reference in the manifest, so the AKS tutorial has you update the image names to include your ACR login server. Without it, the runtime looks on Docker Hub. Attaching ACR grants pull permissions but doesn't rewrite image names.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Deploy an application to AKS

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: Pods in an AKS cluster fail to pull images from your Azure container registry with 401 Unauthorized. The registry isn't ABAC-enabled. What is the recommended fix?

options.text: Make the registry public
Run az aks update --name aks1 --resource-group rg --attach-acr <registry>, which grants AcrPull to the kubelet identity
Give the cluster's control plane identity the Owner role on the registry
Enable the registry admin user and create an imagePullSecret with its password

questions.explanation: The AKS-ACR integration assigns the AcrPull role to the managed identity of the cluster's agent pools (the kubelet identity), so nodes can pull without stored credentials. Admin-user pull secrets and public registries are discouraged, and Owner is far more privilege than pulling needs and is assigned to the wrong identity.
questions.source_title: Authenticate with ACR from AKS

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: Your container registry uses attribute-based access control (ABAC) repository permissions. A colleague runs az aks update --attach-acr, but nodes still can't pull. What should you do?

options.text: Manually assign the Container Registry Repository Reader role to the kubelet managed identity
Assign AcrPull on the resource group instead of the registry
Switch the AKS cluster to use a service principal
Run --attach-acr again with the --force flag

questions.explanation: ABAC-enabled registries don't honor the classic AcrPull role and don't support the --attach-acr integration. You must assign the Container Registry Repository Reader role to the kubelet identity yourself. Repeating the command or assigning AcrPull at a different scope doesn't help.
questions.source_title: Troubleshoot AKS image pull errors from ACR

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: Your AKS cluster has Linux and Windows node pools. A Linux-based Deployment sometimes gets scheduled onto Windows nodes and fails. What should you add to the pod template?

options.text: A Service of type ClusterIP
nodeSelector: kubernetes.io/os: linux
imagePullPolicy: Always
replicas: 1

questions.explanation: A nodeSelector constrains pods to nodes with matching labels, and the AKS sample manifests use kubernetes.io/os: linux so Linux containers only run on Linux nodes. Replica count, pull policy, and Services don't affect which operating system a pod is scheduled on.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Deploy an application to AKS

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: You need to deploy the same manifest into a separate namespace called aks-store-demo. Which commands are correct?

options.text: kubectl create ns aks-store-demo, then kubectl apply -n aks-store-demo -f manifest.yaml
kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml --cluster aks-store-demo
az aks nodepool add --name aks-store-demo
kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml; namespaces are created from the file name

questions.explanation: You create the namespace and then use -n (or metadata.namespace in the manifest) to deploy into it, as in the AKS Automatic quickstart. --cluster selects a kubeconfig cluster, not a namespace, a node pool is compute capacity rather than a namespace, and kubectl never derives a namespace from a file name.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Deploy an AKS cluster using Azure CLI

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: You change the image tag of a Deployment in its manifest from v1 to v2 and run kubectl apply again. What happens by default?

options.text: A second Deployment is created alongside the first
All pods are deleted at once and recreated
The Deployment performs a rolling update, replacing pods gradually with pods that run v2
Nothing changes until you delete the Deployment

questions.explanation: kubectl apply updates the existing Deployment object, and the default RollingUpdate strategy creates new pods from the updated template while scaling down old ones, which avoids downtime. Deployments don't need to be deleted to update, and apply updates the existing object rather than creating a duplicate.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Deploy an application to AKS

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: A container in AKS is repeatedly killed, and kubectl describe pod shows the last state as OOMKilled. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The Service selector doesn't match the pods
The image tag doesn't exist in the registry
The liveness probe path is wrong
The container exceeds its memory limit, so the limit or the app's memory usage must be adjusted

questions.explanation: OOMKilled means the container used more memory than its limit allowed, and Kubernetes terminated it; incorrect resource limits are a documented cause of CrashLoopBackOff. A missing tag causes ImagePullBackOff, a bad liveness probe shows probe failures in events, and a selector mismatch affects routing, not memory.
questions.source_title: Pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff mode

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: kubectl get pods shows a pod with STATUS Running but READY 0/1. Users get no responses through the Service. What does this indicate?

options.text: The container is running but not ready, typically because its readiness probe is failing, so it is removed from the Service endpoints
The image can't be pulled
The node is out of disk space
The pod has been evicted

questions.explanation: READY is the ratio of ready containers to total containers; a container can be running but not ready when its readiness probe fails, and Services only route to ready pods. Image pull problems show ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull, and evictions show a different status.
questions.source_title: List pods in an AKS cluster

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: An app in AKS needs a database password. Following Kubernetes practice, how should you provide it to the container?

options.text: Pass it as a command-line argument in the manifest
Store it in a Kubernetes Secret and reference it from the container env with secretKeyRef (or mount it as a volume)
Hard-code it in the container image
Put it in a ConfigMap and mark the ConfigMap as encrypted

questions.explanation: Secrets are the Kubernetes object for sensitive values, and containers consume them as environment variables or mounted files; missing or misconfigured Secrets and ConfigMaps are a documented cause of crashes. ConfigMaps are for non-sensitive configuration, and images or command arguments expose the value to anyone who can read them.
questions.source_title: Pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff mode

questions.skill_name: Deploy and manage applications on AKS with manifest files
questions.stem: You apply a manifest with a Service of type LoadBalancer. kubectl get service shows EXTERNAL-IP as <pending>. What does this usually mean?

options.text: The cluster has no Linux node pool
The Deployment failed to pull its image
The Service type must be ClusterIP for AKS
Azure is still provisioning the public IP for the load balancer; wait and watch the service until the IP appears

questions.explanation: When a LoadBalancer Service is created, AKS asks Azure to provision a public IP on the load balancer, and the EXTERNAL-IP shows <pending> until that finishes; the quickstart has you watch the service until the address appears. Image pull failures show on pods, ClusterIP would never get a public IP, and node OS doesn't cause a pending IP.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Deploy an AKS cluster using Azure CLI

questions.skill_name: Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
questions.stem: A pod in AKS shows ImagePullBackOff. What should you do first to get the detailed error?

options.text: Run kubectl logs <pod>
Delete and recreate the namespace
Run kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <namespace> and read the Events section
Restart the AKS cluster

questions.explanation: For ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull, the Events in kubectl describe pod show why the pull failed, such as authorization errors, a missing tag, or DNS issues. kubectl logs returns nothing because the container never started, and restarting the cluster or recreating the namespace doesn't diagnose anything.
questions.source_title: Troubleshoot AKS image pull errors from ACR

questions.skill_name: Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
questions.stem: You suspect your AKS nodes can't reach or authenticate to your Azure container registry. Which command checks this from the cluster's perspective?

options.text: az acr check-health --name contoso only from your laptop
az acr task logs --registry contoso
kubectl get nodes
az aks check-acr --resource-group rg --name aks1 --acr contoso.azurecr.io

questions.explanation: az aks check-acr validates that the AKS cluster can access the registry and that the kubelet identity is authorized. Checking registry health from a laptop doesn't test the cluster's network path or identity, kubectl get nodes only lists nodes, and task logs only show ACR build output.
questions.source_title: Troubleshoot AKS image pull errors from ACR

questions.skill_name: Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
questions.stem: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. The current container restarts too quickly to see its output. Which command shows the logs from the previous, crashed container?

options.text: kubectl describe node
az aks show --query provisioningState
kubectl logs <pod> -n <namespace> --previous
kubectl get events --watch-only on the Service

questions.explanation: kubectl logs --previous returns the logs of the last terminated instance of the container, which usually contains the exception or error that caused the crash. Node descriptions and cluster provisioning state don't include application output.
questions.source_title: Pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff mode

questions.skill_name: Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
questions.stem: A new Container Apps revision never becomes healthy. You open Log stream in the portal. Which log type shows image pull failures, probe results, and secret sync errors?

options.text: Activity log
Console logs
System logs
HTTP logs

questions.explanation: System logs contain platform events such as image pull status, probe results, identity errors, and secret sync outcomes. Console logs contain your application's stdout and stderr. HTTP logs record ingress requests, and the Activity log records management operations on the resource.
questions.source_title: Troubleshoot common deployment failures in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
questions.stem: Your container apps send logs to Log Analytics. Which tables hold the application output and the platform events?

options.text: AzureActivity and Heartbeat
ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL for stdout/stderr and ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL for system events
ContainerLogV2 and KubeEvents
AppRequests and AppDependencies

questions.explanation: Container Apps writes console output to ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL and system events to ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL when the environment uses Log Analytics (or the equivalent tables without the suffix when using diagnostic settings). ContainerLogV2 and KubeEvents belong to AKS Container insights, and AppRequests holds Application Insights request telemetry.
questions.source_title: Troubleshoot common deployment failures in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
questions.stem: When you open Log stream for a container app, the portal says the revision is scaled to zero. What should you do to see live logs?

options.text: Delete the revision
Switch to the Logs blade; it streams logs from scaled-to-zero revisions
Disable ingress
Make the revision run a replica, for example by sending a request or setting the minimum replicas to 1

questions.explanation: Log streaming shows output from running replicas. If the revision is scaled to zero there is nothing to stream, so the troubleshooting guide suggests deploying or configuring the revision with a minimum replica count (or generating traffic). Historical logs are queried in Log Analytics, not streamed, and disabling ingress doesn't start a replica.
questions.source_title: Troubleshoot a container app

questions.skill_name: Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
questions.stem: A container app revision is Degraded with 0 ready replicas, and system logs show the probe gets connection refused. What should you check first?

options.text: That the probe port matches the port the app listens on and the ingress targetPort
That the registry is geo-replicated
That the app is in multiple revision mode
That the Log Analytics workspace exists

questions.explanation: Connection refused means nothing is listening on the probed port. The deployment troubleshooting guide says to set the probe port to match the app's listening port and the ingress target port, and to increase delays if the app starts slowly. Logging destination, revision mode, and geo-replication don't cause probe connection failures.
questions.source_title: Troubleshoot common deployment failures in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
questions.stem: You didn't configure any health probes, but a slow-starting container app keeps restarting with startup probe failures. Why?

options.text: When ingress is enabled and no probes are defined, Container Apps applies default probes against the target port
Container Apps always runs a probe on port 80 regardless of ingress
The container image contains a HEALTHCHECK that Container Apps converts to a liveness probe
Probes are created by the KEDA scaler

questions.explanation: With ingress enabled and no probes configured, Container Apps adds default probes that target the ingress target port. A slow-starting app can fail them, so define your own startup probe with suitable delays and thresholds. KEDA doesn't create probes, and the platform doesn't use the Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK.
questions.source_title: Health probes in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
questions.stem: AKS has Container insights enabled. In which Log Analytics table do you query container stdout/stderr logs using the recommended schema?

options.text: ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL
AppTraces
AzureDiagnostics
ContainerLogV2

questions.explanation: Container insights stores the container logs it collects from AKS in the ContainerLogV2 table, the recommended schema with fields such as PodName, PodNamespace, and ContainerName. ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL is for Azure Container Apps, AppTraces is Application Insights log telemetry, and AzureDiagnostics holds resource logs from many services.
questions.source_title: Monitor Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)

questions.skill_name: Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
