questions.stem: You need the logs of every container belonging to pods whose names contain checkout in the last hour. ContainerLogV2 alone isn't enough because you also want pod inventory details. Which pair of tables does Microsoft's sample query join?

options.text: KubeEvents and AppRequests on operation_Id
KubePodInventory and ContainerLogV2 on ContainerID
ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL and KubePodInventory on RevisionName
Heartbeat and Perf on Computer

questions.explanation: The Container insights sample joins KubePodInventory (pod name, namespace, container ID) with ContainerLogV2 on ContainerID to return log lines for matching pods. operation_Id is an Application Insights correlation field, and the Container Apps and VM tables don't contain AKS pod inventory.
questions.source_title: Query container logs in Azure Monitor

questions.skill_name: Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
questions.stem: You need to run commands inside a running container app replica to check DNS resolution to a database. What should you use?

options.text: Revision labels
Azure Monitor metrics
The container console (for example az containerapp exec)
Log stream

questions.explanation: Container Apps provides a container console so you can connect to the shell inside a running container and debug from there. Log stream only shows output, metrics show resource usage, and labels give a revision its own FQDN.
questions.source_title: Observability in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
questions.stem: Users can't reach an app hosted in AKS. Microsoft's inside-out troubleshooting approach says to start where?

options.text: Check the public DNS records first
Recreate the cluster's load balancer
Check that the pod is running and the app inside it responds, using kubectl get pods and kubectl describe pod
Check the Azure subscription quota

questions.explanation: The guidance for app connection issues starts inside the cluster: confirm the pod is Running and Ready and that the app responds, then work outward to the Service, ingress, and network. kubectl describe pod events reveal probe failures, CrashLoopBackOff, or OOMKilled. DNS and load balancer checks come later, and quota rarely causes connectivity errors.
questions.source_title: Troubleshoot app connection issues in an AKS cluster

questions.skill_name: Connect to Cosmos DB for NoSQL with the SDK and run queries
questions.stem: A .NET API creates a new CosmosClient for every HTTP request. Under load you see high latency and port exhaustion. What should you change?

options.text: Use a single CosmosClient instance for the lifetime of the application
Increase the container's RU/s
Switch to strong consistency
Dispose each CosmosClient immediately after the query

questions.explanation: CosmosClient is thread-safe and manages connections and address caches, so Microsoft recommends a singleton for the application's lifetime; creating clients per request opens new connections and can exhaust ports. Disposing faster doesn't remove the connection churn, and consistency or throughput changes don't fix client-side connection problems.
questions.source_title: Performance tips for Azure Cosmos DB and .NET

questions.skill_name: Connect to Cosmos DB for NoSQL with the SDK and run queries
questions.stem: You know both the id and the partition key value of an item. Which operation retrieves it with the lowest RU charge?

options.text: A cross-partition query with ORDER BY c._ts
SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.id = @id without a partition key
A point read, such as ReadItemAsync(id, new PartitionKey(pk))
Reading the change feed from the beginning

questions.explanation: A point read by id and partition key goes straight to the item, and apart from the consistency level its RU charge depends only on the item's size. A query, especially without the partition key, must be planned and may fan out across partitions, which costs more. The change feed isn't a lookup mechanism.
questions.source_title: Optimize request cost in Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Connect to Cosmos DB for NoSQL with the SDK and run queries
questions.stem: Your application runs in a corporate network whose firewall only allows outbound HTTPS on port 443 to a single endpoint. Which Cosmos DB SDK connection mode should you use?

options.text: Session mode
Direct mode over TCP
Gateway mode
Bulk mode

questions.explanation: Gateway mode sends requests over HTTPS to a single gateway endpoint, which suits networks with strict firewall rules, at the cost of an extra network hop. Direct mode connects to many backend replicas over a range of TCP ports and is faster but needs those ports open. Bulk is a throughput optimization and Session is a consistency level, not a connection mode.
questions.source_title: Performance tips for Azure Cosmos DB and .NET

questions.skill_name: Connect to Cosmos DB for NoSQL with the SDK and run queries
questions.stem: Your API filters items by a value supplied by users. Which way of building the Cosmos DB query is recommended?

options.text: Use a stored procedure for every query
Download all items and filter in memory
Use a parameterized query, for example SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.city = @city with the value passed as a parameter
Concatenate the user value into the query string

questions.explanation: Parameterized queries (QueryDefinition with WithParameter in .NET) keep user input out of the query text, preventing injection, and let the service reuse the query plan. String concatenation is unsafe, reading everything wastes RUs, and stored procedures are scoped to a single partition key and add no benefit here.
questions.source_title: Query performance tips for Azure Cosmos DB SDKs

questions.skill_name: Connect to Cosmos DB for NoSQL with the SDK and run queries
questions.stem: A query filters on the partition key, and the container has only a few physical partitions. Which .NET SDK feature can reduce query latency by skipping the separate query plan call?

options.text: Bounded staleness consistency
The change feed processor
Optimistic Direct Execution (EnableOptimisticDirectExecution in QueryRequestOptions)
Bulk execution mode

questions.explanation: Optimistic Direct Execution (.NET SDK 3.38.0 and later) runs single-partition queries directly when the partition key is in the request or query, or the container has a single physical partition, and the results don't need pagination. Bulk mode is for high-volume writes, the change feed is for processing changes, and consistency doesn't affect query planning.
questions.source_title: Query performance tips for Azure Cosmos DB SDKs

questions.skill_name: Connect to Cosmos DB for NoSQL with the SDK and run queries
questions.stem: Your Cosmos DB account is replicated to West US, Central US, and East US. An app running in Central US must read from the nearest replica. What should you configure in the SDK?

options.text: EnableContentResponseOnWrite
The partition key path
ApplicationPreferredRegions (preferred regions) with Central US first
A larger MaxItemCount

questions.explanation: Preferred regions tell the SDK which regional endpoints to use, in order, so reads go to the closest replica and fail over to the next one; Microsoft also recommends running the app in the same region as the account. The partition key, content response, and page size settings don't affect regional routing.
questions.source_title: Performance tips for Azure Cosmos DB and .NET

questions.skill_name: Connect to Cosmos DB for NoSQL with the SDK and run queries
questions.stem: A Java service inserts large documents at high volume and never uses the item returned by createItem. How can you reduce network and CPU usage?

options.text: Use strong consistency
Add a composite index
Create a new client for each write
Set contentResponseOnWriteEnabled(false) on the CosmosClientBuilder

questions.explanation: For workloads with heavy create payloads, the Java SDK best practices recommend turning off content response on write so the service doesn't send the full item back. Consistency and indexes don't change the response payload, and creating clients per write hurts performance.
questions.source_title: Best practices for Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK

questions.skill_name: Connect to Cosmos DB for NoSQL with the SDK and run queries
questions.stem: Your app receives HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) responses from Cosmos DB during peak hours. What do they mean, and what is an appropriate response?

options.text: The request rate exceeded the provisioned RU/s; let the SDK retry after the indicated delay and, if 429s persist, increase throughput or reduce RU consumption
The partition key is invalid; recreate the container
The account has hit its storage limit; delete data
The client is using the wrong region; switch to Gateway mode

questions.explanation: A 429 means the operation was rate-limited because the provisioned throughput (RU/s) was exhausted. The SDKs retry automatically using the retry-after hint, and sustained throttling calls for more RU/s or cheaper operations (for example better indexing or point reads). It isn't a partition key, storage, or region error.
questions.source_title: Request Units in Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Connect to Cosmos DB for NoSQL with the SDK and run queries
questions.stem: An IoT container is partitioned by deviceId, and some devices write about 1 KB every second. Microsoft warns this design will eventually fail. Why, and what is the recommended fix?

options.text: Partition keys must be numeric
A single logical partition can store at most 20 GB, so use a hierarchical partition key such as deviceId then a time value
Logical partitions are limited to 1,000 items; add more containers
Each device needs its own database

questions.explanation: Each logical partition, meaning all items with the same partition key value, is limited to 20 GB. A busy device can exceed that within a year, so the IoT guidance uses hierarchical partition keys (for example deviceId, then timestamp) to spread data. There's no 1,000-item limit, and partition keys don't have to be numeric.
questions.source_title: Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Connect to Cosmos DB for NoSQL with the SDK and run queries
questions.stem: A .NET job imports 5 million items into a Cosmos DB container and must use the provisioned throughput as efficiently as possible. Which SDK option is designed for this?

options.text: Use a stored procedure for each item
Switch to strong consistency
Enable bulk mode (AllowBulkExecution = true) and send many concurrent CreateItem or UpsertItem tasks
Insert items one at a time with await on each call

questions.explanation: Bulk mode lets the .NET SDK group concurrent point operations into batches per partition, which maximizes throughput use for large ingestion jobs. Sequential awaits leave throughput idle, per-item stored procedures add overhead and are limited to one partition key, and consistency doesn't improve ingestion.
questions.source_title: Performance tips for Azure Cosmos DB and .NET

questions.skill_name: Optimize Cosmos DB queries and RUs (indexing, consistency)
questions.stem: Items contain a large description property that is never used in filters or ORDER BY clauses. You want to reduce the RU cost of writes. What should you change in the indexing policy?

options.text: Switch the indexing mode to lazy
Add a composite index on description
Add /description/* (or /description/?) to excludedPaths while keeping /* included
Exclude /* and include only /description/?

questions.explanation: By default every property is indexed, and each indexed term adds write cost. Including the root and excluding unneeded paths is the recommended strategy because new properties are still indexed automatically. Including only description does the opposite of what's needed, lazy mode is obsolete, and a composite index adds even more indexing work.
questions.source_title: Indexing policies in Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Optimize Cosmos DB queries and RUs (indexing, consistency)
questions.stem: A query uses ORDER BY c.lastName ASC, c.firstName ASC. With the default indexing policy it fails with an error about a missing index. What should you add?

options.text: A composite index on /lastName ASC and /firstName ASC
A vector index
A spatial index
A range index on /lastName only

questions.explanation: ORDER BY on multiple properties requires a composite index whose paths and sort orders match the query. A single-property range index can't serve a multi-property sort, and spatial or vector indexes are for geospatial and similarity queries.
questions.source_title: Troubleshoot query issues when using Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Optimize Cosmos DB queries and RUs (indexing, consistency)
questions.stem: A query filters on c.category and sorts by c.price, and it consumes many RUs. Which optimization does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: Add a composite index on (category, price) and include both properties in the ORDER BY clause
Remove the WHERE clause and filter in the client
Increase the page size to 10,000
Switch to eventual consistency

questions.explanation: For queries with both a filter and an ORDER BY, add a composite index over the filter and sort properties and include all the composite index's properties in the ORDER BY so the query uses it. Client-side filtering reads far more data, eventual consistency doesn't change query plan efficiency, and page size doesn't reduce total work.
questions.source_title: Troubleshoot query issues when using Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Optimize Cosmos DB queries and RUs (indexing, consistency)
questions.stem: A container only stores session data that expires through time-to-live, and the app never queries by any property. Which indexing policy fits best?

options.text: indexingMode consistent, no included paths, and /* as the only excluded path
indexingMode none with TTL enabled
Exclude only /_etag/?
Include /* and add composite indexes for every property

questions.explanation: For scenarios where no property needs indexing but TTL is required, the documentation recommends consistent mode with no included paths and /* as the only excluded path, because TTL needs the indexing mode to be consistent rather than none. Indexing everything wastes write RUs, and excluding only _etag still indexes all other properties.
questions.source_title: Indexing policies in Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Optimize Cosmos DB queries and RUs (indexing, consistency)
questions.stem: You switch to an opt-in indexing policy: /* is excluded and only /status/? and /createdAt/? are included. Queries that filter on the partition key /tenantId become expensive. Why?

options.text: Partition key filters never use the index
The _ts property is no longer indexed
With the exclude-root strategy, the partition key path isn't indexed unless you include it explicitly
Opt-in policies disable point reads

questions.explanation: When the root path is excluded, only explicitly included paths are indexed, and the documentation notes that the partition key path isn't indexed by default with that strategy, so include it if you filter on it. Point reads don't depend on the index, and id and _ts are always indexed in consistent mode.
questions.source_title: Indexing policies in Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Optimize Cosmos DB queries and RUs (indexing, consistency)
questions.stem: Your account uses strong consistency, and read RU costs are higher than expected. What is the effect of the consistency level on reads?

options.text: Strong and bounded staleness reads cost about twice the RUs of the more relaxed levels
Session consistency doubles read cost
Only writes are affected by consistency
Strong reads cost the same as eventual reads

questions.explanation: With strong or bounded staleness, the RU cost of any read operation, whether a point read or a query, is roughly doubled compared with session, consistent prefix, or eventual consistency. Consistency doesn't change write RU charges in this way.
questions.source_title: Optimize request cost in Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Optimize Cosmos DB queries and RUs (indexing, consistency)
questions.stem: A user updates their profile and immediately reloads the page through the same client. The app uses the default consistency level. What is guaranteed?

options.text: Nothing; reads are eventual by default
Every client in every region sees the update instantly
Session consistency guarantees read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and monotonic writes within the client session
The read is served from the integrated cache only

questions.explanation: Session consistency is the default and guarantees that within a single session a client reads its own writes and never sees older data after newer data. Other sessions may see the update later. Strong consistency would be needed for global linearizability, and the integrated cache is a separate optional feature.
questions.source_title: Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Optimize Cosmos DB queries and RUs (indexing, consistency)
questions.stem: The account default consistency is Session. Can a single request override it, and how?

options.text: Yes, to any level including strong
Yes, but only for writes
Yes, but only to an equal or weaker level, such as eventual or consistent prefix
No, consistency can only be set at the account level

questions.explanation: The requested consistency level for an operation must match or be weaker than the level configured on the account. You can relax a read to eventual or consistent prefix to save cost, but you can't strengthen it beyond the account default.
questions.source_title: Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Optimize Cosmos DB queries and RUs (indexing, consistency)
questions.stem: Which list shows the Cosmos DB consistency levels from strongest to weakest?

options.text: Session, Strong, Bounded staleness, Consistent prefix, Eventual
Bounded staleness, Strong, Session, Eventual, Consistent prefix
Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix, Eventual
Strong, Session, Bounded staleness, Eventual, Consistent prefix

questions.explanation: Azure Cosmos DB offers five levels, ordered from strongest to weakest: Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix, and Eventual. Stronger levels give fresher reads at the cost of higher latency, lower availability, or more RUs.
questions.source_title: Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Optimize Cosmos DB queries and RUs (indexing, consistency)
questions.stem: Query metrics show Retrieved Document Count far higher than Output Document Count, and the query costs 400 RUs. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A property used in the filter isn't indexed, so many documents are loaded and filtered after retrieval
The container uses session consistency
The client uses Direct mode
The query uses a parameter

questions.explanation: When far more documents are retrieved than returned, the engine is loading documents to evaluate filters it couldn't answer from the index. The troubleshooting guide's example removes an excluded path so the filter becomes indexed, dropping the charge sharply. Connection mode, session consistency, and parameters don't cause this pattern.
questions.source_title: Troubleshoot query issues when using Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Optimize Cosmos DB queries and RUs (indexing, consistency)
questions.stem: A read-heavy app repeatedly reads the same large items and runs the same expensive queries. You want cache hits to cost zero RUs without writing your own caching layer. What should you use?

options.text: The Cosmos DB integrated cache through a dedicated gateway
The change feed processor
Strong consistency
A composite index

questions.explanation: The integrated cache, accessed through a dedicated gateway, serves point reads and queries from memory, and cache hits have an RU charge of zero, which suits read-heavy workloads with repeated reads. Strong consistency increases read cost, a composite index only helps specific queries, and the change feed processes writes.
questions.source_title: Azure Cosmos DB integrated cache

questions.skill_name: Optimize Cosmos DB queries and RUs (indexing, consistency)
questions.stem: What determines the RU charge of a point read, besides the consistency level?

options.text: The length of the partition key path
The number of physical partitions
The size of the item retrieved
The number of indexed properties

questions.explanation: The cost optimization guide states that the only factor affecting the RU charge of a point read, apart from consistency, is the size of the item; for example, a 1 KB item costs about 1 RU. Indexing affects writes and queries, and partition count doesn't change a point read's cost.
questions.source_title: Optimize request cost in Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Store embeddings and run vector search in Cosmos DB
questions.stem: You want to store 1,536-dimension embeddings in Cosmos DB for NoSQL and query them by similarity. Which two definitions are required when you create the container? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.

options.text: A composite index on the embedding path
A vector index (for example diskANN) on the embedding path in the indexing policy
A vector embedding policy that defines the path, data type, distance function, and dimensions
A unique key on the embedding path

questions.explanation: Vector search in Cosmos DB for NoSQL needs a container vector embedding policy, describing each vector path's data type, dimensions, and distance function, plus a vector index entry in the indexing policy. Composite indexes and unique keys apply to scalar properties and can't index embeddings.
questions.source_title: Vector search in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

questions.skill_name: Store embeddings and run vector search in Cosmos DB
questions.stem: Which query returns the five items most similar to a query embedding passed as @embedding?

options.text: SELECT TOP 5 c.title FROM c WHERE CONTAINS(c.embedding, @embedding)
SELECT TOP 5 c.title, VectorDistance(c.embedding, @embedding) AS score FROM c ORDER BY VectorDistance(c.embedding, @embedding)
SELECT TOP 5 c.title FROM c WHERE c.embedding = @embedding
SELECT TOP 5 c.title FROM c ORDER BY c.embedding DESC

questions.explanation: VectorDistance computes the similarity between a stored vector and the query vector, and ordering by it returns the nearest neighbors using the configured vector index and distance function. Equality, plain ORDER BY on an array, and CONTAINS don't perform similarity search.
questions.source_title: Vector search in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

questions.skill_name: Store embeddings and run vector search in Cosmos DB
questions.stem: You try to create a flat vector index for 1,536-dimension embeddings and the request is rejected. Which index types support this dimension count?

options.text: Only flat, after reducing dimensions to 2,048
A composite index
quantizedFlat or diskANN, which support up to 4,096 dimensions
A spatial index

questions.explanation: The flat index supports at most 505 dimensions, while quantizedFlat and diskANN support up to 4,096. Reducing to 2,048 still exceeds the flat limit, and composite and spatial indexes don't index vectors.
questions.source_title: Vector search in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

questions.skill_name: Store embeddings and run vector search in Cosmos DB
questions.stem: Which requirement applies to the quantizedFlat and diskANN vector index types in Cosmos DB for NoSQL?

options.text: The container must use serverless capacity
The container must use strong consistency
At least 1,000 vectors must be inserted
Vectors must have exactly 1,536 dimensions

questions.explanation: The documentation states that the quantizedFlat and diskANN indexes require at least 1,000 vectors to be inserted. They support up to 4,096 dimensions, work with any consistency level, and aren't tied to a capacity mode.
questions.source_title: Vector search in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

questions.skill_name: Store embeddings and run vector search in Cosmos DB
questions.stem: Each physical partition of your container will hold about 20,000 vectors, and you want a good balance of recall, latency, and cost. Which vector index type does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: flat
diskANN with vectorIndexShardKey
No vector index; use full scans
quantizedFlat

questions.explanation: quantizedFlat is recommended when roughly 50,000 or fewer vectors are indexed per physical partition (or search scope). diskANN, optionally sharded by partition key, is the choice for larger partitions. flat is exact but limited to 505 dimensions and slow at scale, and full scans cost far more RUs.
questions.source_title: Tips for optimizing vector indexing and search performance

questions.skill_name: Store embeddings and run vector search in Cosmos DB
questions.stem: A multitenant container stores millions of vectors, and queries always filter by tenantId, the partition key. Several tenants have more than 50,000 vectors. Which configuration does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: A quantizedFlat index without any shard key
A diskANN index with vectorIndexShardKey set to the partition key path
A flat index
A separate container per vector

questions.explanation: For larger partitions (more than 50,000 vectors), the performance tips recommend diskANN with vectorIndexShardKey set to the partition key path, so each tenant's vectors get their own index shard and filtered searches stay fast. flat doesn't scale, quantizedFlat is aimed at smaller scopes, and a container per vector is impractical.
questions.source_title: Tips for optimizing vector indexing and search performance

questions.skill_name: Store embeddings and run vector search in Cosmos DB
questions.stem: Inserting documents that contain large embeddings consumes more RUs than expected. The indexing policy includes /* and also defines a diskANN vector index on /embedding. What should you change?

options.text: Remove the vector embedding policy
Switch to strong consistency
Add the vector path /embedding/* to excludedPaths so it isn't also indexed as a regular property
Add a composite index on /embedding

questions.explanation: Microsoft recommends excluding vector paths from the regular included paths, because indexing every array element as a normal property adds significant write cost while the vector index already covers similarity search. Removing the embedding policy breaks vector search, and consistency or composite indexes don't reduce this cost.
questions.source_title: Vector search in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

questions.skill_name: Store embeddings and run vector search in Cosmos DB
questions.stem: Which distance functions can you set in a Cosmos DB vector embedding policy?

options.text: manhattan, hamming, and jaccard
levenshtein and cosine
cosine, dotproduct, and euclidean
cosine only

questions.explanation: The vector embedding policy supports cosine, dot product, and Euclidean distance functions, and the TypeScript quickstart compares rankings produced by all three. The other options list metrics that Cosmos DB vector search doesn't offer.
questions.source_title: Vector search in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

questions.skill_name: Store embeddings and run vector search in Cosmos DB
questions.stem: A small reference dataset has 2,000 vectors of 384 dimensions, and the business requires exact nearest-neighbor results (100 percent recall). Which index type fits?

options.text: diskANN
quantizedFlat
No index; approximate search is always exact
flat

questions.explanation: The flat index performs exact kNN search with 100 percent recall and supports up to 505 dimensions, so 384-dimension vectors fit. quantizedFlat and diskANN compress vectors or use approximate search, trading a little recall for speed. Approximate search isn't exact by definition.
questions.source_title: Tips for optimizing vector indexing and search performance

questions.skill_name: Store embeddings and run vector search in Cosmos DB
questions.stem: Your RAG app must return the 10 most similar support articles, but only those in the product category the user selected. How should you write the query?

options.text: Store the category inside the embedding vector
Create one container per category
Run the vector query for TOP 10, then remove other categories in the client
Combine a WHERE filter with vector ordering: SELECT TOP 10 ... FROM c WHERE c.category = @category ORDER BY VectorDistance(c.embedding, @q)

questions.explanation: Cosmos DB lets you combine regular filters with VectorDistance ordering in the same query, so the top results already respect the metadata filter. Filtering after a TOP 10 can return fewer than 10 relevant results, a container per category is unnecessary, and embeddings can't carry exact metadata filters.
questions.source_title: Vector search in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

questions.skill_name: Store embeddings and run vector search in Cosmos DB
questions.stem: Your embedding model returns 1,536-dimension vectors, but the vector embedding policy declares 768 dimensions. What should you do?

options.text: Truncate every vector to 768 values before inserting it
Make the policy's dimensions match the model's output size
Leave it as it is; dimensions are only a hint
Switch the distance function to dotproduct

questions.explanation: The vector embedding policy defines the dimensions of the vectors at the path, and stored and query vectors must match it and the embedding model. Truncating vectors corrupts their meaning, and the distance function doesn't change the dimension requirement.
questions.source_title: Vector search in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

questions.skill_name: Implement a Cosmos DB change feed processor
questions.stem: Which four components make up the Cosmos DB change feed processor?

options.text: The monitored container, the lease container, the host (compute instance), and the delegate (your code)
The source container, the dead-letter queue, the scheduler, and the trigger
The lease container, a Service Bus queue, a timer, and an estimator
The monitored container, an Event Grid topic, a webhook, and a function

questions.explanation: The change feed processor has a monitored container that generates the change feed, a lease container that stores state and coordinates workers, hosts that run the processor, and a delegate that handles each batch of changes. Dead-letter queues, Event Grid, and Service Bus aren't part of it.
questions.source_title: Java application using the change feed processor

questions.skill_name: Implement a Cosmos DB change feed processor
questions.stem: You run three instances of the same change feed processor to keep up with writes. How should they be configured so they share the work?

options.text: A different processor name on each host
A different lease container on each host
Same processor name and lease container, and a different instance name on each host
Only one instance can run; the others must be standby

questions.explanation: Instances with the same lease configuration (processor name and lease container) form one deployment and split the leases between them, while each instance needs a unique instance name. Different lease containers or processor names would make each instance process every change independently.
questions.source_title: Java application using the change feed processor

questions.skill_name: Implement a Cosmos DB change feed processor
questions.stem: You need two independent jobs to process the same container's change feed: one updates a search index and one sends emails. To save cost you want one lease container. Is that possible?

options.text: No; every processor needs its own lease container
Yes; use a different processor name for each job so their leases don't collide
Yes, but only if both jobs run on the same host
No; a container's change feed can be read by only one processor

questions.explanation: A lease container can be shared as long as each logical job uses its own processor name, so its leases are tracked separately. Several processors can read the same change feed independently, and they don't need to run on the same host.
questions.source_title: Read the Azure Cosmos DB change feed

questions.skill_name: Implement a Cosmos DB change feed processor
questions.stem: You suspect your change feed processor is falling behind the write rate. Which tool measures how far behind it is?

options.text: The Azure Activity log
The change feed estimator, which compares the leases' state with the latest changes
Cosmos DB query metrics
A composite index

questions.explanation: The change feed estimator measures the difference between the last processed item, recorded in the lease container, and the latest change in the monitored container, and reports it to a delegate (push model) or on demand. Query metrics, the Activity log, and indexes don't show processing lag.
questions.source_title: Use the change feed estimator

questions.skill_name: Implement a Cosmos DB change feed processor
questions.stem: You are getting started with the change feed and want the simplest way to run code whenever items are created or modified, with leases handled for you. What does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: A custom polling loop that queries _ts every second
A timer-triggered function that reads the whole container
An Azure Functions Cosmos DB trigger
An Event Grid subscription on the Cosmos DB account

questions.explanation: Azure Functions is described as the simplest option and is recommended for most change feed scenarios; the Cosmos DB trigger uses the change feed processor and a lease container behind the scenes. Polling by _ts and full reads waste RUs, and Event Grid doesn't deliver per-item change feed events.
questions.source_title: Read the Azure Cosmos DB change feed

questions.skill_name: Implement a Cosmos DB change feed processor
questions.stem: You read the change feed with the pull model and want to switch to the change feed processor without reprocessing changes. Can you convert your stored continuation token into a lease?

options.text: No; continuation tokens and leases both act as bookmarks, but they can't be converted into each other
Yes; the SDK converts it automatically on startup
Only if both use the same processor name
Yes; paste the token into the lease container

questions.explanation: The pull model's continuation tokens and the processor's lease container both record the last processed point, but the documentation states you can't convert continuation tokens to a lease or vice versa. Plan the cut-over, for example by starting the processor from a point in time, and make processing idempotent.
questions.source_title: Change feed pull model in Azure Cosmos DB

questions.skill_name: Implement a Cosmos DB change feed processor
questions.stem: A change feed consumer must remove items from a search index when they are deleted in Cosmos DB, but deletes never arrive in the default (latest version) change feed. What is a common solution?

options.text: Use strong consistency
Read the change feed from the beginning every hour
Enable a composite index on _ts
Use a soft-delete flag (for example isDeleted: true) and set a TTL so the item is removed after the consumer sees the update

questions.explanation: The latest version mode of the change feed captures inserts and updates but not deletes. A soft-delete update is captured as a change that the consumer can act on, and TTL then removes the item. Rereading the feed or changing consistency and indexing doesn't surface deletes.
questions.source_title: Read the Azure Cosmos DB change feed

questions.skill_name: Implement a Cosmos DB change feed processor
questions.stem: Your delegate occasionally throws an exception because a downstream API is unavailable. What should you assume about delivery, and how should you write the handler?

options.text: Failed batches are retried, so changes can be delivered more than once; make processing idempotent
Each change is delivered exactly once even if the delegate fails
The processor stops permanently on the first error
Failed changes are moved to a dead-letter queue automatically

questions.explanation: The change feed processor handles errors by retrying changes that weren't processed correctly, so a batch can be seen again and handlers should be idempotent. There's no exactly-once guarantee and no built-in dead-letter queue, and the processor doesn't stop permanently on a single exception.
questions.source_title: Read the Azure Cosmos DB change feed

questions.skill_name: Implement a Cosmos DB change feed processor
questions.stem: Where can the lease container for a change feed processor be located?

options.text: Only in the same database as the monitored container
Only in an Azure Storage account
Only in Azure Table storage
In the same Cosmos DB account as the monitored container or in a separate account

questions.explanation: The lease container stores processor state and coordinates workers, and it can live in the same account as the monitored container or in a different account. It is a Cosmos DB container, not an Azure Storage resource.
questions.source_title: Java application using the change feed processor

questions.skill_name: Implement a Cosmos DB change feed processor
questions.stem: You create an Azure Functions Cosmos DB trigger, but no lease container exists yet. What does the trigger need?

options.text: Nothing; the trigger keeps its state in memory
A Blob container to store leases
A lease container, which you either create yourself or let the trigger create (CreateLeaseContainerIfNotExists)
A Service Bus queue to store checkpoints

questions.explanation: The Cosmos DB trigger is built on the change feed processor and needs a lease container to track progress; you can point it at an existing container or let it create one. Checkpoints aren't stored in Service Bus or Blob storage, and in-memory state would be lost on restart and couldn't coordinate scaled-out instances.
questions.source_title: Azure Cosmos DB trigger and bindings for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Connect and query Azure Database for PostgreSQL with SDKs
questions.stem: A Python app connects to Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server with Microsoft Entra authentication and no stored password. How does it obtain the credential it passes as the password?

options.text: It uses the storage account key of the server
It reads the server admin password from an environment variable
It calls the PostgreSQL REST API to create a temporary password
It uses azure-identity (for example DefaultAzureCredential) to get an access token for Azure Database for PostgreSQL and passes the token as the password

questions.explanation: In the passwordless (recommended) path of the Python quickstart, the azure-identity library acquires a Microsoft Entra access token for Azure Database for PostgreSQL, and the driver sends that token in place of a password. An admin password is exactly what passwordless avoids, and there's no REST API for temporary passwords or any storage key involved.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Use Python to connect to Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Connect and query Azure Database for PostgreSQL with SDKs
questions.stem: An App Service app with a system-assigned managed identity can get an Entra token, but login to Azure Database for PostgreSQL still fails with an authentication error. What is the most likely missing step?

options.text: The server must use port 6432
A database role for the managed identity hasn't been created and granted privileges by a Microsoft Entra administrator of the server
The managed identity needs the Key Vault Secrets User role
The app must also send the admin password

questions.explanation: The managed identity has to exist as a user inside PostgreSQL. A Microsoft Entra admin on the server creates a database user for the identity and grants it privileges; only then can the token be used to log in. Admin passwords aren't combined with tokens, the port is unrelated, and Key Vault roles don't grant database access.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Connect to Azure databases from App Service using a managed identity

questions.skill_name: Connect and query Azure Database for PostgreSQL with SDKs
questions.stem: Microsoft Entra access tokens for Azure Database for PostgreSQL typically expire after about an hour. What happens to a connection that was opened with a token that has since expired?

options.text: The token is checked when the connection opens, so the open connection keeps working, but new connections need a fresh token
Queries on the connection start failing with permission errors
The server automatically refreshes the token for the client
The connection is closed exactly when the token expires

questions.explanation: The token is validated at connection time, so pooled connections that are already open keep working after it expires. Any new connection must present a valid token, which is why clients and pools need a token-refresh callback. The server doesn't refresh client tokens.
questions.source_title: Improve performance using a cache with Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Connect and query Azure Database for PostgreSQL with SDKs
questions.stem: Your Python code builds SQL like f"SELECT * FROM docs WHERE owner = '{user}'" before calling psycopg. What should you change?

options.text: Escape quotes manually in the user string
Use a stored procedure for every query
Pass values as query parameters, for example cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM docs WHERE owner = %s", (user,))
Switch to the pgbouncer port

questions.explanation: psycopg sends parameters separately from the SQL text, which prevents SQL injection and handles quoting and types correctly. Manual escaping is error-prone, the pooler port doesn't affect injection, and stored procedures aren't required to use parameters safely.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Use Python to connect to Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Connect and query Azure Database for PostgreSQL with SDKs
questions.stem: A script inserts rows with psycopg inside a with psycopg.connect(...) block that doesn't call commit, but no rows appear in the table when you check from another session. Why?

options.text: psycopg writes rows to a temporary table first
The transaction was never committed, so the changes weren't made durable or visible
Inserts require port 6432
Azure Database for PostgreSQL delays inserts by one hour

questions.explanation: psycopg opens a transaction implicitly, and changes only become visible to other sessions once committed. Call conn.commit(), use the connection context manager in a way that commits, or enable autocommit. There's no temporary table or delay, and the port doesn't affect commits.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Use Python to connect to Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Connect and query Azure Database for PostgreSQL with SDKs
questions.stem: A Spring Boot app on Azure must connect to Azure Database for PostgreSQL with a managed identity instead of a password, using Spring Cloud Azure. Which application property enables this?

options.text: spring.datasource.password=managed-identity
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
spring.datasource.azure.passwordless-enabled=true
server.port=6432

questions.explanation: With Spring Cloud Azure, setting spring.datasource.azure.passwordless-enabled to true makes the JDBC connection acquire Entra tokens for the configured identity; Service Connector uses this property for system- and user-assigned identities. A literal password string doesn't work, and the JPA and server port properties are unrelated.
questions.source_title: Integrate Azure Database for PostgreSQL with Service Connector

questions.skill_name: Connect and query Azure Database for PostgreSQL with SDKs
questions.stem: What is the default port for connecting directly to an Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, and which port is used for its built-in connection pooler?

options.text: 5432 for direct connections and 6432 for PgBouncer
1433 for both
443 for both
6432 for direct connections and 5432 for PgBouncer

questions.explanation: Clients connect to PostgreSQL on port 5432, and the built-in PgBouncer listens on port 6432 on the same host name. 1433 is SQL Server's port, and 443 is HTTPS.
questions.source_title: PgBouncer in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Connect and query Azure Database for PostgreSQL with SDKs
questions.stem: Which SSL setting does the Python quickstart use in the connection string for Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server?

options.text: sslmode=require
sslmode=disable
sslmode=allow with a self-signed certificate on the client
ssl=false

questions.explanation: Connections to Azure Database for PostgreSQL are encrypted with TLS, and the quickstart sets sslmode=require. Disabling SSL breaks connections to servers that enforce secure transport and exposes credentials, including tokens.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Use Python to connect to Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Connect and query Azure Database for PostgreSQL with SDKs
questions.stem: You are writing a .NET app that connects to Azure Database for PostgreSQL with Npgsql and a user-assigned managed identity. How do you select that identity with DefaultAzureCredential?

options.text: Set the server parameter azure.extensions to the identity name
Set ManagedIdentityClientId to the identity's client ID in DefaultAzureCredentialOptions
Nothing; DefaultAzureCredential always uses user-assigned identities first
Add the identity's object ID to the connection string as Password

questions.explanation: For a user-assigned identity, DefaultAzureCredential needs the identity's client ID (ManagedIdentityClientId); otherwise it uses the system-assigned identity. The token, not an object ID, is the password, and azure.extensions controls allowed PostgreSQL extensions.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Connect to Azure databases from App Service using a managed identity

questions.skill_name: Model PostgreSQL schemas and choose data types
questions.stem: You run CREATE EXTENSION pgvector; on Azure Database for PostgreSQL and it fails. What is the correct extension name?

options.text: azure_vector
pgvector
vector
pg_vector

questions.explanation: Although the community calls it pgvector, the binary and the extension are named vector, and that name is used both to allowlist it and in CREATE EXTENSION vector.
questions.source_title: Enable and use pgvector in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Model PostgreSQL schemas and choose data types
questions.stem: Before you can create the vector extension in a database on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, what must you do?

options.text: Open a support ticket to enable the extension
Add vector to the allowlist in the azure.extensions server parameter, then run CREATE EXTENSION in each database that needs it
Restart the server in single-user mode
Install the extension binaries with apt-get

questions.explanation: Extensions are allowlisted at the server level with the azure.extensions parameter (check with SHOW azure.extensions;), and then created separately in every database where they are used. It is a managed service, so you don't install binaries or need support tickets.
questions.source_title: Enable and use pgvector in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Model PostgreSQL schemas and choose data types
questions.stem: You define a column as embedding vector and try to create an HNSW index on it. The command fails with "column does not have dimensions". How should the column be defined?

options.text: With an explicit dimension, for example embedding vector(1536)
As embedding text
As embedding jsonb
As embedding float8[]

questions.explanation: pgvector can only index columns whose dimensions are declared, such as vector(1536); a bare vector column can't be indexed. Arrays, JSON, and text columns can't be used with pgvector operators or indexes.
questions.source_title: Optimize performance when using pgvector

questions.skill_name: Model PostgreSQL schemas and choose data types
questions.stem: Your semantic search must search both product titles and product descriptions. How does the Azure tutorial model the data?

options.text: Store embeddings in a separate database
Store a single embedding of the whole row in a JSON column
Create a separate vector column for each data field involved in the search and store each field's embedding there
Concatenate all vectors into one text column

questions.explanation: The tutorial identifies the fields used in search and, for each one, creates a corresponding vector field holding that field's embedding, then searches the vector field and lists the nearest neighbors. JSON or text columns can't be indexed by pgvector, and a separate database complicates joins with the source data.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Create a semantic search with Azure Database for PostgreSQL and Azure OpenAI

questions.skill_name: Model PostgreSQL schemas and choose data types
questions.stem: You want to fill an embedding column from text already stored in the database without writing an external batch job. Which feature can do this inside Azure Database for PostgreSQL?

options.text: The azure_ai extension's azure_openai schema, which can call Azure OpenAI to create embeddings from SQL
The pg_cron extension alone
PgBouncer
The pg_stat_statements extension

questions.explanation: The azure_ai extension lets you generate embeddings with Azure OpenAI directly from SQL (for example in an UPDATE that sets the vector column), while pgvector stores and searches them. pg_stat_statements tracks query statistics, PgBouncer pools connections, and pg_cron only schedules jobs.
questions.source_title: Integrate Azure AI capabilities into Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Model PostgreSQL schemas and choose data types
questions.stem: You want to use DiskANN indexes on Azure Database for PostgreSQL, but you haven't created the vector extension yet. Which statement creates everything you need in one step?

options.text: CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_diskann CASCADE;
ALTER SYSTEM SET azure.extensions = 'diskann';
CREATE INDEX USING diskann;
CREATE EXTENSION diskann;

questions.explanation: pg_diskann depends on the vector extension, and CASCADE automatically creates the dependency in the same database. Both extensions must also be allowed at the server level. diskann isn't the extension's name, CREATE INDEX needs the extension first, and server parameters are changed through Azure, not ALTER SYSTEM.
questions.source_title: Enable and use DiskANN in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Model PostgreSQL schemas and choose data types
questions.stem: Most vector queries search only the last 30 days of documents. Which schema design helps the planner touch only relevant data?

options.text: Partition the table by date range and create the vector index on the partitioned table so each partition gets its own index
Use a single unpartitioned table with no date column
Add a text column with the month name
Store each month in a separate database

questions.explanation: The pgvector performance guide shows range partitioning by date: the planner prunes irrelevant partitions, and an index created on the partitioned table is built per partition (visible as a Merge Append in the plan). A month-name column doesn't enable pruning, and separate databases make queries much harder.
questions.source_title: Optimize performance when using pgvector

questions.skill_name: Model PostgreSQL schemas and choose data types
questions.stem: Your embedding model outputs 3,072 dimensions. What happens if you store them in a vector(3072) column and plan to use HNSW or IVFFlat?

options.text: HNSW automatically reduces the vectors to 2,000 dimensions
The insert fails because vector supports at most 1,024 dimensions
The vectors can be stored, but IVFFlat and HNSW indexes support at most 2,000 dimensions, so the column can't be indexed with them
IVFFlat supports up to 16,000 dimensions

questions.explanation: pgvector lets you store higher-dimensional vectors, but IVFFlat and HNSW indexes are limited to 2,000 dimensions, so indexing fails with an error naming the index type. Options include choosing a model or setting that outputs fewer dimensions. Indexes never reduce dimensions automatically.
questions.source_title: Optimize performance when using pgvector

questions.skill_name: Model PostgreSQL schemas and choose data types
questions.stem: Which pgvector operator returns the cosine distance between two vectors?
questions.explanation: In pgvector, <=> is cosine distance, <-> is Euclidean (L2) distance, and <#> is negative inner product. @> is PostgreSQL's containment operator for arrays and JSON, not a vector distance.
questions.source_title: Enable and use pgvector in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL indexing strategies and pgvector overhead
questions.stem: You are creating an IVFFlat index on a table with 500,000 rows. What value of lists does the Azure guidance suggest as a starting point?

options.text: About 500 (rows / 1000)
500,000 (one list per row)
About 707 (the square root of rows)
1 (the default)

questions.explanation: For tables up to 1 million rows, the guide suggests lists = rows / 1000; for larger tables, sqrt(rows). 500,000 / 1,000 = 500. One list per row defeats the purpose of clustering, and the square-root rule applies above 1 million rows.
questions.source_title: Optimize performance when using pgvector

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL indexing strategies and pgvector overhead
questions.stem: An IVFFlat index returns poor recall. You want more accurate results for one transaction only, without changing the setting for other sessions. What should you run?

options.text: SET hnsw.ef_search = 100;
SET LOCAL ivfflat.probes = 10; inside the transaction
ALTER INDEX ... SET (lists = 1)
REINDEX the table every query

questions.explanation: probes controls how many lists are searched; the default is 1, and more probes give better recall at higher cost. SET LOCAL applies the change only to the current transaction, while plain SET applies it to the connection. lists is fixed at build time, ef_search is an HNSW parameter, and reindexing doesn't improve recall.
questions.source_title: Optimize performance when using pgvector

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL indexing strategies and pgvector overhead
questions.stem: You set ivfflat.probes equal to the index's lists value, and EXPLAIN now shows a sequential scan. Why?

options.text: Sequential scans are always faster for vectors
The index became corrupted
probes can't exceed 10
Searching all lists is an exact search, so the planner doesn't use the index

questions.explanation: When probes equals the number of lists, every list is searched, which makes the search exact, so the guide notes the planner won't use the index. Nothing is corrupted, there's no probes limit of 10, and for large tables an index scan is usually faster for approximate search.
questions.source_title: Optimize performance when using pgvector

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL indexing strategies and pgvector overhead
questions.stem: What are the default HNSW parameters in pgvector, according to the Azure performance guide?

options.text: lists = 100 and probes = 1
m = 8, ef_construction = 16, and hnsw.ef_search = 100
m = 16, ef_construction = 64, and hnsw.ef_search = 40
m = 32, ef_construction = 100, and hnsw.ef_search = 10

questions.explanation: HNSW defaults are m = 16 (maximum connections per layer), ef_construction = 64 (candidate list size during build), and hnsw.ef_search = 40 (candidate list size at query time). lists and probes are IVFFlat parameters.
questions.source_title: Optimize performance when using pgvector

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL indexing strategies and pgvector overhead
questions.stem: HNSW search results are fast but miss some relevant documents. Which change improves recall at query time without rebuilding the index?

options.text: Increase hnsw.ef_search, for example SET hnsw.ef_search = 100
Decrease m
Increase ivfflat.probes
Drop the index and use a sequential scan in production

questions.explanation: hnsw.ef_search sets how many candidates are considered at query time; raising it improves recall at some latency cost and can be changed per session. m is a build-time parameter, probes only applies to IVFFlat, and sequential scans are exact but slow at scale.
questions.source_title: Optimize performance when using pgvector

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL indexing strategies and pgvector overhead
questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares pgvector index types on Azure Database for PostgreSQL?

options.text: HNSW builds faster and uses less memory than IVFFlat
IVFFlat builds faster and uses less memory than HNSW but has a worse speed-recall trade-off, while DiskANN balances accuracy and fast builds
DiskANN only supports exact search
IVFFlat has the best recall of the three

questions.explanation: According to the Azure guide, IVFFlat has faster build times and lower memory use than HNSW but lower query performance for a given recall, and DiskANN offers a good balance of highly accurate queries and fast build times. DiskANN is an approximate nearest neighbor algorithm, not exact search.
questions.source_title: Optimize performance when using pgvector

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL indexing strategies and pgvector overhead
questions.stem: You are loading 2 million embeddings into a new table. When should you create the IVFFlat index?

options.text: Halfway through the load
Never; IVFFlat indexes build themselves
After loading the data, because the build is faster and the resulting layout is better
Before loading, so every insert updates the index

questions.explanation: The guide recommends loading data before indexing whenever possible. For IVFFlat in particular, the lists are computed from the existing data with k-means, so building on an empty table produces poor clusters. Inserting into an existing index is also slower.
questions.source_title: Optimize performance when using pgvector

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL indexing strategies and pgvector overhead
questions.stem: You created CREATE INDEX ON docs USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops). Queries use ORDER BY embedding <-> :q LIMIT 10 and do a sequential scan. Why?

options.text: The index operator class (cosine) doesn't match the query operator (<-> is Euclidean distance); use <=> or build the index with vector_l2_ops
HNSW indexes can't be used with LIMIT
Cosine indexes only work with halfvec
The table needs to be vacuumed first

questions.explanation: An index is only used when the query's distance operator matches the operator class: vector_cosine_ops serves <=>, vector_l2_ops serves <->, and vector_ip_ops serves <#>. LIMIT is the normal pattern for nearest-neighbor queries, and vacuuming doesn't change operator matching.

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL indexing strategies and pgvector overhead
questions.stem: A partial IVFFlat index was created with WHERE tier = 'premium'. A query filters WHERE tier LIKE 'premium' and doesn't use the index. Why?

options.text: LIKE disables all indexes in PostgreSQL
The query's predicate must match the partial index's predicate form; LIKE doesn't match the = condition
Partial indexes don't work with vectors
The index must be rebuilt after every insert

questions.explanation: The planner uses a partial index only when it can prove the query's WHERE clause implies the index predicate. The guide's example shows WHERE tier = 'premium' using the index and WHERE tier LIKE 'premium' not using it. Partial vector indexes are a valid filtering strategy.

questions.stem: A DiskANN index build is taking a long time on a large table. How can you monitor its progress?

options.text: Check the PgBouncer log
Query pg_stat_progress_create_index
Query pg_stat_statements
Run SHOW azure.extensions

questions.explanation: On PostgreSQL 12 and later, pg_stat_progress_create_index reports index build phases; for HNSW and DiskANN they are initializing and loading tuples. pg_stat_statements records query statistics, azure.extensions lists allowed extensions, and PgBouncer doesn't build indexes.

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL indexing strategies and pgvector overhead
questions.stem: Your OpenAI embeddings are normalized to length 1. Which distance operator does the Azure guide recommend for the best performance?

options.text: Inner product (<#>)
Cosine distance (<=>) is always faster
Manhattan distance
Euclidean distance (<->)

questions.explanation: For vectors normalized to length 1, inner product gives the same ranking as cosine similarity and is cheaper to compute, so the guide recommends <#> (with an inner-product operator class). Euclidean distance also ranks the same but isn't the recommended choice, and pgvector has no Manhattan distance operator.

questions.stem: Which DiskANN index parameters and defaults are correct on Azure Database for PostgreSQL?

options.text: lists (default 100) and probes (default 1)
max_neighbors (default 1,000) only
m (default 16) and ef_construction (default 64)
max_neighbors (default 32) and l_value_ib (default 50) at build time, and diskann.l_value_is at query time

questions.explanation: pg_diskann indexes take max_neighbors (default 32) and l_value_ib, the build-time search list size (default 50), and you tune query-time search with diskann.l_value_is. lists and probes belong to IVFFlat, and m and ef_construction belong to HNSW.

questions.skill_name: Configure PostgreSQL compute, memory, and storage for vectors
questions.stem: Creating an HNSW index on millions of rows is slow. Which server parameter governs the memory used by CREATE INDEX, and what is its maximum on flexible server?

options.text: maintenance_work_mem, which can be set up to 2 GB
max_connections, which must be raised
work_mem, which can be set up to 64 GB
shared_buffers, which must be lowered

questions.explanation: maintenance_work_mem sets the memory for maintenance operations such as VACUUM, CREATE INDEX, and ALTER TABLE, and the bulk-load guidance notes it can be set to a maximum of 2 GB on flexible server. work_mem applies to query operations like sorts and hashes, and the other two parameters don't speed up an index build.

questions.skill_name: Configure PostgreSQL compute, memory, and storage for vectors
questions.stem: You want CREATE INDEX on a large table to use several CPU cores. Which parameter controls the number of worker processes for index builds?

options.text: autovacuum_max_workers
max_parallel_maintenance_workers
max_worker_processes is the only parameter involved
max_parallel_workers_per_gather

questions.explanation: max_parallel_maintenance_workers controls how many parallel workers CREATE INDEX can use, as described in the bulk-load guidance. max_parallel_workers_per_gather is for parallel query execution, and autovacuum workers handle vacuuming. max_worker_processes is an overall ceiling, not the specific control.

questions.skill_name: Configure PostgreSQL compute, memory, and storage for vectors
questions.stem: A server with many concurrent vector queries runs out of memory. Which server parameters does Microsoft list as having a direct impact on memory consumption?

options.text: azure.extensions and timezone
ssl_min_protocol_version
work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, and shared_buffers
log_min_duration_statement and log_line_prefix

questions.explanation: The high memory utilization guide lists work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, and shared_buffers as parameters whose configuration affects memory consumption. Extension, time zone, logging, and TLS settings don't drive memory usage in the same way.

questions.skill_name: Configure PostgreSQL compute, memory, and storage for vectors
questions.stem: You scaled a flexible server to a larger compute size and noticed that the default value of maintenance_work_mem increased. Why?

options.text: The value is copied from the client's connection string
Its default is calculated from the memory allocated to the server, so it changes when you change the compute size
maintenance_work_mem always doubles after a restart
Azure resets all parameters to random values after scaling

questions.explanation: On flexible server, the default maintenance_work_mem depends on the resources allocated to the server and is computed from its memory with a documented formula. Scaling changes the memory, so the default changes. Parameters aren't randomized, and clients can't set server defaults through connection strings.
questions.source_title: Resource usage / memory server parameters

questions.skill_name: Configure PostgreSQL compute, memory, and storage for vectors
questions.stem: An exact (non-indexed) vector search over a moderately sized table is slow, and EXPLAIN shows few parallel workers. Which parameter can you raise so the planner may use more workers per Gather node?

options.text: ivfflat.probes
max_parallel_workers_per_gather
maintenance_work_mem
pgbouncer.default_pool_size

questions.explanation: The pgvector guide explains that max_parallel_workers_per_gather limits workers per Gather node, and raising it can speed up exact searches, although the planner may still decide not to parallelize. maintenance_work_mem affects index builds, probes affects IVFFlat searches, and pool size affects PgBouncer.

questions.skill_name: Configure PostgreSQL compute, memory, and storage for vectors
questions.stem: You will load 50 million rows with embeddings into a new table that will have an HNSW index and foreign keys. Which sequence does Microsoft recommend for the initial load?

options.text: Disable maintenance_work_mem during the load
Create all indexes first so that inserts are validated
Load the data first, then create indexes and constraints with a high maintenance_work_mem
Load through PgBouncer with session pooling

questions.explanation: For initial loads, the guidance is to drop or postpone indexes and constraints, load the data, and then re-create them using a high maintenance_work_mem, which speeds up index and foreign key creation. Building indexes first slows every insert, and the pooling mode doesn't change load efficiency.
questions.source_title: Best practices to bulk upload data to Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Configure PostgreSQL compute, memory, and storage for vectors
questions.stem: A team sets work_mem to 1 GB to speed up a reporting query. Shortly after, the server runs out of memory under normal load. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: work_mem is allocated per sort or hash operation in each connection, so many concurrent connections can multiply it far beyond available memory
work_mem is shared by all connections, so 1 GB is too small
The server ignores work_mem above 64 MB
work_mem only affects index builds

questions.explanation: work_mem applies to each sort or hash operation in each session, so total usage can reach many times the setting when many connections run queries at once. That's why the high-memory guide lists it as a key parameter to review. It isn't shared, it isn't specific to index builds (that's maintenance_work_mem), and it isn't silently capped at 64 MB.
questions.source_title: Troubleshoot high memory utilization in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Configure PostgreSQL compute, memory, and storage for vectors
questions.stem: A serverless API opens hundreds of short-lived connections to Azure Database for PostgreSQL, and memory and CPU are high even though queries are simple. What does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: Increase work_mem
Move the database to a larger region
Increase max_connections to the maximum allowed
Use connection pooling, for example the built-in PgBouncer, to reduce the number of backend connections

questions.explanation: Each PostgreSQL connection is a backend process with its own memory, so connection churn and many idle connections waste resources. PgBouncer uses real server connections only while a transaction or query is active and can handle up to 10,000 client connections with low overhead. Raising max_connections or work_mem makes memory pressure worse.

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL vector search and RAG with metadata filters
questions.stem: A table docs has an embedding vector(1536) column. Which query returns the five documents most similar to a query vector :q by cosine distance?

options.text: SELECT id, title FROM docs ORDER BY embedding <=> :q LIMIT 5
SELECT id, title FROM docs WHERE embedding = :q LIMIT 5
SELECT id, title FROM docs GROUP BY embedding LIMIT 5
SELECT id, title FROM docs ORDER BY embedding DESC LIMIT 5

questions.explanation: Nearest-neighbor search in pgvector orders by a distance operator and limits the result: <=> is cosine distance, and smaller distances are more similar. Equality would only match identical vectors, and ordering or grouping by the raw vector has no similarity meaning.
questions.source_title: Enable and use pgvector in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL vector search and RAG with metadata filters
questions.stem: You want every row whose Euclidean distance to a query vector is less than 6, rather than a fixed top-k. Which query is correct?

options.text: SELECT * FROM items WHERE embedding <#> '[3,1,2]' = 6
SELECT * FROM items WHERE vector_dims(embedding) < 6
SELECT * FROM items WHERE embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' < 6
SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding <=> '[3,1,2]' LIMIT 6

questions.explanation: pgvector distance operators return numbers, so you can filter on them; <-> is Euclidean (L2) distance, and the documentation shows exactly this threshold pattern. LIMIT 6 returns six rows regardless of distance, <#> is negative inner product, and vector_dims returns the number of dimensions.
questions.source_title: Enable and use pgvector in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL vector search and RAG with metadata filters
questions.stem: Your search returns the 10 nearest products, but only products in the user's chosen category should be returned. How should you write the query in PostgreSQL?

options.text: Add the metadata filter in the WHERE clause together with the ORDER BY distance and LIMIT, for example WHERE category = $1 ORDER BY embedding <=> $2 LIMIT 10
Store the category inside the embedding
Create a separate database for each category
Run the vector search for 10 rows first and remove other categories in the application

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL lets you combine relational filters with vector ordering in one query, so the database applies the metadata filter as part of retrieval. Filtering after a top-10 search can leave fewer than 10 relevant rows. Embeddings can't encode exact metadata, and a database per category is unnecessary; partial indexes or partitioning can make frequent filters fast.
questions.source_title: Optimize performance when using pgvector

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL vector search and RAG with metadata filters
questions.stem: Stored embeddings were generated with text-embedding-3-small. Search quality is poor, and you discover the search API embeds user queries with a different model. What should you do?

options.text: Normalize only the stored vectors
Increase hnsw.ef_search
Generate query embeddings with the same model (and dimensions) used for the stored embeddings
Switch the distance operator from cosine to Euclidean

questions.explanation: Similarity is only meaningful when stored and query vectors come from the same embedding model and dimension space, which is why the semantic search tutorial generates the query embedding the same way as the data embeddings. Changing the operator, search breadth, or normalization doesn't fix vectors from different models.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Create a semantic search with Azure Database for PostgreSQL and Azure OpenAI

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL vector search and RAG with metadata filters
questions.stem: You want a single SQL statement that embeds the user's search text with Azure OpenAI and returns the nearest rows, without an application round trip for the embedding. Which approach works on Azure Database for PostgreSQL?

options.text: Use PgBouncer to generate the embedding
Use azure_openai.create_embeddings from the azure_ai extension inside the ORDER BY expression, cast to vector
Store the search text and run LIKE '%text%'
Call Azure OpenAI from a PL/pgSQL HTTP request with pg_net

questions.explanation: The azure_ai extension exposes azure_openai.create_embeddings, so a query can embed the input text and order by distance to the stored vectors in one statement, as shown in the semantic search tutorial. PgBouncer only pools connections, and LIKE is keyword matching, not semantic similarity.
