questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL vector search and RAG with metadata filters
questions.stem: A cosine distance query returns a distance of 0.18 between two embeddings. What is their cosine similarity?

options.text: 5.56, the inverse of the distance
0.82, because cosine similarity = 1 - cosine distance
0.18, because distance and similarity are the same

questions.explanation: pgvector's <=> operator returns cosine distance, which is 1 minus cosine similarity. A distance of 0.18 means a similarity of 0.82; smaller distances mean more similar vectors.
questions.source_title: Enable and use pgvector in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL vector search and RAG with metadata filters
questions.stem: Your app already keeps its relational data in Azure Database for PostgreSQL, and you want to add semantic search with the fewest new services. What is the natural choice?

options.text: Store embeddings in Blob storage and scan them from the app
Enable pgvector (and optionally pg_diskann) in the existing database and store embeddings next to the data
Copy all data into a separate search service before you can use embeddings
Use Azure Managed Redis as the system of record for the documents

questions.explanation: Azure Database for PostgreSQL supports built-in vector search through pgvector, with pg_diskann for scalable ANN indexing, so embeddings can live in the same tables and queries can join and filter on existing data. A separate search service or Blob scans add complexity, and Redis is a cache, not a system of record for documents.
questions.source_title: Choose an Azure service for vector search

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL vector search and RAG with metadata filters
questions.stem: To recommend items, you want the centroid (average vector) of all embeddings of items a user liked. Which pgvector feature returns it directly?

options.text: vector_norms(embedding)
l2_distance(embedding, embedding)
COUNT(embedding)
The AVG(embedding) aggregate, which returns a vector

questions.explanation: pgvector supports aggregates such as AVG and SUM on vector columns, and they return a vector. vector_norms returns a vector's Euclidean norm, l2_distance returns a number, and COUNT returns the row count.
questions.source_title: Enable and use pgvector in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL vector search and RAG with metadata filters
questions.stem: After a model change, some inserts fail and you suspect stored vectors have the wrong number of dimensions. Which function checks a vector's dimension count?

options.text: vector_dims(embedding)
cosine_distance(embedding, embedding)
vector_norms(embedding)
array_length(embedding)

questions.explanation: vector_dims returns the number of dimensions of a pgvector value, so you can find rows that don't match the expected size. vector_norms returns the vector's length, and cosine_distance of a vector with itself is 0. array_length works on PostgreSQL arrays, not the vector type.
questions.source_title: Enable and use pgvector in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL vector search and RAG with metadata filters
questions.stem: You use pgvector's <#> operator with normalized embeddings. Why does ORDER BY embedding <#> :q (ascending) return the most similar rows first?

options.text: <#> returns Euclidean distance
Ascending order always returns the least similar rows first
<#> returns cosine similarity
<#> returns the negative inner product, so larger inner products (more similar) produce smaller values

questions.explanation: pgvector's <#> operator returns the negative inner product, so the most similar vectors have the most negative values and sort first in ascending order. This keeps the ORDER BY ... LIMIT pattern consistent with the other distance operators. <=> is cosine distance and <-> is Euclidean distance.
questions.source_title: Enable and use pgvector in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL vector search and RAG with metadata filters
questions.stem: In a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app backed by PostgreSQL, what is the database's role when the user asks a question?

options.text: Generate the final answer text
Store the model weights
Fine-tune the language model on each question
Retrieve the most relevant chunks by vector similarity (plus metadata filters), which the app then adds to the prompt sent to the language model

questions.explanation: In RAG, the question is embedded, the vector store returns the nearest relevant content, often filtered by metadata such as tenant or category, and that content grounds the model's answer. The database doesn't generate answers, fine-tune models, or host model weights.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Create a semantic search with Azure Database for PostgreSQL and Azure OpenAI

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL connection optimization
questions.stem: You want to start using the built-in PgBouncer on an Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server. What do you need to do?

options.text: Create a new server with a different host name
Enable PgBouncer on the server (the pgbouncer.enabled server parameter) and point the app at port 6432 on the same host name
Change the app to port 5433
Install PgBouncer on a separate VM

questions.explanation: PgBouncer is an optional, built-in feature that you enable per server, after which clients connect to the same host name on port 6432 instead of 5432. No separate VM or server is needed, and 5433 isn't the PgBouncer port.
questions.source_title: PgBouncer in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL connection optimization
questions.stem: You try to enable the built-in PgBouncer on a Burstable tier server and can't. Which compute tiers support it?

options.text: All tiers, including Burstable
Burstable only
Memory Optimized only
General Purpose and Memory Optimized

questions.explanation: The PgBouncer documentation states that the built-in PgBouncer is supported on the General Purpose and Memory Optimized compute tiers, in both public and private access networks. To use it, scale the server out of the Burstable tier.
questions.source_title: PgBouncer in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL connection optimization
questions.stem: Why can the built-in PgBouncer serve up to 10,000 client connections with low overhead?

options.text: It spreads connections across several databases
It closes idle clients every second
It uses a real PostgreSQL connection only while a transaction is open or a query is active, and shares server connections between clients
It caches all query results in memory

questions.explanation: PgBouncer's lightweight, asynchronous model uses PostgreSQL connections only when needed, inside an open transaction or while a query runs, so many client connections share a small number of server connections. It doesn't cache results or distribute queries across databases.
questions.source_title: PgBouncer in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL connection optimization
questions.stem: An API opens a new PostgreSQL connection for every HTTP request and closes it afterward. Latency is high because of connection setup. What should you do in the application?

options.text: Use a client-side connection pool (for example psycopg_pool or HikariCP) so connections are reused, optionally in front of PgBouncer
Use a larger embedding model
Increase work_mem
Open a new connection twice per request to warm it up

questions.explanation: Each new connection pays for TCP, TLS, and authentication, and PostgreSQL starts a backend process for it. Reusing pooled connections removes that overhead, and PgBouncer is especially useful when connection churn is frequent. work_mem and the embedding model don't affect connection setup.
questions.source_title: PgBouncer in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL connection optimization
questions.stem: After moving to PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode, a feature that relies on session-level state starts behaving unpredictably. Which code is most likely affected?

options.text: INSERT statements in autocommit mode
Code that sets session variables with SET or uses temporary tables and expects them on later transactions
Simple single-statement SELECT queries
Queries that use parameters

questions.explanation: In transaction pooling, a client gets a server connection only for the length of a transaction, so later transactions may run on a different backend. Session state such as SET values, temporary tables, or session-level advisory locks isn't guaranteed to persist. Stateless statements and parameterized queries work normally.
questions.source_title: PgBouncer in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL connection optimization
questions.stem: A Python service keeps a pool of PostgreSQL connections and authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID. New connections start failing about an hour after startup. Which Microsoft library is designed to handle this with psycopg?

options.text: azure-postgresql-auth, which provides Entra authentication with automatic token management and connection pooling for psycopg2, psycopg3, and SQLAlchemy
azure-keyvault-secrets
azure-monitor-opentelemetry
azure-storage-blob

questions.explanation: Entra tokens expire (typically after about an hour), so new pooled connections need fresh tokens. The Azure PostgreSQL Auth client library for Python provides Entra ID authentication with automatic token management and connection pooling for psycopg2, psycopg3, and SQLAlchemy. The other libraries serve Blob storage, Key Vault, and telemetry.
questions.source_title: Azure PostgreSQL Auth client library for Python

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL connection optimization
questions.stem: The same product-detail queries hit Azure Database for PostgreSQL thousands of times per minute, and the data changes rarely. Which architecture reduces database load the most?

options.text: Enable strong consistency
Cache-aside with Azure Managed Redis: read from Redis first and query PostgreSQL only on a cache miss
Increase max_connections
Add more IVFFlat lists

questions.explanation: Microsoft's caching guidance for PostgreSQL implements cache-aside with Azure Managed Redis so repeated reads are served from memory and PostgreSQL only handles misses. More connections add load, IVFFlat lists only affect vector indexes, and strong consistency is a Cosmos DB concept.
questions.source_title: Improve performance using a cache with Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: PostgreSQL connection optimization
questions.stem: Twenty instances of a web app each keep a client-side pool of up to 50 PostgreSQL connections. After scaling out, new connections fail because the server's connection limit is reached. What is the best fix?

options.text: Route the app through PgBouncer (port 6432) and size the per-instance pools so instances × pool size stays well within limits
Create a vector index
Increase work_mem
Remove client-side pooling and open a connection per query

questions.explanation: Client-side pools multiply with the number of instances: 20 × 50 means up to 1,000 backend connections. PgBouncer lets many client connections share a small number of server connections, and right-sizing pools keeps the total under control. work_mem and vector indexes don't affect connection limits, and opening a connection per query increases churn.
questions.source_title: PgBouncer in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Azure Managed Redis caching, expiration, and invalidation
questions.stem: You implement the cache-aside pattern with Azure Managed Redis in front of a database. What happens on a cache miss?

options.text: The app reads the item from the database, writes it to Redis (usually with an expiration), and returns it
Redis automatically loads the item from the database
The app writes a placeholder value and returns nothing
The request fails until a background job fills the cache

questions.explanation: In cache-aside, the application owns the logic: try the cache, and on a miss load from the system of record, store the value in the cache, and return it. Redis doesn't know about your database and doesn't load data on its own.
questions.source_title: Caching guidance

questions.skill_name: Azure Managed Redis caching, expiration, and invalidation
questions.stem: Cached product prices must never be more than 10 minutes out of date, even if an invalidation message is lost. What should you do when writing them to Redis?

options.text: Store prices without a TTL and refresh them weekly
Set an expiration (TTL) of 10 minutes on each key, for example SET key value EX 600
Use NoEviction so values stay forever
Use a longer key name

questions.explanation: An expiration bounds how long a stale value can survive, so the next read after it expires reloads fresh data. NoEviction controls what happens when memory is full, not freshness, and keys without a TTL can stay stale indefinitely.
questions.source_title: Caching guidance

questions.skill_name: Azure Managed Redis caching, expiration, and invalidation
questions.stem: When a product is updated in the database, readers must see the new price quickly. Which cache-aside step should the update path perform?

options.text: Flush the entire cache on every update
Update the database and then delete (invalidate) the product's cache key so the next read reloads it
Do nothing; TTL alone guarantees immediate consistency
Update only the cache and let the database catch up later

questions.explanation: Removing the key after updating the system of record forces the next read to fetch the current value, which is the usual cache-aside invalidation step. Writing only to the cache risks losing data, flushing everything causes a stampede of misses, and TTL only bounds staleness rather than removing it immediately.
questions.source_title: Caching guidance

questions.skill_name: Azure Managed Redis caching, expiration, and invalidation
questions.stem: Which authentication method does Microsoft recommend for applications connecting to Azure Managed Redis?

options.text: Microsoft Entra ID (for example a managed identity), which new caches use by default
Access keys stored in app settings
A shared password embedded in the container image
Anonymous access over a private endpoint

questions.explanation: Azure Managed Redis uses Microsoft Entra ID by default for new caches, and Microsoft recommends it over access keys because keys bring password management and security risks. Anonymous access and embedded passwords aren't acceptable for production.
questions.source_title: Use Microsoft Entra ID for cache authentication with Azure Managed Redis

questions.skill_name: Azure Managed Redis caching, expiration, and invalidation
questions.stem: A client authenticates to Azure Managed Redis with Microsoft Entra tokens. Connections drop roughly every hour. What does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: Disable TLS
Switch to access keys
Have the client send a new token at least three minutes before the current one expires
Restart the cache every hour

questions.explanation: Entra tokens expire, and the guidance is to send a new token at least three minutes before expiry to avoid connection disruption; Microsoft's client extensions handle this automatically. Access keys are less secure, disabling TLS weakens security, and restarting the cache causes outages.
questions.source_title: Use Microsoft Entra ID for cache authentication with Azure Managed Redis

questions.skill_name: Azure Managed Redis caching, expiration, and invalidation
questions.stem: Your team uses a Redis client library that doesn't support the Redis Cluster API, and you need a sharded Azure Managed Redis cache. Which clustering policy should you choose?

options.text: Non-clustered, because it supports sharding
Any policy; it can be changed later
OSS, because it works with any client
Enterprise, because clients connect to a single endpoint and a proxy routes requests to shards

questions.explanation: With the Enterprise policy, clients use one endpoint and an internal proxy routes requests to shards, so any standard Redis client works. The OSS policy requires cluster-aware clients but can give lower latency through direct shard connections, and non-clustered isn't sharded. The clustering policy can't be changed after the cache is created.
questions.source_title: Choose a clustering policy for Azure Managed Redis

questions.skill_name: Azure Managed Redis caching, expiration, and invalidation
questions.stem: In a cache-aside architecture with Azure Managed Redis and Azure Database for PostgreSQL, which statement about Redis is correct?

options.text: Redis automatically replicates every write back to PostgreSQL
Redis data must never expire
Redis holds values the app can re-create from PostgreSQL; it isn't the system of record
Redis is the system of record, and PostgreSQL is the backup

questions.explanation: In the reference architecture, Managed Redis stores frequently requested values and query results that can be rebuilt from PostgreSQL, which remains the system of record. Redis doesn't write data back to PostgreSQL by itself, and expirations are normal for cached data.
questions.source_title: Cache-aside caching using Azure Managed Redis and Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.skill_name: Azure Managed Redis caching, expiration, and invalidation
questions.stem: A .NET app uses StackExchange.Redis and fails with AuthenticationFailure after a developer pasted an Entra access token into the Password field. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Use the Microsoft.Azure.StackExchangeRedis extension and configure the connection with a token credential (for example DefaultAzureCredential), which acquires and refreshes tokens
Paste the token into the user name field instead
Use the cache's access key permanently
Disable Entra authentication on the cache

questions.explanation: Microsoft provides extension libraries such as Microsoft.Azure.StackExchangeRedis that configure StackExchange.Redis with a token credential, handling user identity, token acquisition, and refresh. Setting a raw token manually goes stale quickly, and falling back to access keys or disabling Entra lowers security.

questions.skill_name: Azure Managed Redis caching, expiration, and invalidation
questions.stem: An Azure Managed Redis cache uses the NoEviction policy. What happens when memory is full, and what should you plan for?

options.text: The cache scales up automatically to the next SKU
The oldest keys are evicted automatically
Keys are written to disk instead
Writes that need more memory fail, so plan explicit cleanup (such as TTLs) and capacity alerts

questions.explanation: With NoEviction, Redis doesn't remove keys to free memory, so memory pressure makes write commands fail. The Well-Architected guidance says to plan explicit cleanup and capacity alerts. Automatic eviction only happens with other policies, and the cache doesn't scale or spill to disk on its own.

questions.stem: You want to give a group of 30 developers data access to an Azure Managed Redis cache through Microsoft Entra ID. What limitation applies?

options.text: Microsoft Entra groups aren't supported, so you add individual users or service principals
Only one Entra user can be added per cache
Groups are supported, but only with access keys enabled
Entra authentication only works for managed identities

questions.explanation: The Well-Architected guidance for Azure Managed Redis says to add only the required users or service principals because Microsoft Entra groups aren't supported for data-plane access. Many individual users and service principals can be added, and Entra authentication isn't limited to managed identities.

options.text: When you create the cache, by enabling the RediSearch module; modules can't be added later
No module is needed; vector search is built into every cache
Any time, by running MODULE LOAD
After creation, through a support request

questions.explanation: Vector search in Redis requires the RediSearch module, and in Azure Managed Redis modules must be enabled during provisioning; you can't add them afterwards or load them manually. Plan vector search before creating the cache.

options.text: Any clustering policy with any eviction policy
The non-clustered policy and volatile-ttl eviction
The OSS clustering policy and the allkeys-lru eviction policy
The Enterprise clustering policy and the NoEviction eviction policy

questions.explanation: RediSearch requires the Enterprise clustering policy and the NoEviction eviction policy, so choosing vector search effectively decides those settings for you. Eviction policies that drop keys would remove indexed documents.

Flash Optimized
Memory Optimized

questions.stem: You are creating a Redis vector index. When should you choose HNSW instead of FLAT?

options.text: When vectors are stored as plain strings
For larger datasets where low latency matters more than exhaustive precision
When you need exact brute-force results on a small dataset
When you want the index to store keys on disk

questions.explanation: FLAT is exact brute-force search, suited to smaller datasets or workloads needing exhaustive search, while HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is an approximate nearest neighbor index suited to larger datasets where latency matters more. Data storage format (hash or JSON) doesn't decide the algorithm.

questions.skill_name: Vector indexing and similarity search in Azure Managed Redis
questions.stem: Which distance metrics can a Redis vector index use?

options.text: L2, COSINE, and IP (inner product)
Levenshtein
Jaccard and Hamming only
Manhattan only

questions.explanation: Redis vector indexes support L2 (Euclidean), COSINE, and IP (inner product). The right choice depends on the embedding model and whether vectors are normalized.

questions.stem: In which Redis data structures can you store vectors for RediSearch, and what else should you store with them?

options.text: Only sorted sets, with no metadata
Only streams
Hashes or JSON documents, with metadata such as document ID, source URL, category, and tenant ID
Only lists, with metadata in a separate cache

questions.explanation: Vectors can be stored in hashes or JSON documents, and the guidance is to store metadata alongside each vector, such as document ID, title, source URL, category, timestamp, tenant ID, or access-control fields, so results can be filtered and traced back to sources.

questions.skill_name: Vector indexing and similarity search in Azure Managed Redis
questions.stem: A support bot must find similar FAQ entries only within the user's product line and tenant. Which Redis vector search capability should you use?

options.text: A separate Redis cache for every tenant
Pub/Sub channels per product line
Hybrid queries that combine metadata filters (for example TAG or numeric filters) with KNN vector search
Plain GET commands on each FAQ key

questions.explanation: RediSearch supports hybrid filtering: metadata filters narrow candidates before or during vector comparison, combined with KNN, range, text, numeric, and tag queries. Separate caches per tenant are costly, GET can't rank by similarity, and Pub/Sub is for messaging.

questions.skill_name: Vector indexing and similarity search in Azure Managed Redis
questions.stem: Your chatbot gets many questions that are phrased differently but mean the same thing, and LLM calls are expensive. How can Azure Managed Redis help?

options.text: As a semantic cache: store prompt embeddings with responses and reuse a cached response when a new prompt is semantically similar
By storing the language model weights
By caching the exact prompt string only, so paraphrases always hit the cache
By replacing the language model entirely

questions.explanation: Semantic caching stores prompts, embeddings, and completions, and uses vector search to return a cached response when a new prompt is similar enough, reducing LLM cost and latency. Exact-string caching misses paraphrases, and Redis doesn't host or replace the model.

questions.stem: Which statement about semantic caching with Azure Managed Redis is correct?

options.text: It requires the OSS clustering policy
It only works with the Flash Optimized tier
It is a checkbox on the cache that works without RediSearch
It is an application or gateway pattern built on Redis vector search, not a separate managed feature you switch on

questions.explanation: The semantic cache tutorial explains that semantic caching is implemented in the application (for example with RedisVL) or at a gateway such as Azure API Management, while Managed Redis supplies the endpoint and RediSearch vector search. It therefore needs RediSearch, with Enterprise clustering and NoEviction, and Flash Optimized doesn't support RediSearch.

options.text: RedisBloom and RedisTimeSeries
RediSearch and RedisJSON
All four modules
No modules can be used with geo-replication

questions.explanation: Only the RediSearch and RedisJSON modules can be used with active geo-replication, which lets you search JSON and vector data across caches synchronized in an active-active configuration. RedisBloom and RedisTimeSeries aren't supported with it.
