questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: An order service sends each order to exactly one of several competing worker instances for processing. Which Service Bus entity fits?

options.text: A queue
An Event Grid custom topic
A topic with a single subscription per message
A topic with one subscription per worker instance

questions.explanation: A queue delivers each message to one of the competing consumers, which load-balances work across instances. With a topic, every subscription gets its own copy of each message, so one subscription per worker would process every order multiple times. Event Grid is for discrete event notifications rather than durable work queues.
questions.source_title: Service Bus queues, topics, and subscriptions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Billing, shipping, and analytics services each need their own copy of every OrderPlaced message. Which Service Bus design should you use?

options.text: A topic with one subscription per service
One queue shared by all three services
Three queues, with the sender writing the same message to each
A queue with sessions enabled

questions.explanation: Topics provide publish-subscribe messaging: each subscription receives an independent copy of every message sent to the topic, and each service reads from its own subscription. A shared queue gives each message to only one consumer, writing to three queues couples the sender to every consumer, and sessions are for ordered processing.
questions.source_title: Service Bus queues, topics, and subscriptions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Your consumer crashes in the middle of processing, and the business can't lose any message. Which receive mode should you use, and what delivery guarantee does it provide?

options.text: Receive-and-delete, which gives exactly-once delivery
Receive-and-delete, which gives at-least-once delivery
Peek-lock, which gives at-most-once delivery
Peek-lock, which gives at-least-once delivery

questions.explanation: In peek-lock (the default), the message is locked and only removed when it is settled (completed), so if the consumer fails the lock expires and the message becomes available again: at-least-once delivery. Receive-and-delete removes the message as soon as it is received, so a crash loses it: at-most-once.
questions.source_title: Prevent message loss and duplicate processing in Azure Service Bus

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: With peek-lock, which settlement action removes a successfully processed message from the queue?

options.text: Defer
Peek
Abandon
Complete

questions.explanation: Completing a message tells the broker processing succeeded, and the message is deleted. Abandon releases the lock so the message can be delivered again, defer sets it aside to be retrieved later by sequence number, and peek reads a message without locking or removing it.
questions.source_title: Message transfers, locks, and settlement

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: A handler sometimes needs 4 minutes to process a message, but the queue's lock duration is 1 minute. Other consumers then receive the same message while it's still being processed. What should you do?

options.text: Switch to receive-and-delete
Renew the message lock while processing (for example by configuring automatic lock renewal in the processor)
Enable duplicate detection
Increase MaxDeliveryCount to 100

questions.explanation: When a lock expires, the message becomes visible again and another receiver can take it. The lock holder can extend the lock (RenewMessageLockAsync, or automatic renewal through settings such as MaxAutoLockRenewalDuration), or you can raise the lock duration within its limit. Receive-and-delete risks losing messages, and delivery count and duplicate detection don't stop the lock from expiring.
questions.source_title: Message transfers, locks, and settlement

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: A malformed message keeps failing and is retried repeatedly. What does Service Bus do by default, and which setting controls it?

options.text: After the delivery count exceeds MaxDeliveryCount (default 10), the message is moved to the dead-letter queue
The message is deleted after 3 failed attempts
The queue is disabled after 10 failures
The message is retried forever unless you delete it manually

questions.explanation: Each time a locked message is abandoned or its lock expires, its delivery count increases. When it exceeds MaxDeliveryCount, which defaults to 10, Service Bus moves it to the dead-letter queue so it no longer blocks processing. Service Bus doesn't delete poison messages or disable the queue.
questions.source_title: Service Bus messaging exceptions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: A queue's size keeps growing and senders start getting QuotaExceeded errors, although the main queue is nearly empty. What is a likely cause?

options.text: Duplicate detection stores too many message IDs
The dead-letter queue is filling up; dead-lettered messages count toward the entity's size and aren't removed automatically
The queue has too many sessions
The lock duration is too short

questions.explanation: The exceptions guide notes that dead-lettered messages take up space as they accumulate and are a common cause of QuotaExceeded. Messages stay in the dead-letter queue until a consumer receives them, so you need a process that inspects and clears it. Duplicate detection, locks, and sessions don't fill an entity like this.
questions.source_title: Service Bus messaging exceptions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: You want to inspect the dead-lettered messages of the queue orders. Which path do you receive from?

options.text: orders/dlq
orders-poison
$deadletter/orders
orders/$deadletterqueue

questions.explanation: Every queue and subscription has a dead-letter subqueue with the path <entity>/$deadletterqueue (the SDKs also expose it through a sub-queue option). The -poison suffix is the Azure Storage queue convention used by Functions, and the other paths don't exist.
questions.source_title: Asynchronous messaging options

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Messages in a queue have a time-to-live of 1 hour, and you need to audit messages that expire before anyone processes them. What should you configure on the queue?

options.text: Increase the lock duration
Enable dead-lettering on message expiration
Set MaxDeliveryCount to 1
Enable duplicate detection

questions.explanation: With dead-lettering on message expiration enabled, messages whose time-to-live expires move to the dead-letter queue instead of being discarded silently. Lock duration, duplicate detection, and MaxDeliveryCount don't affect what happens to expired messages.
questions.source_title: Service Bus queues, topics, and subscriptions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Dead-lettered messages from many queues pile up, and you want them all collected in one place for a single remediation service. Which property helps?

options.text: forwardDeadLetteredMessagesTo on each queue or subscription, pointing to a central queue
defaultMessageTimeToLive
enablePartitioning
requiresSession

questions.explanation: forwardDeadLetteredMessagesTo automatically forwards dead-lettered messages from a queue or subscription to another queue or topic, so you can centralize handling. TTL controls expiry, partitioning distributes the entity across brokers, and sessions enable ordered processing.
questions.source_title: Service Bus queues, topics, and subscriptions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Messages in the dead-letter queue are several weeks old. What happens to them if no one processes them?

options.text: They are deleted after 14 days
They return to the main queue after their TTL
They stay there; messages in the dead-letter queue don't expire and aren't cleaned up automatically
They move to a dead-letter queue of the dead-letter queue

questions.explanation: The dead-letter queue retains messages until a consumer explicitly receives them. Time-to-live isn't observed for messages that have already been dead-lettered, so you need an operational process to drain and resolve them.
questions.source_title: Asynchronous messaging options

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: A producer sometimes resends a payment message after a timeout, causing double charges. You want Service Bus to drop the repeated message automatically. What should you do?

options.text: Use receive-and-delete mode
Enable sessions and use random SessionId values
Create the queue with duplicate detection enabled and set a stable, unique MessageId on each payment message
Shorten the lock duration

questions.explanation: Duplicate detection discards a message whose MessageId was already seen within the detection time window. It must be enabled when the queue or topic is created, and the sender must set the MessageId to a value derived from the business operation. Sessions, receive mode, and lock duration don't detect duplicates.
questions.source_title: Service Bus messages, payloads, and serialization

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Your solution needs guaranteed first-in, first-out delivery and automatic duplicate detection. Which queueing service fits?

options.text: Azure Storage queues
Azure Service Bus queues
Azure Event Hubs consumer groups
Azure Event Grid

questions.explanation: The comparison guide recommends Service Bus queues when you need guaranteed FIFO ordered delivery (through sessions) and automatic duplicate detection. Storage queues don't guarantee ordering or detect duplicates, Event Grid is an eventing service, and Event Hubs is a streaming platform.
questions.source_title: Storage queues and Service Bus queues compared

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: All messages for the same customer must be processed in order, but different customers can be processed in parallel. Which Service Bus feature should you use?

options.text: Duplicate detection, with the customer ID as the MessageId
Partitioning, with one partition per customer
Sessions, with the customer ID as the SessionId
Scheduled messages

questions.explanation: Sessions group related messages by SessionId; a receiver that accepts a session gets an exclusive lock and processes that session's messages in order, while other receivers handle other sessions in parallel. Duplicate detection would drop all but one message per customer, partitioning doesn't guarantee ordering per customer, and scheduling only delays delivery.
questions.source_title: Message sessions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: You want to enable sessions on an existing production queue that was created without them. What must you do?

options.text: Restart the namespace
Create a new queue with sessions enabled, because sessions must be enabled when the entity is created
Run az servicebus queue update --enable-session true
Set SessionId on new messages; the queue enables sessions automatically

questions.explanation: Session support must be enabled at the time a queue or subscription is created, so you create a new session-enabled entity and move producers and consumers to it. Setting SessionId on messages doesn't change the queue, and restarting the namespace isn't possible or relevant.
questions.source_title: Message sessions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Sessions are enabled on a queue. A legacy sender keeps sending messages without a SessionId. What happens?

options.text: The messages go straight to the dead-letter queue
Those sends fail, because clients must send messages as part of a session on a session-enabled queue
The broker assigns a random SessionId
The messages are delivered to any receiver

questions.explanation: When sessions are enabled on a queue or subscription, clients can no longer send or receive regular messages; they must set a SessionId when sending and accept a session to receive. Clients can still peek. Service Bus doesn't assign session IDs automatically.
questions.source_title: Message sessions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Every subscription on the topic orders receives all messages, but the EU-fulfillment subscription should get only messages where region = 'EU'. What should you configure?

options.text: Replace the subscription's default rule with a filter rule such as the SQL filter region = 'EU'
Create a separate topic for EU messages and change all senders
Filter the messages in the subscriber's code after receiving them
Enable sessions with SessionId = EU

questions.explanation: Subscriptions select messages through rules; a new subscription has a default rule that accepts everything (a true filter, equivalent to 1=1). Replacing it with a SQL or correlation filter on the region property delivers only matching messages. Client-side filtering wastes throughput, a new topic couples senders to consumers, and sessions don't filter.
questions.source_title: Topic filters and actions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: A subscription filter only needs to match messages whose Subject is 'red' and CorrelationId is 'high'. Which filter type is the most efficient?

options.text: No filter, with client-side checks
A correlation filter
A SQL filter with LIKE patterns
A boolean true filter

questions.explanation: Correlation filters match on equality against system and user properties such as Subject, CorrelationId, and custom properties, and they are cheaper for the broker to evaluate than SQL filter expressions. A true filter passes everything, and client-side checks waste delivery capacity.
questions.source_title: Topic filters and actions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: For the subscription ColorRed, you want to accept messages where color = 'red' and also set the quantity property to half its value before delivery. What should you use?

options.text: A SQL filter with a SQL rule action
A correlation filter only
Auto-forwarding to another queue
Duplicate detection

questions.explanation: A subscription rule consists of a filter condition and, optionally, an action that annotates the selected message, for example a SQL action that sets quantity = quantity / 2 when color is red. Correlation filters select messages but don't modify them, and duplicate detection and auto-forwarding don't change properties.
questions.source_title: Topic filters and actions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Which statement about Service Bus filtering is correct?

options.text: Queues support SQL filters on receive
Filters can only inspect the message body
Filtering is a feature of topic subscriptions; queues don't support subscription filters
Each topic can have only one subscription with a filter

questions.explanation: Subscription rules (SQL, boolean, and correlation filters) let each subscription select messages from a topic; queues don't support filtering. Filters evaluate message properties, not the body, and a topic can have many subscriptions, each with its own rules.
questions.source_title: Service Bus queues, topics, and subscriptions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: A reminder message must become available to receivers only 24 hours after it is sent. What should the sender do?

options.text: Schedule the message with a scheduled enqueue time 24 hours in the future
Defer the message after receiving it
Set the lock duration to 24 hours
Set the message time-to-live to 24 hours

questions.explanation: Scheduled messages (ScheduledEnqueueTime or ScheduleMessageAsync) are accepted immediately but stay invisible until the scheduled time, and the sequence number returned lets you cancel them. TTL makes messages expire rather than appear later, deferral happens on the receiver side, and lock duration has a much lower maximum and only applies after a message is received.
questions.source_title: Service Bus messages, payloads, and serialization

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: A consumer receives a message that can't be processed until a related message arrives. It wants to set the message aside and fetch it later by ID. Which action should it use, and how is the message retrieved later?

options.text: Abandon the message, and later receive it by MessageId
Defer the message, and later receive it with its sequence number
Dead-letter it, and later resubmit it
Complete it, and later restore it from a backup

questions.explanation: Deferral keeps the message in the queue but hides it from normal receives; it can only be retrieved explicitly by its sequence number, so the consumer must store that number. Abandon makes it available to any receiver immediately, dead-lettering marks it as failed, and complete deletes it.
questions.source_title: Message transfers, locks, and settlement

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Messages arriving in the subscription audit of the topic orders must be moved automatically into the queue audit-processing in the same namespace, with no code. What should you configure?

options.text: Auto-forwarding (forwardTo) on the subscription, set to the queue
A SQL filter action
A scheduled message
Duplicate detection on the queue

questions.explanation: Auto-forwarding chains a queue or subscription to another queue or topic in the same namespace, and Service Bus moves messages automatically. Filter actions modify properties, scheduled messages delay visibility, and duplicate detection removes repeats.
questions.source_title: Service Bus queues, topics, and subscriptions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: A startup uses the Basic tier of Service Bus, and the team now wants publish-subscribe with topics. What must change?

options.text: Move to at least the Standard tier, because the Basic tier supports queues only
Enable sessions on the Basic namespace
Create a topic with the --basic flag
Use Premium only for queues

questions.explanation: The Basic tier offers queues only; topics and subscriptions require the Standard or Premium tier. There's no flag to create topics in Basic, and sessions are an unrelated feature.
questions.source_title: Service Bus queues, topics, and subscriptions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Your messages carry document payloads of up to 20 MB. Which Service Bus option supports this without splitting messages?

options.text: The Basic tier with batching
The Premium tier, which supports large messages (up to 100 MB)
The Standard tier, which supports up to 256 MB
Any tier, because Service Bus has no size limit

questions.explanation: The Standard tier limits messages to 256 KB, while the Premium tier supports large messages up to 100 MB. Batching combines small messages into one send but doesn't raise the per-message limit. For very large payloads, another option is the claim-check pattern with Blob storage.
questions.source_title: Storage queues and Service Bus queues compared

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: An app with a managed identity must only send messages to a queue, following least privilege. Which role should you assign at the queue scope?

options.text: Contributor
Azure Service Bus Data Sender
Azure Service Bus Data Owner
Azure Service Bus Data Receiver

questions.explanation: Azure Service Bus Data Sender allows sending messages, which is all the app needs. Data Receiver allows receiving, Data Owner allows full data-plane access, and Contributor is a management-plane role that doesn't give the least-privilege data access you want.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Use identity-based connections with triggers and bindings

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: A ServiceBusProcessor handler throws an exception for a message. With the default settings of the .NET processor, what happens to that message?

options.text: It is deleted immediately
It is moved to the dead-letter queue on the first failure
It isn't completed; the message is abandoned and redelivered, and after MaxDeliveryCount it is dead-lettered
It is completed anyway because AutoCompleteMessages is true

questions.explanation: With AutoCompleteMessages enabled (the default), the processor completes a message only after the handler returns without throwing. If the handler throws, the message is abandoned, its delivery count increases, and once MaxDeliveryCount is exceeded it moves to the dead-letter queue.
questions.source_title: Service Bus messaging exceptions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: You need to send hundreds of small messages efficiently without exceeding the maximum message size. What is the recommended approach in the SDK?

options.text: Send each message on a new client
Use receive-and-delete mode
Concatenate all payloads into one message regardless of size
Create a ServiceBusMessageBatch, add messages with TryAddMessage until it's full, and send the batch

questions.explanation: A message batch tracks its size as you add messages and tells you when it's full, so each send stays within the size limit while reducing round trips. Creating clients per message is expensive, a single concatenated message can exceed limits, and receive mode only affects consumers.
questions.source_title: Service Bus queues, topics, and subscriptions

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Peek-lock gives at-least-once delivery, so a consumer can occasionally process the same message twice. What should you do in the consumer?

options.text: Make processing idempotent, for example by recording processed MessageIds
Switch to receive-and-delete
Use a longer TTL
Set MaxDeliveryCount to 1

questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery means duplicates can happen, for example when a lock expires after processing but before completion. Idempotent handlers, such as checking a stored MessageId, make duplicates harmless. Receive-and-delete trades duplicates for possible message loss, and the other settings don't prevent redelivery.
questions.source_title: Prevent message loss and duplicate processing in Azure Service Bus

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: A client sends a request message and needs the reply delivered back to it. Which message properties support this request-response pattern?

options.text: TimeToLive only
PartitionKey only
ScheduledEnqueueTime
ReplyTo (and ReplyToSessionId for session-based replies), with CorrelationId linking the reply to the request

questions.explanation: ReplyTo names the entity where the reply should be sent, ReplyToSessionId lets the requester receive replies through a specific session, and CorrelationId lets it match a reply to its request, for example by echoing the request's MessageId. Scheduling, TTL, and partition key don't route replies.
questions.source_title: Service Bus messages, payloads, and serialization

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: A consumer uses a high prefetch count, and you notice messages being redelivered and their delivery counts increasing. What is a likely cause?

options.text: Prefetched messages are locked while they wait in the client buffer, and their locks can expire before the handler reaches them
Prefetch converts the queue to receive-and-delete
Prefetch only works with sessions
Prefetch disables lock renewal on the server

questions.explanation: Prefetching pulls messages into a local buffer to increase throughput, but in peek-lock mode each prefetched message's lock is already running. If messages sit in the buffer longer than the lock duration, the locks expire and the messages are delivered again. Keep the prefetch count in line with processing speed.
questions.source_title: Message transfers, locks, and settlement

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: A consumer receives a message from queue A and must send a result to queue B. Either both operations succeed or neither does. What can you use?

options.text: Two separate operations with retries
Duplicate detection on queue B
Auto-forwarding from A to B
A Service Bus transaction that groups the complete on queue A and the send to queue B in the same namespace

questions.explanation: Service Bus supports transactions that group operations such as completing a received message and sending new messages to entities in the same namespace, so they commit or roll back together. Separate operations can leave partial results, and duplicate detection or auto-forwarding don't give atomicity.
questions.source_title: Message transfers, locks, and settlement

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Which Service Bus message property should a sender set to a unique, application-defined value so that duplicate sends can be detected?

options.text: TimeToLive
MessageId
ContentType
Subject

questions.explanation: MessageId is the application-defined identifier of the message; when duplicate detection is enabled, Service Bus uses it to discard repeated messages within the detection window. ContentType describes the payload, Subject is an application label, and TimeToLive controls expiration.
questions.source_title: Service Bus messages, payloads, and serialization

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: Temporary reply queues created per client session are sometimes left behind when clients crash. How can Service Bus remove unused queues automatically?

options.text: Set auto-delete on idle (AutoDeleteOnIdle) on the queues so they are deleted after a period with no activity
Enable duplicate detection
Set MaxDeliveryCount to 1
Set the message time-to-live to 1 minute

questions.explanation: AutoDeleteOnIdle (the --auto-delete-on-idle parameter) deletes a queue automatically after it has been idle for the configured interval, which suits temporary entities. MaxDeliveryCount, duplicate detection, and message TTL affect messages, not the lifetime of the queue itself.
questions.source_title: az servicebus queue (CLI reference)

questions.skill_name: Azure Service Bus queues, topics, subscriptions, and dead-lettering
questions.stem: While investigating the dead-letter queue, you want to know why each message ended up there. Where do you look?

options.text: The namespace's Activity log
The DeadLetterReason and DeadLetterErrorDescription properties of each dead-lettered message
The message's ScheduledEnqueueTime
The queue's lock duration

questions.explanation: When Service Bus or an application dead-letters a message, it records properties such as DeadLetterReason (for example MaxDeliveryCountExceeded or TTLExpiredException) and DeadLetterErrorDescription on the message. Lock duration and scheduling properties don't explain dead-lettering, and the Activity log tracks management operations.
questions.source_title: Asynchronous messaging options

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: An Event Grid subscription uses the default retry policy, and the webhook endpoint is down. How long and how many times does Event Grid try to deliver an event?

options.text: Up to 7 days or 100 attempts
Exactly 3 attempts within 1 minute
Up to 24 hours (1,440 minutes) or 30 attempts, whichever comes first
Until the endpoint recovers, with no limit

questions.explanation: By default Event Grid retries delivery for 24 hours (1,440 minutes) or 30 times, whichever limit is reached first, using an exponential backoff schedule. After that the event is dead-lettered if a dead-letter location is configured, otherwise it is dropped.
questions.source_title: Set dead-letter location and retry policy (Event Grid)

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: Events older than 2 hours are useless to your handler. How should you configure the event subscription?

options.text: Set maxDeliveryAttempts to 120
Set the retry policy's event time-to-live to 120 minutes
Set the subscription expiration time to 2 hours from now
Configure a custom retry schedule of every 2 hours

questions.explanation: The retry policy has two settings: maximum delivery attempts (1 to 30) and event time-to-live (1 to 1,440 minutes). Setting the TTL to 120 minutes stops retries after 2 hours. The retry schedule itself can't be configured, and the subscription expiration deletes the whole subscription at a given time.
questions.source_title: Set dead-letter location and retry policy (Event Grid)

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: You want events that Event Grid couldn't deliver to be kept for later analysis instead of being dropped. What should you configure?

options.text: A dead-letter destination, a container in an Azure Storage account, on the event subscription
Longer TTL on the custom topic itself
A Service Bus dead-letter queue on the topic
A second event subscription to the same endpoint

questions.explanation: Event Grid dead-lettering writes undeliverable events to a blob container in a storage account that you specify on the event subscription (for example with --deadletter-endpoint). Without it, events are dropped when retries end. Service Bus DLQs belong to Service Bus, topics have no such TTL setting, and a second subscription to the same failing endpoint fails too.
questions.source_title: Set dead-letter location and retry policy (Event Grid)

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: Which values are valid when you customize an Event Grid subscription's retry policy?

options.text: Maximum delivery attempts from 1 to 100 and a custom backoff schedule
A fixed retry every 10 seconds
Event time-to-live up to 7 days
Maximum delivery attempts from 1 to 30 and event time-to-live from 1 to 1,440 minutes

questions.explanation: Max delivery attempts must be an integer from 1 to 30, and event TTL must be from 1 to 1,440 minutes; the default for both is the maximum. You can't configure the retry schedule, which uses exponential backoff, and TTL can't exceed 24 hours.
questions.source_title: Set dead-letter location and retry policy (Event Grid)

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: An Azure Function subscribed to a Storage account's events should run only for blobs created under the container images whose names end with .jpg. Which filter settings should you use?

options.text: includedEventTypes Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated, subjectBeginsWith /blobServices/default/containers/images/blobs/, and subjectEndsWith .jpg
subjectEndsWith images and subjectBeginsWith .jpg
No filter; check the extension in the function
An advanced filter on data.url StringContains images only

questions.explanation: Event type filters select BlobCreated events, and subject filters match the blob path prefix and suffix, as in Microsoft's subscription schema example. Filtering in the function still delivers and bills every event, a single contains check on the URL is less precise, and the last option reverses prefix and suffix.
questions.source_title: Filter events for Event Grid

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: You need to deliver only events whose data.color is blue, red, or green. Which kind of filter should you use?

options.text: An event type filter listing the colors
A dead-letter filter
A subject filter with subjectBeginsWith blue
An advanced filter with key data.color, operator StringIn, and the three values

questions.explanation: Advanced filters compare a key in the event, including fields inside data, against values using operators such as StringIn, NumberGreaterThan, or StringContains; StringIn matches any of the listed values. Subject and event type filters only inspect those specific fields, and there's no dead-letter filter.
questions.source_title: Filter events for Event Grid

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: An event subscription has two advanced filters: data.region StringIn [EU] and data.amount NumberGreaterThan 1000. Which events are delivered?

options.text: Only events that match both filters (region is EU and amount is greater than 1000)
Only the first filter is evaluated
All events, because advanced filters are informational
Events that match either filter

questions.explanation: When a subscription has several advanced filters, an event must satisfy all of them (logical AND). Within one filter, multiple values are combined with OR, so StringIn [EU, US] would match either value.
questions.source_title: Filter events for Event Grid

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: You create an Event Grid custom topic and publish events from your app. How must the request be authenticated?

options.text: With a client certificate only
With the storage account key of the subscriber
With an access key (aeg-sas-key header), a SAS token, or Microsoft Entra ID
Anonymously, because custom topics are public

questions.explanation: Publishers authenticate to a custom topic with its access key, a SAS token generated from it, or a Microsoft Entra token for an identity with a publisher role. Topics aren't anonymous, subscriber storage keys aren't used for publishing, and client certificates aren't the documented mechanism.
questions.source_title: Authenticate event delivery to event handlers

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: When you create an Event Grid custom topic, which input schemas can you choose for the events you publish?

options.text: Only Avro
Only the Service Bus message format
Only CloudEvents
Event Grid schema, CloudEvents v1.0 schema, or a custom schema mapped to Event Grid fields

questions.explanation: The input schema of a custom topic is set when it is created: the Event Grid schema (the default), the CloudEvents v1.0 schema, or a custom event schema with input mappings to Event Grid fields. Avro and Service Bus formats aren't Event Grid input schemas.
questions.source_title: Map custom fields to Event Grid schema

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: Your existing system emits events with fields named eventName and eventSubject, and you can't change the publisher. How can you publish them to Event Grid?

options.text: Use the CloudEvents schema; it accepts any field names
Rename the fields in every subscriber
Create the custom topic with the custom input schema and map eventName and eventSubject to Event Grid's eventType and subject, setting defaults where needed
Event Grid can't accept events that use other field names

questions.explanation: Custom input schema mapping lets a topic map your fields to the Event Grid schema (id, eventTime, subject, eventType, dataVersion), with default values for subject, event type, and data version when they are missing. CloudEvents has its own required attributes, and subscribers can't fix publisher-side schema problems.
questions.source_title: Map custom fields to Event Grid schema

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: Which statement about CloudEvents in Azure Event Grid is correct?

options.text: CloudEvents can only be delivered to Event Hubs
Event Grid natively supports the JSON format of CloudEvents v1.0 for system and custom events, and it is the preferred format for interoperability
CloudEvents requires a custom schema mapping
CloudEvents is only supported for IoT Hub events

questions.explanation: Event Grid natively supports CloudEvents v1.0 in JSON with the HTTP protocol binding, for system events such as Blob Storage and IoT Hub and for custom events. It is described as the preferred format because it's an open, extensible standard that improves interoperability. Event Grid also keeps its own proprietary schema.
questions.source_title: CloudEvents v1.0 schema with Azure Event Grid

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: You create an event subscription that targets your own HTTPS webhook using the Event Grid schema. Before any events are delivered, Event Grid sends a SubscriptionValidationEvent. What must your endpoint do?

options.text: Return the validationCode from the event in a validationResponse (or complete the manual validation URL)
Do nothing; validation is optional
Send a reply event to the topic
Return HTTP 401 to prove it is protected

questions.explanation: To prevent abuse, Event Grid confirms that the endpoint wants the events through a validation handshake: the endpoint echoes the validationCode in a validationResponse, or someone browses to the validationUrl. Until validation succeeds, nothing is delivered. Returning 401 fails validation.
questions.source_title: Authenticate event delivery to event handlers

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: You subscribe a webhook with the CloudEvents v1.0 delivery schema. How does Event Grid confirm the endpoint?

options.text: It uses the CloudEvents abuse protection handshake (an HTTP OPTIONS request that the endpoint answers with WebHook-Allowed-Origin) instead of the Event Grid validation event
It skips validation for CloudEvents
It requires the endpoint to be an Azure Function
It sends a SubscriptionValidationEvent with a validationCode

questions.explanation: When the CloudEvents schema is used for delivery, Event Grid uses the CloudEvents v1.0 abuse protection mechanism, an OPTIONS request that the endpoint must answer with the allowed origin header, in place of the Event Grid validation event. Validation is always required, and any HTTPS endpoint that implements it can be used.
questions.source_title: Authenticate event delivery to event handlers

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: Which requirement applies to a webhook endpoint that receives events pushed from Event Grid?

options.text: It must be hosted in Azure
It must be in the same region as the topic
It must accept FTP uploads
It must use HTTPS and handle the webhook validation

questions.explanation: Any public endpoint can be an event handler if it uses encryption in transit (HTTPS), can read the event format, and handles webhook validation. It doesn't have to be hosted in Azure or in the same region.
questions.source_title: Azure Event Grid push delivery concepts

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: An Event Grid topic delivers events to a Service Bus queue. Security requires no keys or connection strings. How should delivery be authenticated?

options.text: Store the Service Bus connection string in the event subscription
Use the topic access key on the Service Bus queue
Make the Service Bus namespace public and anonymous
Enable a managed identity on the topic and assign it a Service Bus data sender role on the queue, then use managed identity for delivery

questions.explanation: Event Grid can deliver to Service Bus, Event Hubs, and Storage queues using its managed identity: enable a system- or user-assigned identity on the topic and add it to the right role on the destination. Connection strings are exactly what you wanted to avoid, Service Bus doesn't allow anonymous sends, and topic keys only authenticate publishers to Event Grid.
questions.source_title: Authenticate event delivery to event handlers

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: Which description best matches when to choose Azure Event Grid over Service Bus or Event Hubs?

options.text: Processing high-value business commands that need ordering, transactions, and dead-letter handling
Reacting to discrete events, such as a blob being created, with push delivery to many subscribers
Ingesting millions of telemetry records per second for stream analytics
Long-term storage of messages for months

questions.explanation: Event Grid is an eventing service for discrete events that report state changes and pushes them to subscribers. Service Bus is a message broker for high-value commands with features like sessions, transactions, and DLQs, and Event Hubs is built for high-volume streaming telemetry. None of them is long-term message storage.
questions.source_title: Asynchronous messaging options

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: Your event handler sometimes receives the same Event Grid event twice and events don't always arrive in the order they were published. Is this expected?

options.text: No; Event Grid guarantees exactly-once, ordered delivery
Only for CloudEvents
Only if dead-lettering is disabled
Yes; Event Grid delivers at least once and doesn't guarantee order, so handlers should be idempotent and use the event id and time

questions.explanation: Retries can cause duplicate deliveries, and events are delivered independently, so ordering isn't guaranteed. Handlers should be idempotent, for example by tracking event ids, and use eventTime or sequence data if order matters. This is true for both schemas and regardless of dead-lettering.
questions.source_title: Azure Event Grid push delivery concepts

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: You want to be notified when a secret in Key Vault is about to expire so a function can rotate it. Which Event Grid event should the function subscribe to, and when does it fire?

options.text: Microsoft.KeyVault.SecretExpired, on the expiration date only
Microsoft.KeyVault.VaultAccessPolicyChanged, daily
Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated, when the secret is rotated
Microsoft.KeyVault.SecretNearExpiry, about 30 days before the secret's expiration date

questions.explanation: Key Vault publishes SecretNearExpiry when the current version of a secret is about to expire; the event fires 30 days before the expiration date. That gives time to create a new version. SecretExpired fires only once it has already expired, and the other events are unrelated.
questions.source_title: Azure Key Vault as Event Grid source

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: A SaaS platform must publish events for thousands of tenants, each with its own subscribers, while managing authentication and partitioning centrally. Which Event Grid feature fits?

options.text: One custom topic per event type with no tenant information
A separate Azure subscription per tenant
Event domains
Service Bus sessions

questions.explanation: Event domains manage large numbers of topics, typically one per tenant, under one endpoint, with centralized authentication and access control per domain topic. Separate subscriptions per tenant are unmanageable, a topic without tenant information can't isolate subscribers, and Service Bus sessions are a messaging feature.
questions.source_title: Azure Event Grid push delivery concepts

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: Your Event Grid handler returns HTTP 400 Bad Request for a malformed event. What does Event Grid do?

options.text: It doesn't retry this error; the event is dead-lettered if a dead-letter location is configured, otherwise dropped
It sends the event to all other subscriptions
It disables the subscription
It retries the event 30 times over 24 hours

questions.explanation: Event Grid treats some errors, such as 400 Bad Request and 413 Request Entity Too Large, as failures that retrying won't fix, so it doesn't retry them and moves the event to dead-letter storage if configured. Transient errors like 503 are retried with backoff. Subscriptions aren't disabled by individual failures.
questions.source_title: Set dead-letter location and retry policy (Event Grid)

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: Using the Azure CLI, how do you create an event subscription on a custom topic that dead-letters to a blob container and stops retrying after 10 attempts or 2 hours?

options.text: az servicebus queue create ... --max-delivery-count 10
az storage container create ... --event-ttl 120
az eventgrid topic create ... --retry 10
az eventgrid event-subscription create ... --deadletter-endpoint <storage-id>/blobServices/default/containers/<container> --max-delivery-attempts 10 --event-ttl 120

questions.explanation: Dead-letter destination and retry policy are set on the event subscription: --deadletter-endpoint takes the storage container resource ID, and the retry policy uses max delivery attempts and event TTL in minutes. Topic creation doesn't define retries, and the Service Bus and Storage commands configure other services.
questions.source_title: az eventgrid topic event-subscription (CLI reference)

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: In the Event Grid event schema, which property identifies the publisher-defined path to the event subject, such as /blobServices/default/containers/images/blobs/cat.jpg?

options.text: dataVersion
eventType
subject
topic

questions.explanation: subject is the publisher-defined path to the event subject, which is what subjectBeginsWith and subjectEndsWith filters match. eventType names the kind of event (for example Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated), topic is the full resource path of the event source, and dataVersion is the schema version of the data object.
questions.source_title: Filter events for Event Grid

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: A subscriber wants blob events delivered from a system topic, but only for one of the storage account's containers. Which filter does Microsoft show for limiting events to a specific resource path?

options.text: An advanced filter on topic StringIn
isSubjectCaseSensitive set to true
subjectBeginsWith with the resource path prefix
includedEventTypes with the container name

questions.explanation: The filtering guide uses subjectBeginsWith (or the --subject-begins-with CLI parameter) to limit events to a specific resource, because the subject contains the resource path. Event types describe what happened, not where, and case sensitivity only changes how subject filters compare text.
questions.source_title: Filter events for Event Grid

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: You create a webhook subscription in the portal. Where do you enable dead-lettering and customize the retry policy?

options.text: On the custom topic's Networking blade
In the Function app's host.json
In the storage account's lifecycle policy
On the Additional features tab of the event subscription

questions.explanation: In the portal, the event subscription's Additional features tab is where you enable dead-lettering to a blob container and customize the retry policy, while the Filters tab holds event type, subject, and advanced filters. Topic networking, storage lifecycle rules, and host.json don't configure Event Grid delivery.
questions.source_title: Filter events for Event Grid

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: An Azure Function uses the Event Grid trigger. What do you need to do about the subscription validation handshake?

options.text: Use the CloudEvents schema only
Disable validation on the topic
Write code that echoes the validationCode
Nothing extra; the Event Grid trigger handles validation automatically

questions.explanation: When you subscribe with the Azure Functions Event Grid trigger, Event Grid authenticates with the function's key and the trigger extension handles validation, so no custom handshake code is needed. You only implement the handshake yourself for generic HTTP webhooks. Validation can't be disabled.
questions.source_title: Authenticate event delivery to event handlers

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes Event Grid's retry behavior when an endpoint returns a transient error such as 503 Service Unavailable?

options.text: Event Grid waits and retries with an exponential backoff schedule until the max attempts or the event TTL is reached
Event Grid retries immediately every second
Event Grid lets you choose a linear retry schedule
Event Grid never retries 503 responses

questions.explanation: For transient failures, Event Grid retries on an exponential backoff schedule, stopping when the maximum number of attempts or the event TTL is reached. The schedule isn't configurable, and 503 is a retryable status.
questions.source_title: Set dead-letter location and retry policy (Event Grid)

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: Your handler can process events far more efficiently in groups. Which delivery setting reduces the number of HTTP calls to a webhook?

options.text: Batching, configured with max events per batch and a preferred batch size in kilobytes on the event subscription
A longer event TTL
Advanced filters
Dead-lettering

questions.explanation: Event Grid output batching delivers several events per HTTP request, controlled by max events per batch and preferred batch size on the event subscription. TTL, dead-lettering, and filters don't change how many events are sent per request.
questions.source_title: Azure Event Grid push delivery concepts

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: A team plans to process a sustained stream of millions of IoT telemetry readings per second with replay and partitioned consumers. Which service fits better than Event Grid?

options.text: Azure Key Vault
Azure Event Hubs
Azure App Configuration
Azure Event Grid custom topics

questions.explanation: Event Hubs is designed for high-throughput streaming of telemetry, with partitions, consumer groups, and retention for replay. Event Grid is designed for discrete, reactive events pushed to handlers, and Key Vault and App Configuration aren't messaging services.
questions.source_title: Asynchronous messaging options

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: You expect a temporary event subscription to be needed only until the end of a migration. How can you make Event Grid remove it automatically?

options.text: Set the event TTL to 1 minute
Set max delivery attempts to 1
Set an expiration time (expirationTimeUtc) on the event subscription
Delete the topic

questions.explanation: An event subscription can have an expiration time, after which Event Grid removes it automatically. TTL and delivery attempts only control retries for individual events, and deleting the topic removes every subscription, not just the temporary one.
questions.source_title: az eventgrid topic event-subscription (CLI reference)

questions.skill_name: Azure Event Grid filters, custom events, and retries
questions.stem: Event Grid can't deliver an event and dead-lettering isn't configured on the subscription. What happens to the event when retries are exhausted?

options.text: It is dropped
It stays in the topic forever
It is delivered to all other subscriptions
It is written to the Activity log for replay

questions.explanation: Without a dead-letter location, Event Grid drops events once the retry policy (attempts or TTL) is exhausted. To keep them, configure a blob container as the dead-letter destination. Topics don't store events indefinitely, and the Activity log doesn't hold event payloads.
questions.source_title: Set dead-letter location and retry policy (Event Grid)

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: How many triggers and bindings can a single Azure Functions function have?

options.text: Exactly one trigger, and zero or more input and output bindings
One trigger and exactly one output binding
Any number of triggers and exactly one binding
No trigger if it has an output binding

questions.explanation: Every function has exactly one trigger, which starts it; the trigger is a special kind of input binding. On top of that a function can have any number of input and output bindings, including none. A function can't run without a trigger.
questions.source_title: Azure Functions triggers and bindings

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: A function triggered by a queue message must write a blob whose name equals the message text. How can you do this without code that builds the blob name?

options.text: Use a blob output binding with path container/{queueTrigger}
Set the blob name in host.json
Read the message in code and call the Blob REST API
Use an HTTP output binding

questions.explanation: Binding expressions resolve values at runtime; in a queue-triggered function, {queueTrigger} resolves to the message text, so a blob output path of container/{queueTrigger} creates a blob named after the message. Calling the REST API works but is extra code, the HTTP output binding returns HTTP responses, and host.json doesn't name blobs.
questions.source_title: Azure Functions binding expressions and patterns

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: You are building a serverless REST API with Azure Functions. Which trigger and binding combination receives a request and returns the response?

options.text: An HTTP trigger with an HTTP output binding
A Service Bus trigger with an HTTP output binding
A Blob trigger with an HTTP input binding
A timer trigger with a queue output binding

questions.explanation: The HTTP trigger runs a function from an HTTP request, and the HTTP output binding returns the response, which is the basis of serverless APIs and webhooks. Timer, Blob, and Service Bus triggers start functions from schedules, storage changes, or messages, not from client HTTP calls.
questions.source_title: Azure Functions HTTP triggers and bindings

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: An HTTP-triggered function must only be callable by clients that present the function's key. Which authorization level should you set?

options.text: user
function
system
anonymous

questions.explanation: With the function authorization level, callers must supply a function (or host) key, either in the x-functions-key header or the code query parameter. anonymous requires no key, admin requires the master key, and user and system aren't HTTP trigger authorization levels for this purpose.
questions.source_title: Azure Functions HTTP triggers and bindings

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: A queue-triggered function keeps failing on one message. What do Azure Functions and Queue storage do with the message by default?

options.text: The message is sent to a Service Bus dead-letter queue
After 5 failed attempts the message is moved to a poison queue named <queue>-poison
The message is retried forever
The message is deleted after the first failure

questions.explanation: The Queue storage trigger retries a failing message up to maxDequeueCount, 5 by default, and then moves it to a poison queue named <original-queue>-poison so you can inspect it. Service Bus dead-letter queues apply to the Service Bus trigger, not Queue storage.
questions.source_title: Azure Queue storage trigger and bindings for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: A Service Bus-triggered function throws an exception while processing a message. What happens by default?

options.text: The message isn't completed; it is retried, and after the entity's MaxDeliveryCount it moves to the dead-letter queue
The message is completed and lost
The function app stops
The message is moved to a <queue>-poison queue after 5 attempts

questions.explanation: The Service Bus trigger completes the message only when the function succeeds; on failure the message is abandoned and redelivered, and Service Bus dead-letters it once the delivery count exceeds MaxDeliveryCount. The -poison queue is the Queue storage convention, and a single failure doesn't stop the app.
questions.source_title: Azure Service Bus bindings for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: A function must write several messages to a Storage queue in a single invocation using an output binding (.NET). Which parameter type supports this?

options.text: HttpResponseData
QueueClient only
ICollector<T> or IAsyncCollector<T>
A single string

questions.explanation: For multiple queue messages, the Queue output binding supports ICollector<T> and IAsyncCollector<T> (or QueueClient), where each Add writes a message. A plain string writes a single message, and HttpResponseData is for HTTP responses.
questions.source_title: Azure Queue storage trigger and bindings for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: A team wants to use Blob storage bindings with a Premium block blob storage account and finds they don't work. What should they do?

options.text: Use an HTTP trigger to read blobs
Switch to the Flex Consumption plan
Enable soft delete on the account
Use a Standard general-purpose v2 storage account, because Blob bindings don't support Premium blob storage accounts

questions.explanation: The Blob storage bindings documentation states that Premium Blob storage accounts aren't supported and recommends a Standard general-purpose v2 account instead. The hosting plan, HTTP triggers, and soft delete don't change binding support.
questions.source_title: Azure Blob storage bindings for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: In the Python v2 programming model, how are triggers and bindings declared?

options.text: Only in a function.json file next to each function
In host.json
With decorators on functions registered to a FunctionApp object, such as @app.route or @app.timer_trigger
In requirements.txt

questions.explanation: The Python v2 model defines all functions on a FunctionApp object and declares triggers and bindings with decorators like @app.route and @app.timer_trigger. function.json belongs to the older v1 model, host.json holds host settings, and requirements.txt lists dependencies.
questions.source_title: Python developer reference for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: In a Java function app, how do you bind a method to an HTTP trigger and a queue output?

options.text: By listing bindings in pom.xml only
By naming the method httpTrigger
With annotations from com.microsoft.azure.functions.annotation, such as @FunctionName, @HttpTrigger, and @QueueOutput
By extending a base class called HttpFunction

questions.explanation: The Java programming model uses annotations from the com.microsoft.azure.functions.annotation package to declare the function name, trigger, and input and output bindings. Base classes, method names, or POM entries alone don't define bindings.
