questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: A Service Bus-triggered function must connect with its managed identity instead of a connection string. The binding's Connection property is ServiceBusConnection. Which app setting should you add?

options.text: ServiceBusConnection = Endpoint=sb://...;SharedAccessKey=...
AzureWebJobsServiceBus = managed
ServiceBusConnection__fullyQualifiedNamespace = contoso.servicebus.windows.net
ServiceBusConnection__identity = true only

questions.explanation: Identity-based connections use settings with the connection name as a prefix, such as <CONNECTION>__fullyQualifiedNamespace, which tells the extension to authenticate with the app's managed identity. The identity also needs a data role such as Azure Service Bus Data Receiver. A SharedAccessKey string is what you want to remove, and the other settings aren't valid ways to switch to identity-based connections.
questions.source_title: Configure connections to remote services in Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: You store identity-based connection settings for a function app in Azure App Configuration instead of app settings. How must the setting names be written?

options.text: Use : or / as the key separator, for example ServiceBusConnection:fullyQualifiedNamespace, instead of the double underscore
Use the double underscore exactly as in app settings
App Configuration can't store these settings
Use a dot, for example ServiceBusConnection.fullyQualifiedNamespace

questions.explanation: The double underscore is how environment variables express hierarchy. When the setting comes from App Configuration (or Key Vault), the documentation says to use a valid key separator such as : or / in place of __ so the name resolves correctly.
questions.source_title: Configure connections to remote services in Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: A function must run every day at 02:30. Which timer trigger schedule (NCRONTAB, six fields) is correct?
questions.explanation: The Functions timer trigger uses six-field NCRONTAB expressions: second, minute, hour, day, month, day of week. 0 30 2 * * * fires at 02:30:00 every day. The five-field form omits seconds, and the other expressions put values in the wrong fields.
questions.source_title: Timer trigger for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: You are creating a new .NET function app in November 2026. Which execution model should you use?

options.text: The in-process model
The isolated worker model
A function.json-only model with no .NET code
The v1 runtime

questions.explanation: The isolated worker model runs your .NET code in a separate worker process and is the supported model going forward; support for the in-process model ended in November 2026, and the v1 runtime is long out of support. In the isolated model, host.json mainly controls host runtime logging, and your application controls its own logs.
questions.source_title: Differences between the isolated worker model and the in-process model for .NET on Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: A function on the Flex Consumption plan must run when blobs are uploaded, and the blob trigger in polling mode isn't an option. Which blob trigger source should you use?

options.text: A timer trigger that lists the container every second
An HTTP trigger called by the uploader
A Queue storage trigger without any event subscription
The Event Grid-based blob trigger (source set to EventGrid)

questions.explanation: The Event Grid source for the blob trigger delivers blob events with lower latency than container polling, and it's the supported blob trigger option on Flex Consumption. Polling the container with a timer is slow and costly, an HTTP call requires every uploader to cooperate, and a queue trigger needs something to put messages in the queue.
questions.source_title: Azure Blob storage bindings for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: A function is triggered by an HTTP request and must read a document from Cosmos DB by the id in the route, then save a new document. Which binding set fits?

options.text: Two HTTP triggers
A Cosmos DB trigger and an HTTP output binding
A timer trigger and a Cosmos DB input binding
An HTTP trigger, a Cosmos DB input binding using {id} from the route, and a Cosmos DB output binding

questions.explanation: The HTTP trigger starts the function, a Cosmos DB input binding can look up a document using a binding expression from the route, and a Cosmos DB output binding saves documents. The Cosmos DB trigger reacts to changes rather than HTTP requests, and a function can only have one trigger.
questions.source_title: Azure Cosmos DB trigger and bindings for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: You want an HTTP-triggered function to be reachable at /api/products/42, with 42 passed to the function as an integer parameter. What should you configure?

options.text: The FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME setting
A binding expression {queueTrigger}
A route template on the HTTP trigger, such as products/{id:int}
A timer schedule

questions.explanation: HTTP triggers accept a route template, and route parameters can have constraints like {id:int}, which makes the value available to the function and its bindings. {queueTrigger} is for queue messages, and the other settings don't define URLs.
questions.source_title: Azure Functions HTTP triggers and bindings

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: What is the main benefit of using input and output bindings instead of calling service SDKs directly in a function?

options.text: They remove the need for a trigger
They connect the function to other services declaratively, so you don't write data-access and connection code
They guarantee exactly-once processing
They make the function run on GPUs

questions.explanation: Bindings give you a declarative way to pass data into and return data from a function without custom data-access code; the runtime handles connections and serialization. They don't change hardware, replace the trigger, or guarantee exactly-once processing.
questions.source_title: Java developer reference for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: A Cosmos DB-triggered function receives batches of changed documents. Which parameter type should it accept in C# to process a batch?

options.text: IEnumerable<T> or IReadOnlyList<T> of a JSON-serializable type
A TimerInfo object
A QueueClient
A single HttpRequest

questions.explanation: The Cosmos DB trigger delivers changes as a batch of documents, which you bind to a collection of a JSON-serializable type. HttpRequest belongs to HTTP triggers, QueueClient to queue bindings, and TimerInfo to timer triggers.
questions.source_title: Azure Cosmos DB trigger and bindings for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Azure Functions triggers and bindings (serverless APIs)
questions.stem: A function uses a Service Bus output binding to send a message after processing an HTTP request. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Output bindings require the in-process model
The Service Bus output binding also triggers the function
Output bindings can only write to Storage
The output binding sends the value returned or assigned in the function to the configured queue or topic

questions.explanation: The Service Bus output binding sends messages to a queue or topic using the value your function returns or assigns to the binding. The trigger is separate, output bindings exist for many services, and they're supported in the isolated worker model and other languages.
questions.source_title: Azure Service Bus bindings for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: You are creating a new serverless function app with event-driven scaling. Which hosting plan does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: Shared App Service plan
Free App Service plan
Flex Consumption
Consumption (legacy)

questions.explanation: The hosting options documentation calls the Consumption plan legacy and recommends Flex Consumption for new serverless function apps, with migration of existing Consumption apps. Azure Functions doesn't support the Free or Shared App Service tiers.
questions.source_title: Azure Functions hosting options

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: Which capabilities does the Flex Consumption plan add compared with the legacy Consumption plan? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.

options.text: Virtual network integration
Deployment slots
Unlimited execution time with no grace period on scale-in
Always ready instances to reduce cold starts

questions.explanation: Flex Consumption adds always ready instances, per-function scaling, and virtual network integration while still scaling to zero. It doesn't currently support deployment slots, and although there's no enforced maximum timeout, running executions get a 60-minute grace period during scale-in.
questions.source_title: Azure Functions Flex Consumption plan hosting

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: You plan to migrate a Consumption plan function app to Flex Consumption. The app uses staging deployment slots for swaps. What should you consider?

options.text: Slots are converted automatically into Flex instances
Flex Consumption doesn't currently support deployment slots, so you need another release strategy
Slots only work on Flex Consumption
Slots require the Free tier

questions.explanation: The migration guide says to check deployment slot usage because Flex Consumption doesn't currently support deployment slots. You would need a different approach, such as separate apps, or a plan that supports slots like Premium or Dedicated.
questions.source_title: Migrate Consumption plan apps to the Flex Consumption plan

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: How are deployment packages handled on the Flex Consumption plan compared with Premium?

options.text: Flex Consumption mounts an Azure Files share for content, like Premium
Flex Consumption requires container images
Flex Consumption only supports FTP
Flex Consumption uses its own package deployment to a Blob storage container, while ZIP deploy isn't supported on Flex

questions.explanation: Flex Consumption hosts deployment packages in a Blob storage container and supports only its own package deployment technology; ZIP deployment is listed as not supported. Premium and Consumption on Windows use Azure Files content settings that Flex doesn't need. Flex Consumption doesn't support container images.
questions.source_title: Deployment technologies in Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: Where do you configure the maximum execution time for all functions in a function app?

options.text: The functionTimeout property in host.json
The WEBSITES_PORT app setting
local.settings.json in Azure
The Dockerfile

questions.explanation: functionTimeout in host.json sets the timeout for function executions in the app, using a timespan string. When an execution exceeds it, a timeout error occurs and the worker process restarts. WEBSITES_PORT is for containers on App Service, local.settings.json is only used locally, and a Dockerfile doesn't control function timeouts.
questions.source_title: Azure Functions hosting options

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: A developer committed local.settings.json, which contains connection strings, to Git. What is the correct practice?

options.text: Commit it so Azure reads the settings during deployment
Exclude local.settings.json from source control; it's for local development only, and app settings in Azure hold the deployed values
Rename it to host.json
Encrypt it and keep it in the repository

questions.explanation: local.settings.json stores app settings for the local Functions runtime only, can contain secrets, and should stay out of source control (the generated .gitignore excludes it). In Azure, values come from application settings, which you can publish deliberately with --publish-local-settings. host.json holds host configuration, not secrets.
questions.source_title: Code and test Azure Functions locally

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: Which statement about host.json is correct?

options.text: It stores connection strings for triggers
It only applies when running locally
Its settings configure the Functions host and apply both when running locally and in Azure
It's ignored by function apps written in Python

questions.explanation: host.json configures the Functions host, for example logging, extension settings, and functionTimeout, and it applies both locally and in Azure. Connection strings and other app settings belong in application settings (or local.settings.json locally), and host.json applies to all languages.
questions.source_title: host.json reference for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: You are publishing with Azure Functions Core Tools and also want the values in local.settings.json created as app settings in Azure. Which command does this?

options.text: az functionapp create --local-settings
func azure functionapp publish <app> --publish-local-settings
func start --publish
func pack --settings

questions.explanation: func azure functionapp publish deploys the project, and --publish-local-settings creates app settings in the function app from local.settings.json. func start runs locally, az functionapp create has no such option, and func pack creates a deployment package without deploying settings.
questions.source_title: Develop Azure Functions locally by using Core Tools

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: An HTTP-triggered API must never have a cold start, needs virtual network access, and runs continuously under steady load with occasional bursts. Which plan characteristic addresses the cold-start requirement on Premium?

options.text: A grace period of 10 minutes
Prewarmed and always ready instances, with at least one instance always running
Running on the Free tier
Scale to zero when idle

questions.explanation: The Premium plan mitigates cold starts with prewarmed and always ready instances, keeping a minimum of one instance running, and it supports virtual networks. Scaling to zero causes cold starts, the grace period concerns scale-in, and Functions doesn't support the Free tier.
questions.source_title: Event-driven scaling in Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: During scale-in on the Flex Consumption or Premium plan, how long can currently executing functions continue to run?

options.text: Up to 10 seconds
Up to 24 hours
They are stopped immediately
Up to 60 minutes

questions.explanation: The grace period for executing functions during scale-in can extend up to 60 minutes on Flex Consumption and Premium, compared with up to 10 minutes on the Consumption plan. Executions aren't killed immediately.
questions.source_title: Event-driven scaling in Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: A function app runs on a Dedicated (App Service) plan and goes idle overnight, causing slow first requests. What should you enable?

options.text: The Free tier
Scale to zero
A shorter functionTimeout
Always On

questions.explanation: On a Dedicated plan, Always On keeps the app running continuously, which is the cold-start mitigation for that plan; there's no dynamic scaling to zero. A shorter timeout doesn't keep the app warm, and Functions doesn't support the Free tier. Even with Always On, individual executions are still limited by functionTimeout.
questions.source_title: Event-driven scaling in Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: You want to run Azure Functions as containers with custom dependencies, alongside other microservices that use Dapr and revisions. Which hosting option fits?

options.text: The legacy Consumption plan
Azure Functions on Azure Container Apps
The Free App Service tier
Azure Container Registry Tasks

questions.explanation: Functions on Azure Container Apps runs function apps as containers with custom dependencies and gets Container Apps features such as KEDA scaling, Dapr, revisions, and sidecars, scaling to zero and out to 1,000 instances (default maximum 10). The legacy Consumption plan doesn't support containers, Functions doesn't support the Free tier, and ACR Tasks only builds images.
questions.source_title: Azure Functions on Azure Container Apps overview

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: In Azure, how does Python function code read configuration values such as a storage account name?

options.text: From requirements.txt
As environment variables populated from the function app's application settings
From local.settings.json deployed with the code
From host.json

questions.explanation: Application settings in the function app's configuration are exposed to code as environment variables in Azure, while local.settings.json provides the same values only during local development. host.json configures the host, and requirements.txt lists packages.
questions.source_title: Python developer reference for Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: A queue-triggered function on Flex Consumption should never scale beyond 20 instances so it doesn't overload a downstream database. What should you configure?

options.text: The maximum instance count for the app's scale settings
functionTimeout in host.json
A deployment slot
The extension bundle version

questions.explanation: Flex Consumption lets you limit scale-out with a maximum instance count, which applies to on-demand instances in each per-function scale group. functionTimeout limits execution length, Flex doesn't support slots, and the extension bundle version doesn't control scaling.
questions.source_title: Event-driven scaling in Azure Functions

questions.skill_name: Configure and deploy function apps
questions.stem: A function app on the Linux Consumption plan still runs the Functions v3 runtime. What does Microsoft announce for these apps?

options.text: v3 is the recommended runtime for new apps
They will be upgraded to v4 automatically with no action
They stop running after September 30, 2026, so migrate to the v4 runtime (and to Flex Consumption)
They move to the Free tier

questions.explanation: The infrastructure-as-code guidance warns that function apps still running the end-of-life v3 runtime on Linux in a Consumption plan stop running after September 30, 2026, and must migrate to v4. New serverless apps should also use Flex Consumption, because Linux Consumption is retired.
questions.source_title: Automate resource deployment for your function app

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: A developer accidentally deletes a secret from a key vault that has soft delete enabled with the default settings. What can you do?

options.text: Wait for it to reappear automatically after 24 hours
Recover the secret, because deleted objects remain recoverable for the retention period (90 days by default)
Nothing; deletion is permanent
Restore it only from an Azure Backup vault

questions.explanation: Soft delete works like a recycle bin: deleted vaults and objects stay recoverable for a configurable retention period, 90 days by default, and can be recovered or purged during that time. Deletion isn't immediately permanent, no separate backup service is required, and objects don't come back by themselves.
questions.source_title: Azure Key Vault soft delete and purge protection

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: Security policy requires that no one, including administrators, can permanently delete secrets before the soft-delete retention period ends. What should you enable?

options.text: Purge protection
Secret expiration dates
Azure RBAC authorization
A private endpoint

questions.explanation: Purge protection blocks purging (permanent deletion) of the vault and its objects until the retention period has passed, protecting against malicious insiders. Once enabled it can't be turned off. RBAC controls who can perform actions, private endpoints control network access, and expiration dates don't prevent deletion.
questions.source_title: Azure Key Vault soft delete and purge protection

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: You delete a secret named DbPassword in a soft-delete-enabled vault and immediately try to create a new secret with the same name. The request fails with a conflict. Why?

options.text: Secret names can never be reused
The deleted secret still exists in a soft-deleted state; you must recover it or purge it before reusing the name
You need the Key Vault Secrets User role
The vault must be restarted

questions.explanation: A soft-deleted secret keeps its name reserved until it is recovered or purged (and purging isn't allowed while purge protection is on, until the retention period ends). Names can be reused after purging. Vaults don't restart, and Secrets User only grants read access.
questions.source_title: Azure Key Vault soft delete and purge protection

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: A web app's managed identity must only read secret values from a key vault that uses the Azure RBAC permission model. Which role should you assign?

options.text: Key Vault Secrets User
Key Vault Secrets Officer
Owner
Key Vault Contributor

questions.explanation: Key Vault Secrets User grants read access to secret contents, which is all the app needs. Secrets Officer can also create, update, and delete secrets. Key Vault Contributor manages the vault resource (management plane) and doesn't grant data access in the RBAC model, and Owner is far too broad.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Use Azure Key Vault with a virtual machine in .NET

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: When you create a new key vault, which permission model does Microsoft's guidance use for granting apps and users access?

options.text: Sharing the vault's access key with each app
Anonymous access restricted by IP
Storing the vault password in app settings
Azure RBAC (for example with -EnableRbacAuthorization), assigning built-in roles such as Key Vault Secrets User

questions.explanation: The guidance creates vaults with Azure RBAC authorization enabled (and purge protection) and grants access with built-in data roles. Key Vault has no shared access key or vault password, and anonymous access isn't supported.
questions.source_title: Apps, API keys, and Azure Key Vault secrets

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: Which code correctly creates a client to read secrets from the vault contoso-kv in .NET without storing credentials?

options.text: new SecretClient(new Uri("https://contoso-kv.azurewebsites.net"))
new KeyVaultClient(connectionString)
new SecretClient(new Uri("https://contoso-kv.vault.azure.net"), new DefaultAzureCredential())
new SecretClient("contoso-kv", "admin-password")

questions.explanation: SecretClient takes the vault URI (https://<vault-name>.vault.azure.net) and a token credential; DefaultAzureCredential is the recommended passwordless option. Vaults don't have passwords or connection strings, and azurewebsites.net is App Service's domain.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Azure Key Vault secret client library for .NET

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: The same code uses DefaultAzureCredential on a developer laptop and in an Azure web app. Which identities does it typically use in each place?

options.text: The vault's admin key in both places
The developer's signed-in Azure CLI (or IDE) credentials locally, and the app's managed identity in Azure
Anonymous access locally and a certificate in Azure
A hard-coded client secret in both places

questions.explanation: DefaultAzureCredential tries a chain of credential sources: locally it can use the developer's Azure CLI or IDE sign-in, as in the quickstarts, and in Azure it uses the resource's managed identity. That's why the same code works without secrets in both environments.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Azure Key Vault secret client library for .NET

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: Your code calls GetSecret("ApiKey") without specifying a version. The secret has three versions. Which value is returned?

options.text: A random version
The first version ever created
The latest (current) version
An error, because the version is required

questions.explanation: Getting a secret by name without a version returns the latest version of that secret; to read an older one, pass its version identifier. That's why apps that always read the latest version pick up rotated values without code changes.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Azure Key Vault secret client library for .NET

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: What happens when you call set_secret with an existing secret name and a new value?

options.text: A second secret with the same name is created
Key Vault creates a new version of the secret; previous versions are kept
The existing value is overwritten and the old value is lost
The call fails because the secret exists

questions.explanation: Secrets are versioned: setting a value on an existing name creates a new current version while older versions remain retrievable by version ID. This is what makes rotation and rollback possible. Names stay unique within a vault.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Azure Key Vault secret client library for Python

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: A storage account key stored in Key Vault must be rotated automatically without downtime for apps using it. Microsoft's tutorial for resources with two sets of credentials uses which approach?

options.text: A timer that rotates both keys at the same moment
A key rotation policy on the secret
Delete and recreate the storage account every 90 days
An Event Grid SecretNearExpiry event triggers a function that regenerates the alternate key and stores it as a new secret version

questions.explanation: For resources with two credentials, the function regenerates the key that isn't currently in use and adds it to Key Vault as a new secret version, so apps keep working with the other key during the switch. The trigger is an Event Grid subscription on SecretNearExpiry. Rotation policies apply to cryptographic keys, and rotating both credentials at once causes downtime.
questions.source_title: Automate rotation of a secret with two sets of credentials

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: You subscribe a function to the Key Vault SecretNearExpiry event, but it never fires for your API key secret. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: SecretNearExpiry only works for certificates
The secret has no expiration date set, so it can never be near expiry
The function needs the Key Vault Administrator role
Event Grid only supports Key Vault in Premium tier

questions.explanation: SecretNearExpiry is raised about 30 days before a secret's expiration date, so the secret must have an expiration date (for example set with az keyvault secret set --expires). The event works for secrets, and the function doesn't need vault admin rights to receive events.
questions.source_title: Apps, API keys, and Azure Key Vault secrets

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: Which statement about automatic rotation in Azure Key Vault is correct?

options.text: Only certificates can be rotated
Secrets and keys both rotate automatically when they expire
Rotation requires deleting the old object first
Cryptographic keys support a rotation policy that rotates them automatically; secrets are rotated with your own logic, typically triggered by Event Grid near-expiry events

questions.explanation: Keys have a rotation policy with lifetime actions (rotate, notify), where the minimum rotation interval is seven days. Secrets don't have a built-in rotation engine, so rotation is implemented with functions or automation reacting to events such as SecretNearExpiry. Rotation creates new versions instead of deleting old ones.
questions.source_title: Configure cryptographic key auto-rotation in Azure Key Vault

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: You configure a key rotation policy and want an Event Grid notification 30 days before the key expires. What else is required?

options.text: An expiry time on the rotation policy and an expiration date on the key
Purge protection disabled
A Premium-tier App Configuration store
A secret with the same name as the key

questions.explanation: The notification time in a key rotation policy raises a near-expiry Event Grid event, and it requires an expiry time on the rotation policy and an expiration date on the key. Secrets, purge protection settings, and App Configuration aren't part of this.
questions.source_title: Configure cryptographic key auto-rotation in Azure Key Vault

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: An app retrieves secrets in a hot code path, and calls to Key Vault occasionally fail with transient errors. Which client configuration does the tutorial show?

options.text: Disable TLS to reduce latency
Create a new SecretClient for every request
Switch to anonymous access
Configure SecretClientOptions with an exponential retry policy (delay, max delay, max retries)

questions.explanation: The tutorial configures SecretClientOptions.Retry with exponential mode, delays, and a maximum number of retries so transient failures are retried safely. Creating clients per request adds overhead, and disabling TLS or using anonymous access isn't possible or safe. Caching secret values in the app also reduces calls.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Use a managed identity to connect Key Vault to a web app

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: Your application must sign tokens with an RSA private key, and the private key must never leave Key Vault. Which object type should you store?

options.text: A secret containing the PEM private key
An App Configuration key-value
An environment variable in App Service
A key, and perform sign operations through the Key Vault keys API

questions.explanation: Key Vault keys support cryptographic operations such as sign and decrypt inside the service, so the private key material isn't returned to the app. Storing the PEM as a secret means the app downloads the private key. App Configuration and environment variables aren't designed for private key protection.
questions.source_title: Azure Key Vault secret client library for .NET

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: You need RSA keys protected by a hardware security module (RSA-HSM) for customer-managed key encryption. What does this require in Key Vault?

options.text: The Standard tier with soft delete disabled
The Premium tier of Key Vault
A Basic tier vault
Any tier, because all keys are HSM-backed

questions.explanation: RSA-HSM keys are only available in the Premium tier of Key Vault; Standard vaults use software-protected keys. Soft delete settings don't affect key protection type, and Key Vault has no Basic tier.
questions.source_title: Use customer-managed keys to encrypt App Configuration data

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: An app stores a JSON object with several values as a single Key Vault secret. What must the app do?

options.text: Serialize the object to a string (for example JSON or Base64) before setting it, and deserialize it after reading
Split it into keys
Nothing; Key Vault stores native JSON objects
Store it as a certificate

questions.explanation: A secret value is a string. The JavaScript developer guide notes that you must serialize values such as JSON or Base64 data before setting them and deserialize them after retrieval. Keys are for cryptographic material, and certificates are for X.509 certificates.
questions.source_title: Set, update, and rotate Key Vault secrets with JavaScript

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: You must load a TLS certificate, including its private key, that is stored in Key Vault. How can the app retrieve the full certificate with the private key?

options.text: Certificates with private keys can't be retrieved
Read it as a secret, because Key Vault stores the certificate's public and private key pair as a secret
Read it from the certificate endpoint, which always includes the private key
Read it from the keys endpoint, which returns the private key

questions.explanation: Key Vault stores a certificate's public and private key pair as a secret with the same name, so an app can retrieve the full certificate through the secrets API. The certificates endpoint returns the public certificate and metadata, and the keys endpoint doesn't return private key material.
questions.source_title: Reload secrets and certificates from Key Vault automatically

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: In the JavaScript SDK, which statement about deleting a secret is correct?

options.text: beginDeleteSecret starts a long-running operation and returns a poller you can wait on
Deleting a secret also deletes the vault
deleteSecret deletes the secret synchronously and permanently
You can only delete secrets in the Azure portal

questions.explanation: Deletion is a long-running operation in the SDK: beginDeleteSecret returns a poller that completes when the secret is deleted (moved to the soft-deleted state in a soft-delete-enabled vault). It doesn't permanently purge the secret or affect the vault, and SDKs and the CLI can delete secrets.
questions.source_title: SecretClient class (JavaScript)

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: A Python app sets a secret and then reads it back. Which library and class does the quickstart use?

options.text: azure-storage-blob with BlobClient
requests with the vault's admin password
azure-keyvault-secrets with SecretClient, authenticated with DefaultAzureCredential
azure-appconfiguration with AzureAppConfigurationClient

questions.explanation: The Python quickstart uses SecretClient from azure-keyvault-secrets with a vault URL and DefaultAzureCredential from azure-identity, then calls set_secret and get_secret. The other libraries target Blob storage and App Configuration, and Key Vault has no admin password.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Azure Key Vault secret client library for Python

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: A secret's properties show recoveryLevel Recoverable+Purgeable and recoverableDays 90. What do these tell you?

options.text: The secret will be rotated every 90 days
The secret can only be read 90 times
The secret expires in 90 days
The secret can be recovered for 90 days after deletion and can also be purged during that time, because purge protection isn't enabled

questions.explanation: recoverableDays is the number of days a deleted secret can be recovered, and the recovery level describes the protection: Recoverable+Purgeable means soft delete is on but purge protection isn't, so it can be purged before the period ends. These properties don't describe expiry, read limits, or rotation.
questions.source_title: Set, update, and rotate Key Vault secrets with JavaScript

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: Container apps, functions, and VMs in your solution all need the same set of Key Vault permissions, and you want one identity you can grant once and reuse. Which kind of managed identity fits?

options.text: A personal Microsoft account
The Key Vault's own identity
A system-assigned identity, which can be shared across resources
A user-assigned managed identity attached to each resource

questions.explanation: A user-assigned managed identity is a standalone resource that can be attached to multiple Azure resources, so one role assignment covers them all; system-assigned identities are tied to a single resource's lifecycle. The vault's identity and personal accounts aren't meant for app access.
questions.source_title: Manage secrets in Azure Container Apps

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: A deployment pipeline must create and update secrets in a key vault (RBAC model) but should not manage keys, certificates, or vault access. Which role fits with least privilege?

options.text: Key Vault Secrets Officer
Key Vault Crypto Officer
Key Vault Secrets User
Key Vault Administrator

questions.explanation: Key Vault Secrets Officer can perform all actions on secrets, including create, update, and delete, but not on keys or certificates. Secrets User can only read secret contents, Administrator covers every data-plane object, and Crypto Officer manages keys rather than secrets.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Use Azure Key Vault with a virtual machine in .NET

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: You store a third-party API key in Key Vault and want it to expire after 180 days so near-expiry events can drive rotation. How can you set this with the Azure CLI?

options.text: az keyvault update --retention-days 180
az keyvault secret set --vault-name <vault> --name MyApiKey --value <value> --expires <date 180 days ahead>
az keyvault secret show --ttl 180
az keyvault secret set --rotation-policy 180d

questions.explanation: The --expires parameter of az keyvault secret set sets the secret's expiration date, which the apps-and-API-keys guidance uses with 180 days; Key Vault then raises SecretNearExpiry about 30 days earlier. Secrets don't have rotation policies, retention days configure soft delete, and show only reads.
questions.source_title: Apps, API keys, and Azure Key Vault secrets

questions.skill_name: Secure secrets with Azure Key Vault (rotation and retrieval)
questions.stem: Several services cache a connection string from Key Vault. You want them notified the moment a new version of that secret is created so they can reload it. Which Key Vault event should they subscribe to through Event Grid?

options.text: Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated
Microsoft.KeyVault.SecretNewVersionCreated
Microsoft.KeyVault.SecretNearExpiry
Microsoft.KeyVault.VaultDeleted

questions.explanation: Key Vault publishes SecretNewVersionCreated when a new version of a secret is created, so subscribers can refresh cached values right away. SecretNearExpiry fires 30 days before expiration, BlobCreated is a Storage event, and vault deletion isn't the signal for a new secret version.
questions.source_title: Azure Key Vault as Event Grid source

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: The key AppName:DbEndpoint must have different values for Test, Staging, and Production in one App Configuration store. How should you model this?

options.text: Create three stores with different names for the key
Use feature flags
Append the environment to every value
Use the same key with labels Test, Staging, and Production

questions.explanation: Labels differentiate key-values that share a key, and a common use is one label per environment. Apps select the label they need while key names in code stay the same. Separate stores add management overhead, encoding environments in values is error-prone, and feature flags are for toggling functionality.
questions.source_title: Keys and values in Azure App Configuration

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: A .NET app calls AddAzureAppConfiguration with default options. New keys added with the label dev don't appear in the app. Why?

options.text: Labels can't be read by .NET apps
The app needs the App Configuration Data Owner role
By default the provider loads only key-values with no label; you must select the dev label explicitly
New keys are only visible after 24 hours

questions.explanation: The .NET provider loads key-values without a label unless you specify selectors, so keys labeled dev are ignored until you select that label (for example by selecting keys with labels null and dev). Read access only needs Data Reader, and keys are visible immediately.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Use dynamic configuration in an ASP.NET Core app

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: An app must pick up configuration changes without restarting, but you want to avoid inconsistent states while several keys are being edited and keep requests to the store low. What does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: Store all configuration in one large JSON key and poll it constantly
Restart the app after every change
Watch a single sentinel key and refresh all configuration only when the sentinel changes; update the sentinel last
Poll every key individually every second

questions.explanation: A sentinel key is updated after you finish changing the other keys. The provider monitors only the sentinel and reloads everything when it changes, which keeps configuration consistent and reduces requests to the store. Polling every key frequently adds load and can load half-finished changes.
questions.source_title: Azure App Configuration best practices

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: You configured dynamic refresh in ASP.NET Core with ConfigureRefresh and a sentinel key, but the app never sees updates. What is a likely missing piece?

options.text: The app must use access keys instead of Entra ID
The sentinel key must be deleted after each update
Dynamic refresh only works in Python
Refresh must actually be triggered, for example with the App Configuration refresh middleware or by calling TryRefreshAsync

questions.explanation: ConfigureRefresh tells the provider what to watch and how long values are cached, but it doesn't refresh on every read; refresh runs when the middleware (UseAzureAppConfiguration) or your code calls TryRefreshAsync. Deleting the sentinel isn't the pattern, and authentication type and language don't change this.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Use dynamic configuration in an ASP.NET Core app

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: A controller reads settings through IOptions<Settings>, and it never shows updated values even though refresh is configured. What should you change?

options.text: Use IOptionsSnapshot<T> or IOptionsMonitor<T>, because IOptions<T> doesn't read configuration again after the app starts
Store settings in Key Vault instead
Use a static variable
Restart the app every minute

questions.explanation: The dynamic configuration tutorial notes that IOptions<T> doesn't read configuration data after the app has started, so it can't reflect refreshed values; IOptionsSnapshot<T> (per request) or IOptionsMonitor<T> do. Static variables and scheduled restarts are workarounds, and Key Vault isn't the fix here.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Use dynamic configuration in an ASP.NET Core app

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: You toggle a feature flag in App Configuration. With default settings in the ASP.NET Core quickstart, how soon does the app see the change?

options.text: Within about 30 seconds, the default feature flag refresh interval
Immediately, on the next request
Only after a restart
After 24 hours

questions.explanation: The default refresh interval for feature flags is 30 seconds, configurable through feature flag options, so the app picks up the change without restarting or redeploying. It isn't instant, and 24 hours is the App Service Key Vault reference cache, not App Configuration feature flags.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Add feature flags to an ASP.NET Core app

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: An app needs a database password and other settings. How should you combine App Configuration and Key Vault?

options.text: Store the password in Key Vault and create a Key Vault reference in App Configuration; the app resolves it with an identity that can read the vault
Store all settings in Key Vault and drop App Configuration
Store the password directly as an App Configuration value
Put the password in a feature flag

questions.explanation: App Configuration can hold Key Vault references: it stores the secret's URI rather than its value, and the provider uses the app's credentials to fetch the secret from Key Vault. The app's identity therefore needs read access to the secret too. Best practice is to keep secrets in Key Vault, not as plain configuration values.
questions.source_title: Azure App Configuration best practices

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: A secret referenced from App Configuration is rotated in Key Vault, but the app keeps using the old value. How can the .NET provider pick up rotated secrets without restarting?

options.text: Set the feature flag refresh interval to 0
Change the label of the reference every time
Configure a secret refresh interval for Key Vault references (SetSecretRefreshInterval)
Delete the App Configuration store

questions.explanation: The provider caches resolved Key Vault secrets. Setting a secret refresh interval makes it reload secrets and certificates from Key Vault periodically, so rotated values are picked up automatically. Relabeling keys or changing feature flag refresh doesn't affect secret caching.
questions.source_title: Reload secrets and certificates from Key Vault automatically

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: An application only reads configuration from App Configuration using Microsoft Entra ID. Which role should its identity have?

options.text: App Configuration Reader
App Configuration Data Reader
App Configuration Data Owner
Reader on the subscription

questions.explanation: App Configuration Data Reader grants read access to the data plane (key-values, snapshots, feature flags). App Configuration Reader is a control-plane role that reads the resource but not its data, Data Owner adds write and delete, and subscription Reader doesn't grant data access.
questions.source_title: Access Azure App Configuration using Microsoft Entra ID

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: You want to deploy a new set of configuration changes safely, test it, and be able to roll back to a known-good set instantly. Which App Configuration feature helps most?

options.text: Increasing the sentinel refresh interval
Configuration snapshots, which are immutable point-in-time versions of key-values
Using longer key names
Disabling labels

questions.explanation: Snapshots capture a consistent, immutable set of configuration that you can build and test before production and progressively roll out, keeping last-known-good snapshots for rollback. Refresh intervals, key names, and labels alone don't give an immutable versioned set.
questions.source_title: Secure your Azure App Configuration deployment

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: A multitenant app stores per-tenant settings in one App Configuration store and also needs environment variations. What does the Azure Architecture Center recommend?

options.text: Use the tenant ID as the label for every key
Use key prefixes for tenant-specific settings and keep labels for other purposes, such as environments
Store tenant settings in feature flags
Create one store per environment and one label per tenant

questions.explanation: If tenant IDs become labels, labels can't be used for anything else, so the guidance suggests key prefixes for tenant-specific settings and labels for purposes such as environments or versions. Feature flags are for turning features on and off.
questions.source_title: Multitenancy and Azure App Configuration

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: A Python console app should reload settings when a key named sentinel changes. Which provider API does the tutorial use?

options.text: os.environ["sentinel"]
azure.keyvault.secrets.SecretClient
A timer that re-imports the module
load(...) with refresh_on=[WatchKey("sentinel")] and a call to refresh

questions.explanation: The Python provider's load function accepts refresh options, including WatchKey for the sentinel; calling refresh checks the sentinel and reloads all values if it changed. Environment variables and Key Vault clients don't watch App Configuration, and re-importing modules isn't the provider's mechanism.
questions.source_title: Tutorial: Use dynamic configuration in Python

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: Your AKS workloads read configuration from Kubernetes ConfigMaps, and you want those ConfigMaps populated and refreshed from Azure App Configuration without changing app code. What should you use?

options.text: The Azure App Configuration Kubernetes Provider
A Kubernetes CronJob that runs kubectl edit
Container insights
An ACR task

questions.explanation: The App Configuration Kubernetes Provider runs in the cluster and generates ConfigMaps (and Secrets for Key Vault references) from an App Configuration store, with optional periodic refresh. ACR tasks build images, Container insights collects logs and metrics, and manual kubectl edits aren't automated or reliable.
questions.source_title: Azure App Configuration Kubernetes Provider reference

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: Your App Configuration store has replicas in two regions. How do the App Configuration providers use them by default?

options.text: They discover replicas automatically and fail over to them when the primary endpoint is unavailable
Replicas are only for backups and can't serve reads
They write to all replicas on every read
They ignore replicas unless you list each one in code

questions.explanation: Replica discovery is on by default in the providers (replicaDiscoveryEnabled defaults to true in the Kubernetes provider), so clients discover replicas and use them for failover, and load balancing across replicas can also be enabled. Replicas serve reads, and providers don't write on reads.
questions.source_title: Azure App Configuration Kubernetes Provider reference

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: A JavaScript app calls load() from the App Configuration provider without options. Which key-values are loaded?

options.text: Only feature flags
All key-values that have no label
Only keys that start with the app name
All key-values with every label

questions.explanation: By default the JavaScript provider's load method loads all configuration with no label. Use selectors in the options (key filter and label filter) to load other labels or limit keys, and enable feature flags separately.
questions.source_title: JavaScript configuration provider

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: How does the ASP.NET Core quickstart connect to App Configuration without storing a connection string?

options.text: A Key Vault reference to the store itself
options.Connect(new Uri(endpoint), new DefaultAzureCredential()), with the identity granted a data role on the store
Anonymous access to the store's endpoint
Using the store's primary access key in appsettings.json

questions.explanation: The provider can connect with the store endpoint and a token credential such as DefaultAzureCredential, which avoids connection strings; the identity needs App Configuration Data Reader (or Owner for writes). Access keys are secrets to manage, and stores don't allow anonymous reads.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Add feature flags to an ASP.NET Core app

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: How should you reference a key-value that explicitly has no label when querying App Configuration through its REST API?

options.text: Leave out the key
Use the label default
Use the null label value \0, URL-encoded as %00
Use an asterisk

questions.explanation: By default a key-value has no label; to explicitly select key-values without a label, use \0 (URL-encoded as %00). default is just a normal label name, and an asterisk matches any label rather than no label.
questions.source_title: Keys and values in Azure App Configuration

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: Which data does Microsoft recommend keeping outside App Configuration, referencing it from elsewhere if needed?

options.text: Secrets (in Key Vault) and large files (in Azure Storage)
Environment-specific endpoints
Logging levels
Feature flags

questions.explanation: App Configuration is meant for configuration you would otherwise put in files or environment variables. The best practices article suggests storing secrets in Key Vault, files in Azure Storage, and similar data in their natural stores, while feature flags, endpoints, and log levels fit App Configuration well.
questions.source_title: Azure App Configuration best practices

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: A CI/CD pipeline imports key-values into an App Configuration store using its service principal. Which role does it need?

options.text: App Configuration Data Reader
Key Vault Secrets User
App Configuration Reader
App Configuration Data Owner

questions.explanation: Writing, updating, and deleting key-values requires the data-plane App Configuration Data Owner role. Data Reader only reads data, App Configuration Reader is a control-plane role without data access, and Key Vault roles don't apply to App Configuration.
questions.source_title: Access Azure App Configuration using Microsoft Entra ID

questions.skill_name: Azure App Configuration
questions.stem: An ASP.NET Core app reads configuration section TestApp:Settings and binds it to a Settings class. How should the keys be named in App Configuration so they map to that section?

options.text: As a single key TestApp containing all settings as plain text
As TestApp_Settings_Message using underscores only
With the : delimiter, for example TestApp:Settings:Message and TestApp:Settings:FontSize
With the label Settings and keys Message and FontSize

questions.explanation: App Configuration keys are free-form strings, and hierarchical names using a delimiter such as : map to .NET configuration sections, so TestApp:Settings:Message binds to the Message property of the TestApp:Settings section. Labels create variants of a key, not hierarchy levels.
questions.source_title: Keys and values in Azure App Configuration

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: You add the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro to an ASP.NET Core app. Which two steps send traces, metrics, and logs to Application Insights? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.

options.text: Set the APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING environment variable to the resource's connection string
Install the Application Insights classic SDK alongside the distro
Set the instrumentation key in web.config
Call builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry().UseAzureMonitor() in Program.cs

questions.explanation: Enabling the distro means adding UseAzureMonitor() and supplying the connection string, typically through the APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING environment variable. Instrumentation keys alone are legacy, and installing the classic SDK next to the distro isn't needed and can duplicate telemetry.
questions.source_title: Azure Monitor Distro client library for .NET

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: Where should production apps get the Application Insights connection string when using the OpenTelemetry Distro?

options.text: From the user's browser cookies
From a query string parameter
From an environment variable (or a configuration file for Java), not hard-coded in code
Hard-coded in the source code

questions.explanation: Microsoft recommends setting the connection string in code only for local development and test; for production, use an environment variable, or a configuration file for Java. That keeps environment-specific values out of builds and lets you change them without redeploying.
questions.source_title: Enable OpenTelemetry in Application Insights

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: You upgrade from the Application Insights .NET SDK 2.x to 3.x, which is built on OpenTelemetry. The app configured only an instrumentation key. What must you change?

options.text: Remove all telemetry configuration
Add adaptive sampling settings
Provide a connection string, because SDK 3.x requires a connection string and can fail at startup without one
Nothing; instrumentation keys remain required

questions.explanation: The migration guide says to use TelemetryConfiguration.ConnectionString instead of an instrumentation key; SDK 3.x requires a connection string and can fail at startup if it isn't configured. Adaptive sampling is replaced by other sampling options, and removing configuration stops telemetry.
questions.source_title: Migrate from Application Insights classic SDKs to OpenTelemetry

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: Telemetry volume from a busy Node.js service is too high. Using the Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro, how do you keep about 10 percent of traces?

options.text: Set samplingRatio to 0.1 (and tracesPerSecond to 0 to use the ratio instead of a rate limit)
Set the log level to Error
Delete the Application Insights resource
Set maxDeliveryAttempts to 10

questions.explanation: The distro supports fixed-percentage sampling with samplingRatio and rate-limited sampling with tracesPerSecond; the documented example keeps about 10 percent of traces with samplingRatio 0.1 and tracesPerSecond 0. Log levels affect logs, not trace sampling, and maxDeliveryAttempts is an Event Grid setting.
questions.source_title: Configure OpenTelemetry in Application Insights

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: With sampling enabled in several microservices, you worry that a trace will be kept in one service but dropped in another. How does Application Insights reduce this risk?

options.text: It samples based on a hash of the trace ID, so all services make the same decision for the same trace
Every service always keeps 100 percent of dependencies
Sampling is disabled for distributed traces
Upstream services send a sampling flag that downstream services must obey

questions.explanation: Application Insights samples based on a hash of the trace ID to keep traces complete, so services sampling at the same rate make consistent decisions for a given trace. The FAQ notes that upstream sampling decisions in W3C headers don't drive the downstream decision; the trace ID hash does.
questions.source_title: Application Insights FAQ

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: With OpenTelemetry and Application Insights, in which tables are distributed tracing spans stored?

options.text: customEvents only
exceptions and pageViews
traces only
requests and dependencies

questions.explanation: Spans for distributed tracing are stored in the requests and dependencies tables (AppRequests and AppDependencies in Log Analytics). Application log records go to the traces table for legacy reasons. customEvents, exceptions, and pageViews hold other telemetry types.
questions.source_title: Application Insights telemetry data model

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: You need to find every telemetry item (requests, dependencies, logs) that belongs to one end-to-end transaction across services. Which field ties them together?

options.text: cloud_RoleInstance
itemCount
client_IP
operation_Id, which corresponds to the W3C trace-id

questions.explanation: Every telemetry item in a distributed trace shares the same operation_Id, which Application Insights maps from the W3C trace-id; the transaction diagnostics view shows all telemetry with that Operation ID. Role instance, client IP, and item count don't identify a transaction.
questions.source_title: Investigate failures, performance, and transactions with Application Insights

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: In the W3C Trace Context standard used by OpenTelemetry, what identifies the overall transaction and what identifies an individual operation within it?

options.text: The HTTP request ID and the thread ID
A 16-byte trace-id for the transaction and an 8-byte span-id for each operation
A GUID session ID and a sequence number
An 8-byte trace-id and a 16-byte span-id

questions.explanation: Each trace gets a globally unique 16-byte trace-id, and each activity within it gets a unique 8-byte span-id. These travel between services in the traceparent header so each service can continue the same trace.
questions.source_title: Distributed tracing and W3C Trace Context (Power Platform guidance)

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: In the Application Map, all your services appear under one confusing name. How do you give each service its own cloud role name with OpenTelemetry?

options.text: Use a separate Application Insights resource per HTTP route
Add a custom metric named role
Rename the Log Analytics workspace
Set the service.name resource attribute (for example with OTEL_SERVICE_NAME) for each service

questions.explanation: Application Insights maps the OpenTelemetry resource attributes service.name (with service.namespace) to the cloud role name, and service.instance.id to the role instance. Setting them per service, for example through OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, makes the map show distinct components.
questions.source_title: Configure OpenTelemetry in Application Insights

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: A Java service uses the Application Insights Java agent built on OpenTelemetry. You want a business method to appear as its own span with minimal code. What is the simplest option?

options.text: Add the method name to the connection string
Write a log line at the start and end of the method
Create a custom metric
Annotate the method with @WithSpan

questions.explanation: The simplest way to add your own spans in Java is OpenTelemetry's @WithSpan annotation, and spans populate the requests and dependencies tables. Log lines become traces rather than spans, metrics aggregate numbers, and the connection string only identifies the destination.
questions.source_title: Add and modify OpenTelemetry in Application Insights

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: You must add a property such as tenantId to every span before it is exported to Application Insights. Which OpenTelemetry extensibility point fits?

options.text: A KQL function
A Container Apps scale rule
A span processor registered with the distro
An Event Grid filter

questions.explanation: Span processors hook into span start and end and can add or modify attributes before export; the migration guide shows registering one with the distro to add a custom property. KQL runs at query time and can't change stored telemetry, and Event Grid filters and scale rules are unrelated.
questions.source_title: Migrate from Application Insights classic SDKs to OpenTelemetry

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: Health-check requests to /healthz flood Application Insights. How can you stop collecting them with OpenTelemetry?

options.text: Lower the sampling ratio to 0
Delete them in Log Analytics every day
Configure the HTTP instrumentation library to exclude those requests
Disable the Application Insights resource

questions.explanation: The filtering guide shows configuring instrumentation libraries (such as the HTTP instrumentation) to ignore specific incoming requests, so they are never recorded. Deleting data afterward doesn't stop ingestion costs, a sampling ratio of 0 drops everything, and disabling the resource stops all monitoring.
questions.source_title: Filter OpenTelemetry in Application Insights

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: In a Node.js app, the Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro is initialized after Express and the database client are imported, and outgoing calls aren't tracked. What should you change?

options.text: Initialize it after the first request
Use a different Application Insights resource
Initialize the distro before loading application libraries (for ESM, preload the distro loader)
Increase the sampling ratio

questions.explanation: Instrumentation must be enabled before the libraries it instruments are loaded; the guidance for Node.js says to enable it first, and ESM apps must preload the distro loader. Initializing later, changing resources, or changing sampling doesn't fix missing instrumentation.
questions.source_title: Filter OpenTelemetry in Application Insights

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: A project already initializes the Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro, and a teammate adds the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro initialization as well. What does Microsoft advise?

options.text: Initialize both to get double coverage
Don't initialize both distros together; use one
It doesn't matter, because they share state
Initialize the Azure Monitor Distro first, then the Microsoft distro

questions.explanation: The configuration guidance states that the Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro and the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro shouldn't be initialized together; Azure Monitor stays the destination with a single distro. Running both risks duplicate or conflicting pipelines.
questions.source_title: Configure OpenTelemetry in Application Insights

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: Your .NET app used EnableAdaptiveSampling in the classic Application Insights SDK. After moving to the OpenTelemetry-based SDK 3.x, what replaces it?

options.text: The functionTimeout setting
KQL sample operators
Sampling configured with TracesPerSecond or SamplingRatio
Event Grid retry policies

questions.explanation: The migration guide maps EnableAdaptiveSampling to the OpenTelemetry-based options TracesPerSecond (rate-limited) or SamplingRatio (fixed percentage). KQL sample operators only affect query results, and the other settings belong to other services.
questions.source_title: Migrate from Application Insights classic SDKs to OpenTelemetry

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: You want to record the distribution of order processing times (for percentiles) as a custom metric with OpenTelemetry. Which instrument fits?

options.text: A histogram created from a Meter
A log message
A span attribute
A counter

questions.explanation: Histograms record value distributions, which Application Insights can aggregate into percentiles; the add-and-modify guide includes a histogram example using the metrics API. Counters only add up values, and span attributes or log messages aren't aggregated as metrics.
questions.source_title: Add and modify OpenTelemetry in Application Insights

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: An OpenTelemetry span has kind CLIENT, for example an outgoing HTTP call to a payment API. In which Application Insights table does it appear?

options.text: requests
availabilityResults
pageViews
dependencies

questions.explanation: Spans that represent incoming work (SERVER and CONSUMER kinds) become requests, while outgoing or internal work (CLIENT, PRODUCER, and INTERNAL kinds) becomes dependencies. pageViews and availabilityResults come from browser telemetry and availability tests.
questions.source_title: Application Insights telemetry data model

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: A Java app gets its Application Insights connection string from a system property, an environment variable, and a configuration file, each with a different value. Which one wins?

options.text: The system property, then the environment variable, then the configuration file
The last one read alphabetically
The configuration file always wins
The environment variable always wins

questions.explanation: For Java, the documented precedence when the connection string is set in more than one place is: system property, then environment variable, then configuration file. Knowing the order prevents surprises when environments set it in different ways.
questions.source_title: Configure OpenTelemetry in Application Insights

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: You want an Azure Functions app (v4) to emit its host and worker telemetry using OpenTelemetry. Which host.json setting is shown in Microsoft's migration guidance?

options.text: "extensionBundle": "OpenTelemetry"
"logging": "none"
"telemetryMode": "OpenTelemetry"
"functionTimeout": "OpenTelemetry"

questions.explanation: Setting telemetryMode to OpenTelemetry in host.json switches the Functions host to emit OpenTelemetry-based telemetry, which you then export to Application Insights or another OTLP destination. functionTimeout controls execution time, and the other values aren't valid settings for this.
questions.source_title: Migrate apps from Azure Functions version 1.x to 4.x

questions.skill_name: Trace distributed systems with OpenTelemetry
questions.stem: In Application Insights, you open one failed request and want to see the full end-to-end chain of calls across services with timings. Which experience should you use?

options.text: Live metrics only
Transaction diagnostics (end-to-end transaction details)
Azure Advisor
The Activity log

questions.skill_name: Write KQL queries to analyze logs and metrics
questions.stem: You want the number of requests in 5-minute buckets over the last day from Application Insights. Which query is correct?

options.text: requests | where timestamp > ago(1d) | summarize count() by bin(timestamp, 5m)
requests | summarize count() by timestamp | where timestamp > 1d
requests | project bin(5m) | count()
requests | take 5m | count

questions.explanation: ago(1d) filters to the last day, and summarize count() by bin(timestamp, 5m) groups rows into 5-minute buckets. Grouping by the raw timestamp creates one group per distinct time, take returns a number of rows rather than a time window, and project doesn't aggregate.

questions.skill_name: Write KQL queries to analyze logs and metrics
questions.stem: A query ends with | render timechart | where count_ > 10 and fails. Why?

options.text: render must be the last operator in the query
where can't follow summarize
render only works on string columns
timechart requires a join

questions.explanation: The render operator tells the client how to visualize results, and it must be the last operator in the query, working on a single tabular result. Move the where clause before render. String columns, summarize ordering, and joins aren't the problem.

questions.skill_name: Write KQL queries to analyze logs and metrics
questions.stem: You need the 95th percentile request duration per hour. Which aggregation should you use?

options.text: summarize max(duration) by bin(timestamp, 1h)
summarize avg(duration) * 0.95 by bin(timestamp, 1h)
summarize count() by duration
summarize percentile(duration, 95) by bin(timestamp, 1h)

questions.explanation: percentile(column, 95) returns the value below which 95 percent of samples fall, grouped per hour with bin. max shows only the worst case, scaling an average doesn't produce a percentile, and counting by duration gives a distribution table rather than the 95th percentile.

questions.skill_name: Write KQL queries to analyze logs and metrics
questions.stem: Two tables are joined with StormEvents | join PopulationData on State and no kind is specified. Which join flavor is used?

options.text: fullouter
leftouter
innerunique, which removes duplicate keys from the left side before matching
inner

questions.explanation: The default join flavor in KQL is innerunique: duplicate key values on the left side are reduced to one row before matching, so results can differ from a SQL-style inner join. Specify kind=inner when every left row should be matched.

questions.skill_name: Write KQL queries to analyze logs and metrics
questions.stem: You want every request, along with its matching custom event if one exists, and requests without events must still appear. Which join kind should you use?

options.text: leftouter
innerunique
rightanti
inner

questions.explanation: leftouter returns all rows from the left table and only matching rows from the right, filling non-matches with empty values. Inner joins drop requests without matches, and rightanti returns only right-side rows that have no match.

questions.skill_name: Write KQL queries to analyze logs and metrics
questions.stem: What is the difference between project and extend in KQL?

options.text: extend removes columns and project adds them
project selects (and can rename or compute) only the listed columns, while extend adds new calculated columns and keeps all existing ones
project can only be used after summarize
They are identical

questions.explanation: project outputs exactly the columns you list, optionally renaming or computing them; extend keeps every existing column and appends new calculated ones. Both can be used anywhere in the pipeline.

questions.skill_name: Write KQL queries to analyze logs and metrics
questions.stem: You reuse the same time window in several parts of a query. How do you define it once?

options.text: With a let statement, for example let startTime = ago(14d); and then use startTime in the query
With a variable declared using var
By repeating ago(14d) everywhere; KQL has no variables
With the set operator

questions.explanation: let binds a name to a scalar or tabular expression for the rest of the query, as in Microsoft's telemetry samples that define the start date, end date, and group interval up front. KQL has no var keyword, and set is used for request properties rather than query variables.

questions.skill_name: Write KQL queries to analyze logs and metrics
questions.stem: You want the number of distinct users per day from customEvents. Which aggregation is correct?

options.text: summarize count() by user_Id
distinct user_Id | count by day
summarize sum(user_Id) by bin(timestamp, 1d)
summarize dcount(user_Id) by bin(timestamp, 1d)

questions.explanation: dcount returns an estimate of the number of distinct values, here unique users per day bucket. count() by user_Id gives events per user, sum makes no sense for IDs, and the last option isn't valid KQL.

questions.skill_name: Write KQL queries to analyze logs and metrics
questions.stem: In a workspace-based Application Insights resource queried from Log Analytics, which table holds the requests your app received?

options.text: ContainerLogV2
requests_v2
AzureActivity
AppRequests

questions.explanation: Application Insights telemetry types map to Log Analytics tables: requests become AppRequests, traces become AppTraces, dependencies become AppDependencies, and so on. ContainerLogV2 holds AKS container logs, and AzureActivity holds management operations.

questions.skill_name: Write KQL queries to analyze logs and metrics
questions.stem: You need the 10 operations with the most failed requests in the last 24 hours. Which query is correct?

options.text: requests | summarize count() by success | top 10
requests | where timestamp > ago(24h) and success == false | summarize failures = count() by name | top 10 by failures desc
requests | top 10 by success
requests | take 10 | where success == false

questions.explanation: Filter first to the time window and failed requests, then count per operation name and keep the top 10 by that count. take returns arbitrary rows before filtering, and grouping by success only produces two groups.

questions.skill_name: Write KQL queries to analyze logs and metrics
questions.stem: A chart of hourly request counts has gaps where no requests occurred, and you need zeros there for anomaly detection. Which operator should you use?

options.text: distinct
summarize count() by bin(timestamp, 1h)
project-away
make-series with default = 0

questions.explanation: make-series builds a time series over a fixed range and step and fills empty buckets with the default value you set, which series functions like series_decompose need. summarize only emits buckets that contain data, and the other operators don't create series.

questions.skill_name: Write KQL queries to analyze logs and metrics
questions.stem: You search a high-volume log table for a whole word. Which operator is generally faster: has or contains?

options.text: contains, because it uses the index
has, because it matches indexed terms, while contains matches any substring
Neither; you must use matches regex
They always perform the same

questions.explanation: has looks for a whole term and can use the term index, so it is usually much faster than contains, which scans for any substring. Use contains only when you truly need substring matches, and regular expressions are the slowest choice.
